docs.title: Session M2-03: Copilot Spaces & context management
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Copilot in Practice Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-02 Duration: 3 hours (1 hr trainer content + 2 hr lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Give Copilot the context a task needs. Use one Storefront API to select Space sources, add repository instructions, compare context levels, and store reusable prompts. Before implementation, inspect CLI /env and /instructions to find and correct a stale module-style instruction.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Create a Copilot Space and choose the smallest source set for a task
  • Write repository instructions and reusable prompt files
  • Tell instruction discovery apart from the model following an instruction
  • Compare the same task across context levels

docs.title: Session materials
docs.text: Resource Location Lab exercises lab/ Lab starter files lab/starter/ Lab solution files lab/solution/

docs.title: Key topics
docs.text:
• Copilot Spaces: selected context sources
  • .github/copilot-instructions.md: project-level instructions
  • .github/prompts/*.md: reusable prompt files
  • VS Code instruction settings
  • Before/after context comparison
  • Runtime instruction inspection in the standalone CLI

docs.title: Give each task the source files it needs
Context selection
docs.text:
Choose sources a reviewer can explain:

  • repository instructions;
  • relevant source files and tests;
  • architecture or API documents;
  • task notes.

docs.title: Context packet exercise
docs.text:
Task: add validation to an API endpoint

Packet:
- route file
- corresponding tests
- API contract
- repository conventions

Ask learners why each source is needed and what is excluded.

docs.title: Evaluate the result
docs.text:
• Does it follow the selected repository files?
  • Is the scope limited to the task?
  • Are assumptions listed for review?
  • Do relevant tests pass?

docs.title: Agenda and time plan
docs.text: Time Topic 0:00 Why context fails 0:08 Context layers 0:18 Spaces 0:30 Instructions and prompt files 0:42 Keeping context fresh 0:50 Before/after demo 0:58 Lab handoff

docs.title: The context problem
docs.text:
Copilot can't apply information it can't see. Extra context adds noise.

Common failures:

  • the relevant contract is absent;
  • stale documentation conflicts with source code;
  • broad context hides the key constraint;
  • local preferences are mistaken for team standards.

docs.title: A practical context hierarchy
docs.text:
Task intent and acceptance criteria
               ↓
Repository instructions and prompt workflow
               ↓
Curated Space: code, docs, issues, specifications
               ↓
Current file and explicit references
               ↓
Memory, when available

Specific task constraints override generic guidance. Clarify conflicts.

docs.title: Copilot Spaces
docs.text:
A Space is a selected set of sources for a recurring topic or workflow.

Good candidates:

  • source repositories and key paths;
  • architecture and API documentation;
  • issues and specifications;
  • team guidance for a domain.

docs.title: Curate for a purpose
docs.text:
Space: Storefront API
├── API specification
├── product route and model
├── architecture note
├── error-handling conventions
└── repository instructions

Exclude unrelated services, production data, secrets, abandoned proposals, and documents nobody keeps current.

Trainer cue: Ask learners what they would remove first if the answer became noisy.

docs.title: Sharing Spaces
docs.text:
Before sharing:

  1. Name the audience and task.
  2. Add purpose-specific instructions.
  3. Test with a known question and compare against the source files.
  4. Remove or replace stale sources.

docs.title: Repository-level instructions
docs.text:
Create .github/copilot-instructions.md for project-wide guidance:

# Repository guidance

- Use TypeScript strict mode.
- Validate request input at the route boundary.
- Keep business logic in `src/services/`.
- Run `npm test` before proposing completion.
- Do not add dependencies without reviewer approval.

Write rules a reviewer can check. Avoid vague goals such as "produce high-quality code."

docs.title: Reusable prompt files
docs.text:
Place team prompts under .github/prompts/:

---
description: Review an API change against its contract
---

Read the selected route, service, tests, and API contract.
List mismatches before suggesting changes.
Do not edit files outside the selected feature.
End with the focused validation command.

docs.title: Inspect what the CLI loaded
docs.text:
/env
/instructions

Find the copied stale CommonJS note and its route-file scope. Compare it with package.json and the current ES-module route.

Correct only that training note, restart, and inspect again. Leave personal, managed, and security instructions alone.

Discovery is not proof of application. Check the proposed code too.

docs.title: VS Code instruction settings
docs.text:
{
  "github.copilot.chat.codeGeneration.useInstructionFiles": true
}

Settings change between IDE versions. Check the setting in your learners' version.

docs.title: Copilot Memory
docs.text:
Memory can retain knowledge across sessions, where available. Ask three questions:

  1. Source: Where did this fact come from?
  2. Scope: Does it apply to this user, repository, or task?
  3. Freshness: How will it be corrected when the code changes?

Never store secrets.

docs.title: Demo: without grounded context
docs.text:
Prompt:

Add a low-stock report endpoint.

Discuss:

  • Which endpoint?
  • Which inputs and error schema?
  • Where is validation normally performed?
  • Which tests prove the behavior?

Don't score the response by confidence or length.

docs.title: Demo: with a context packet
docs.text:
Using the Storefront API specification, product route, product model, architecture
note, and repository instructions, propose the smallest low-stock endpoint change.

First list acceptance criteria and assumptions. Do not add dependencies.
End with two checks to run and cite the files used.

Compare assumptions, source references, and the checks each response proposes.

docs.title: Concrete code target
docs.text:
function parseThreshold(value) {
  if (value === undefined) return 10;
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(value)) {
    throw new Error("threshold must be a non-negative integer");
  }
  return Number(value);
}

Ask where the static report route must appear relative to /:id.

docs.title: Keep context fresh
docs.text: Trigger Action API contract changes Update Space sources and prompts Repository convention changes Review instruction files Output contradicts source Remove stale sources and retest

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
You will:

  1. keep one Storefront API for the full lab;
  2. select the smallest source set;
  3. add repository instructions and a low-stock endpoint;
  4. compare one logging task across context levels;
  5. store and test three reusable prompt files.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Relevant context beats a large packet.
  2. Select Space sources for a named purpose and audience.
  3. Instructions state project-wide rules. Prompt files define reusable tasks.
  4. Memory needs a source, a scope, and a way to correct it.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Which source would you remove from a context packet, and why?

  • Which source is authoritative?
  • What must stay out of the Space?

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-03 lab: Spaces and context management
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Deliverable: A context package for one Storefront API, with comparison results

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
Use one Storefront API for the whole lab. Select sources for a Copilot Space, add repository instructions, compare the same task across context levels, and store reusable prompt files beside the project.

Stage Work Time 1 Prepare the project and select Space sources 30 min 2 Add instructions and inspect what the CLI loaded 30 min 3 Compare one task across context levels 30 min 4 Build and test a prompt library 30 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Use only the synthetic Storefront API files supplied with this lab.

You need:

  • GitHub Copilot in your editor;
  • Copilot Spaces access;
  • Node.js and npm;
  • the standalone Copilot CLI with /env and /instructions.

Create a writable copy:

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-03
cp -R sessions/session-m2-03-spaces-and-context/lab/starter/ecommerce-project \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-03/storefront-api
cp sessions/session-m2-03-spaces-and-context/lab/starter/context-comparison.md \
  sessions/session-m2-03-spaces-and-context/lab/starter/stale-storefront.instructions.md \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-03/storefront-api/
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-03/storefront-api
npm install
npm start

Open http://localhost:3000/api/products. The response should contain the seeded products.

docs.title: Stage 1: Prepare the project and select Space sources (30 minutes)
Inspect the context before adding it
docs.text:
Read these files:

Source Decision it supports README.md Project purpose, setup, and endpoints docs/api-spec.md Required HTTP behavior docs/architecture.md Layers, response envelopes, and naming src/models/product.js Product fields and validation src/routes/products.js Current route patterns

Write context-notes.md:

# Storefront API Context Notes

## Task
Add a low-stock report endpoint.

## Required sources
## Excluded sources
## Conflicts or stale statements
## Acceptance criteria

Keep the source set small. Leave out unrelated repositories, private discussions, and production data.

docs.title: Create the Space
docs.text:
Create a Space named Storefront API Lab. Add the five files and these instructions:

Answer from the selected Storefront API sources. Follow docs/api-spec.md and
docs/architecture.md. Use the Product validation and response patterns already in
the project. State when a requested behavior is not defined by the sources.

Ask:

What files and acceptance criteria should guide a low-stock report endpoint?
Do not write code yet.

Check every claim against the sources.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
• context-notes.md names the task and acceptance criteria.
  • Every selected source has a reason to be present.
  • Each claim in the first answer is supported by a selected file.
  • The Space contains the selected sources.

docs.title: Stage 2: Add repository instructions (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Create .github/copilot-instructions.md in the Storefront API:

# Storefront API Instructions

- Use ES modules.
- Keep route handlers under `src/routes/`.
- Follow the `{ data: ... }` success envelope.
- Return errors as `{ error: { code, message, details? } }`.
- Use `Product.validate()` before product data changes.
- Add no dependency unless the task requires it and a reviewer approves it.
- Keep examples and tests on synthetic data.

docs.title: Inspect a stale instruction before implementation (10 minutes)
docs.text:
In this copied workspace only, create .github/instructions/ and copy stale-storefront.instructions.md into it as storefront-style.instructions.md. Read the file before starting the CLI. It deliberately conflicts with the current ES-module contract.

Start copilot from the Storefront project and run:

/env
/instructions

Inspect instruction source paths and any file-match scope. Leave personal, organization, and security instructions alone. In context-comparison.md, name the project instruction and the stale route note, then compare both with package.json and an existing route.

Ask Copilot to identify the conflict without editing. Correct only the stale training note to require ES modules. Restart the CLI and inspect /env and /instructions again. A listed file shows discovery. It doesn't show that the model followed the instruction.

Ask Copilot to plan the low-stock endpoint:

Plan a GET /api/products/reports/low-stock endpoint for this project. It should
accept an optional non-negative integer threshold and default to 10. Return only
products whose stock is at or below the threshold. Follow repository instructions.
Do not edit files.

Review the plan against the API spec, architecture, and model. Check the route order too: a static route must not be hidden behind /:id.

Then ask for the smallest implementation and a check:

Implement the accepted low-stock endpoint plan. Keep the current API behavior.
Run the smallest useful check and show the result.

Check manually:

curl "http://localhost:3000/api/products/reports/low-stock?threshold=80"
curl "http://localhost:3000/api/products/reports/low-stock?threshold=-1"

Compare your instruction file with lab/solution/ecommerce-project/.github/copilot-instructions.md.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
• The plan uses ES modules and existing response envelopes.
  • The route is placed before /:id.
  • Invalid thresholds produce a structured 400 response.
  • Existing product routes still work.
  • context-notes.md records one instruction Copilot followed and one item you still had to review.
  • CLI inspection identified the stale training source and its corrected text.

docs.title: Stage 3: Compare one task across context levels (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Open context-comparison.md. Use the same task in every experiment:

Add request-logging middleware to the Storefront API. Record timestamp, method,
URL, response time, and status code. Use info for 2xx, warn for 4xx, and error for
5xx. Add no logging package.

Run four experiments without changing the task:

  1. No project context: Ask from an empty window.
  2. Repository context: Open the Storefront API with copilot-instructions.md.
  3. Space: Ask in the live Space with the selected project sources.
  4. Prompt file: Use a structured repository prompt for the task.

Record:

  • import style;
  • file placement;
  • response and error conventions;
  • added assumptions;
  • number of corrections;
  • claims that cite or clearly follow a source.

Score each response against the project requirements, not how well it reads. Keep extra context only when it removes wrong assumptions.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
• All four experiments use the same task text.
  • Each score cites a concrete output difference.
  • The comparison identifies one useful source and one source that added no value.
  • The final choice states the smallest context set that supports the task.

docs.title: Stage 4: Build and test a prompt library (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Create these files in storefront-api/.github/prompts/:

  1. investigate-bug.prompt.md
  2. generate-api-docs.prompt.md
  3. migration-checklist.prompt.md

Each prompt needs front matter with a short description. Name the inputs it accepts, the sections it should return, and a check to run.

docs.title: Test the prompts on the same project
docs.text:
• Run investigate-bug against an invalid minPrice query scenario.
  • Run generate-api-docs against the low-stock endpoint.
  • Run migration-checklist for a proposed Express major-version update. Do not install it.

Review each result:

  • Did it stay inside the selected Storefront API sources?
  • Did it separate known facts from assumptions?
  • Did it name a check another engineer can run?
  • Did it avoid changing code when the prompt only requested analysis?

Compare with lab/solution/ecommerce-project/.github/prompts/.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
• All three prompt files appear in .github/prompts/.
  • Each prompt was tested on the Storefront API.
  • Each output includes a check to run.
  • The migration prompt stops before package changes.
  • Stale or duplicate instructions were removed.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
Submit the storefront-api/ workspace with:

  1. context-notes.md and the live Space's source list.
  2. .github/copilot-instructions.md.
  3. The completed context-comparison.md.
  4. Three tested prompt files under .github/prompts/.
  5. Low-stock endpoint check results and the final context choice.

docs.title: Command reference
docs.text: Copilot CLI environment and instruction commands.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-03: Context workflows
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Before teaching
docs.text: Copy the Storefront project and check that /env and /instructions work in the standalone CLI. Check that learners have Spaces and GitHub Copilot access.

docs.title: Session objective
docs.text: Teach learners to select the few files a task needs and check the answer against those files.

docs.title: Minute-mapped delivery plan (60 minutes)
docs.text: Time Segment Trainer outcome 0:00 to 0:08 Diagnose the context problem Learners tell missing information from excess noise. 0:08 to 0:18 Context hierarchy Learners rank task, instructions, curated sources, and local references. 0:18 to 0:30 Curated context workflows The group writes a purpose, audience, and source list. 0:30 to 0:42 Instructions and reusable prompts Learners separate project-wide rules from repeatable tasks. 0:42 to 0:50 Keeping context fresh Learners check source, scope, and freshness. 0:50 to 0:58 Scripted before/after demo The group compares two responses with the source files. 0:58 to 1:00 Close and lab handoff Learners start by selecting sources for their Space.

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
• Missing contracts make Copilot invent assumptions.
  • Broad, stale, or conflicting sources can hide the rule the task needs.
  • A confident answer does not show that the right source was used.
  • Select the fewest files a reviewer needs to check the answer.

docs.title: Opening exercise
docs.text:
Display this request:

Add validation to the checkout endpoint.

Ask learners what is missing.

Expected answers: endpoint location, input contract, error shape, repository conventions, focused tests.

Then ask what should stay out.

Expected answers: unrelated repositories, production records, secrets, ownerless stale documents.

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
1. Task intent and acceptance criteria define the outcome.
  2. Repository instructions give project-wide conventions.
  3. Reusable prompt files encode repeatable workflows.
  4. Spaces bring code, docs, issues, and specifications together.
  5. Current files and named references supply local context.
  6. Memory needs a source, a scope, and a way to correct it.
  7. Specific task requirements override generic guidance.
  8. Conflicts need clarification. More context does not resolve them.

docs.title: Source-ranking exercise
docs.text:
For a fictional quantity-validation change, rank:

  • current API contract;
  • focused route tests;
  • architecture note;
  • unrelated product roadmap;
  • production request log.

Include the contract, tests, and architecture note. Exclude the roadmap and the production log.

docs.title: Trainer-created context card
docs.text:
Purpose: answer questions about the fictional Checkout API validation behavior.
Audience: workshop participants.

Include:
- docs/api-contract.md
- src/routes/checkout.ts
- src/services/checkout.ts
- tests/checkout.test.ts
- .github/copilot-instructions.md

Exclude:
- production data
- secrets and credentials
- unrelated services
- abandoned proposals

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
• A Space holds this packet. Check sharing and access settings in the Space before you share it.
  • Test the packet with a known question whose answer exists in the sources.
  • Ask learners why each source is in and why the others are out.

docs.title: Segment 4: Instructions and reusable prompts (0:30 to 0:42)
Repository instruction example
docs.text:
# Repository guidance

- Validate request input at the route boundary.
- Keep business logic in src/services/.
- Preserve the documented error response shape.
- Run the focused test before proposing completion.
- Do not add dependencies without reviewer approval.

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
• Write instructions a reviewer can check, not "write high-quality code."
  • Show /env and /instructions in the CLI. They show which files were found and their scope. They don't show that the model followed them.
  • Use the stale CommonJS note in the copied project only. Compare it with the ES-module contract, correct the note, restart, and inspect again. Don't touch personal, managed, or security rules.
  • Keep project-wide conventions separate from one feature's requirements.

docs.title: Reusable prompt example
docs.text:
---
description: Review a low-stock endpoint change
---

Read the selected contract, route, service, tests, and repository guidance.
List mismatches before proposing changes.
Do not edit files outside the selected feature.
End with assumptions, cited evidence, and the focused validation command.

docs.title: Pair exercise
docs.text: Ask pairs to label each sentence as a project-wide instruction, a task-specific prompt, an acceptance criterion, or vague guidance. Move feature-specific behavior out of repository-wide rules.

docs.title: Segment 5: Keeping context fresh (0:42 to 0:50)
docs.text:
For every source or remembered fact, ask:

  1. Source: Where did this come from?
  2. Scope: Which repository, audience, and task does it apply to?
  3. Freshness: After which change should you check it again?
Trigger Action API contract changes Update packet sources and retest a known question. Repository convention changes Review instruction and prompt files. Output conflicts with source files Remove the stale source and decide which source governs.

Memory is a preview feature in some plans. Check that it's available before you demo it, and never store secrets in it.

docs.title: Scripted demo: Low-stock reporting with and without grounding (0:50 to 0:58)
docs.text: Compare the two responses against clear criteria. Don't claim a product surface always cites or follows context.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use four excerpts from the Storefront API lab:

docs/api-spec.md:

Product list responses use the existing data envelope.
Invalid query values use the existing VALIDATION_ERROR response.

src/routes/products.js:

router.get('/:id', async (req, res) => {
  // Existing dynamic route.
});

src/models/product.js defines product stock as a non-negative integer.

The lab task requires GET /api/products/reports/low-stock, an optional non-negative integer threshold, and a default threshold of 10.

docs.title: Pass A: Minimal prompt
docs.text:
Add a low-stock report endpoint.

Submit it without project context, or reveal a prepared generic proposal. Record assumptions about the route, threshold, error shape, and test command.

Look for a route placed after /:id, invalid thresholds accepted, invented errors, or missing checks. The request lacks the files needed to judge the proposal.

docs.title: Pass B: Grounded prompt
docs.text:
Using only the API specification, product route, product model, and
repository instructions, propose the smallest low-stock endpoint change.
First list acceptance criteria and assumptions.
Do not add dependencies. Reject negative or non-integer thresholds.
End with the source files used and two checks to run.

Require acceptance criteria before code. Compare the plan with the API specification and route order. Ask whether Number.isInteger(Number(value)) would wrongly accept "2".

The grounded response should state the threshold rules, place the static route before /:id, avoid new dependencies, name its source files, and list two checks.

It may include a code proposal such as:

function parseThreshold(value) {
  if (value === undefined) return 10;
  if (!/^\d+$/.test(value)) {
    throw new Error('threshold must be a non-negative integer');
  }
  return Number(value);
}

Check the existing project before choosing the error type and message.

docs.title: Group variant
docs.text:
Give half the room only the minimal request and the other half the four-source packet and grounded prompt. Each group writes a plan, not code. Swap plans and compare them on correctness, scope, named assumptions, traceability to a source file, and test cases. Reveal the code proposal in the debrief.

If the surface is unavailable, use printed responses. If time runs out, compare acceptance criteria and skip code generation.

docs.title: "Should we add the whole repository?"
docs.text: No. Start with the fewest files that support the task. Add a file only when the answer is missing specific information.

docs.title: "Do instructions guarantee compliance?"
docs.text: No. Use tests, repository checks, and review to see whether the result follows them.

docs.title: "Which source wins when docs and code disagree?"
docs.text: Ask the source owner to clarify before implementation.

docs.title: "Can we store team conventions in memory?"
docs.text: Keep long-lived team rules in reviewed repository files.

docs.title: "Why did the grounded response still miss a rule?"
docs.text: Context gives Copilot more information. It doesn't guarantee correct use. State the rule, test it, and review the result.

docs.title: Closing and lab handoff (0:58 to 1:00)
docs.text: Keep only the sources the task needs. Open lab/README.md. Learners use the same Storefront API to select sources, add repository instructions, compare context, and test reusable prompts.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-04: Copilot for code review & pull requests
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Copilot in Practice Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-03 Duration: 3 hours (1 hr trainer content + 2 hr lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Follow one pull request from change brief to final human decision. Inspect a flawed change, run /review and /security-review on its local diff, and compare those findings with Copilot PR review. Then correct the code and resolve a conflict. Keep the diff, test output, and reviewer decision.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Generate PR summaries and review comments with Copilot
  • Configure automatic Copilot reviews for a repository or organization
  • Judge Copilot review quality and blind spots
  • Run general and security review on a local patch before committing
  • Triage unsupported claims and check fixes with regression tests
  • Resolve a merge conflict manually and keep both branches' intended behavior

docs.title: Session materials
docs.text: Resource Location Lab exercises lab/ Lab starter files lab/starter/ Lab solution files lab/solution/

docs.title: Key topics
docs.text:
• PR summaries and commit message generation
  • Copilot code review, manual and automatic
  • Local /review and /security-review, then review of the correction diff
  • Review comments with one-click fixes
  • Manual merge conflict resolution and tests
  • Quality gates and team adoption

docs.title: Diffs, test results, and human judgment
Review is a human responsibility
docs.text:
Automation raises questions. A reviewer decides whether a change is correct, safe, maintainable, and in scope.

Issue and acceptance criteria
        ↓
Proposed change and checks
        ↓
Human review
        ↓
Accept, request revision, or implement manually

docs.title: Review rubric
docs.text:
• Correctness against acceptance criteria
  • Tests and check results
  • Security, dependency, and permission implications
  • Scope and maintainability
  • Repository conventions and human approval

docs.title: Conflict-resolution exercise
docs.text:
1. Read both branch intentions.
  2. Write the merged behavior and tests before editing.
  3. Resolve the conflict manually in the sandbox.
  4. Run checks and request review.

docs.title: Review the same diff through separate passes
docs.text:
1. Record the human verdict before assisted review.
  2. Leave the patch uncommitted and run /review.
  3. Run /security-review against that same local patch.
  4. Triage both outputs, then commit and request Copilot PR review.
  5. Repeat the local commands on the correction diff before committing fixes.

Keep the original verdict. Record no-findings results.

docs.title: A finding needs support
docs.text:
Claim Check Exposed password field Inspect the actual response and add a regression test Database compromise The mock route never executes SQL; reject that claim Leaked credential The strings are fake and unused; reject a live-leak claim Pagination defect Check page-one behavior separately from security review

Record: review source, file/line, impact, check, and triage decision.

docs.title: Security review has a narrow scope
docs.text:
/security-review examines current local changes. It's read-only and doesn't replace repository security scanning.

A clean result doesn't make a change secure. The human reviewer decides.

docs.title: Agenda and time plan
docs.text: Time Topic 0:00 Review workflow and roles 0:08 Summaries and descriptions 0:18 Local commands and PR review 0:28 Defect and triage demo 0:43 Suggestions and conflicts 0:51 Limits and adoption 0:58 Lab handoff and Q&A

docs.title: Copilot across a PR lifecycle
docs.text:
Issue and acceptance criteria
          ↓
Branch and bounded commits
          ↓
Draft summary and PR description
          ↓
Automated checks + Copilot first pass
          ↓
Human review and author response
          ↓
Approval, revision, or close

docs.title: Commit messages and PR descriptions
docs.text:
Copilot drafts text from the visible change. Authors check that:

  • the user-visible behavior is accurate;
  • tests and results aren't invented;
  • breaking changes and migrations are named;
  • security and dependency implications are named;
  • issue links and acceptance criteria match the work.

A polished summary can still be wrong.

docs.title: A reviewable PR template
docs.text:
## Problem
What user-visible problem does this solve?

## Change
List the bounded implementation choices.

## Validation
- [ ] Focused tests
- [ ] Existing checks
- [ ] Manual edge case

## Risk and rollback
Name data, dependency, security, and recovery considerations.

docs.title: Requesting Copilot review
docs.text:
1. Check that the PR is ready for a first pass.
  2. Request the Copilot review from the PR.
  3. Treat the comments as hypotheses.
  4. Resolve them, reject them with a reason, or implement a checked fix.
  5. Request human review with the diff, findings, and check results.

Copilot review doesn't replace required reviewers.

docs.title: Automatic review configuration
docs.text:
You can configure automatic review at repository or organization scope.

Before enabling:

  • choose eligible repositories;
  • decide who triages comments;
  • keep branch protection and required human approvals;
  • watch noise, missed findings, and review delay;
  • know how to turn it off.

docs.title: Quality gates
docs.text:
Gate Checks Ready for first pass Clear description, focused diff, tests available Ready for human review Checks pass; AI comments triaged Ready for approval Acceptance criteria met; risks reviewed Ready for merge Required approvals and branch protections satisfied

Copilot review comes before human approval. It never replaces it.

docs.title: Demo PR: intentional defect
docs.text:
export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}

The requirement says suspended users must never view invoices.

if (user.status === "suspended") return false;
return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;

Ask which tests should accompany this suggestion.

docs.title: Demo narrative: complete lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Open the issue and read acceptance criteria aloud.
  2. Inspect the focused branch diff before generated prose.
  3. Generate or improve the PR description; correct unsupported claims.
  4. Run required checks and request Copilot review.
  5. Classify each comment: valid, uncertain, noise, or out of scope.
  6. Apply one checked fix and add a regression test.
  7. Request human review and record the final decision.

docs.title: Reviewing suggested fixes
docs.text:
Before applying:

  • restate the finding in your own words;
  • reproduce the defect or find the violated requirement;
  • inspect the complete patch, not only highlighted lines;
  • add a test that fails before the fix;
  • run broader checks in proportion to the risk.

One-click application saves typing. The reviewer still decides.

docs.title: What review may catch
docs.text:
• localized correctness issues;
  • missing error handling or tests;
  • suspicious patterns visible in the diff;
  • inconsistent naming or repository conventions.

docs.title: What it may miss
docs.text:
• unstated product intent;
  • cross-system behavior absent from context;
  • runtime, operational, or legal risk;
  • subtle authorization and data-boundary flaws;
  • plausible but misleading changes.

docs.title: Merge conflict resolution
docs.text:
Base behavior + branch A intent + branch B intent
                        ↓
              write merged acceptance criteria
                        ↓
                resolve conflict in sandbox
                        ↓
                 run tests and human review

Don't blindly choose "ours" or "theirs."

docs.title: Adoption patterns
docs.text:
Start: Optional first-pass review on a few repositories.

Measure: Actionable findings, false positives, review time, rework, and defects that reach users.

Adapt: Tune scope, guidance, and escalation.

Expand: Only when quality and developer experience hold up.

Know how to pause reviews for a repository that needs an exception.

docs.title: Facilitation prompts
docs.text:
• Which comment needs domain expertise to evaluate?
  • Which code reference or test would resolve an uncertain comment?
  • Which repositories should not use automatic review?
  • How will the team detect over-reliance?

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
You will:

  1. follow one pull request from a flawed change brief;
  2. classify human and Copilot findings;
  3. apply only fixes supported by code references or test results;
  4. resolve the prepared conflict without losing either branch goal;
  5. record the final human decision.

Deliverable: Review notes, the corrected project, conflict results, the initial and correction outputs from /review and /security-review, and the private training PR reference.

docs.title: Remember
docs.text:
1. Check generated summaries against the diff.
  2. AI review is a first pass. A human decides.
  3. Suggested fixes need reproduction, inspection, and tests.
  4. Conflict resolution starts from the intended merged behavior.
  5. Measure adoption and keep it reversible.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Which review decision needs a human, and what should they check?

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-04 lab: Code review workflows
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Deliverable: A reviewed change record, corrected starter project, and conflict review

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
Review a deliberately flawed change. Support each comment with a code reference or test result, apply targeted fixes, and decide whether to accept the change. Compare your own review with Copilot-assisted review. Use only synthetic data.

Exercise Topic Time 1 Human, code, and security review of one diff 40 min 2 Validate and correct the starter project 35 min 3 Resolve a conflict and check the result 25 min 4 Review the results and make a final decision 20 min

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• the standalone Copilot CLI with /review and /security-review (check /help);
  • Copilot pull-request review;
  • a private training repository you may push to (the trainer provides an empty one);
  • Git, the authenticated GitHub CLI (gh auth status), Node.js, and npm.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Starter assets:

  • lab/starter/review-project/: Express API under review, with src/api.js, src/utils.js, and Jest/Supertest tests in tests/api.test.js
  • lab/starter/code-changes.md: intentionally flawed changes to review
  • lab/starter/partner-review-checklist.md: structured review worksheet
  • lab/starter/fix-evaluation-template.md: finding, fix, and test record
  • lab/starter/conflict-scenario/: manual merge-conflict scenario (README.md, utils-with-conflict.js)

Create a workspace outside the curriculum folder:

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-04
cp -R lab/starter/review-project ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-04/review-project
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-04/review-project
npm install
npm test
git init
printf 'node_modules/\n' > .gitignore
git add .gitignore package.json package-lock.json src tests
git commit -m "Record review baseline"
git branch -M main
git switch -c feature/add-user-management

Expected: npm install adds no new dependencies and npm test reports that the existing API tests pass.

If install or tests fail: Fix the environment. Don't change package versions to hide a failure.

Add the trainer's private repository as origin and push the baseline:

git remote add origin <private-training-repository-url>
git push -u origin main

The baseline must be the same commit locally and remotely, so the PR contains only the intended change. If the remote already has commits, ask for an empty repository. Never force-push or push the intentional defects to a public repository.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Review one diff through three passes (40 minutes)
Steps
docs.text:
1. Read the change brief. Open lab/starter/code-changes.md. It lists changes to src/api.js and src/utils.js, each with an intended defect.

  2. Open lab/starter/fix-evaluation-template.md. Use its single triage table for human, local-command, and PR findings throughout the lab. Each finding names a file or function, the affected acceptance criterion, and the code or test output that supports it.

  3. Read the baseline. Open src/api.js, src/utils.js, and tests/api.test.js. Note the existing behavior so you can separate it from introduced defects.

  4. Apply the change brief on feature/add-user-management. Keep the changes uncommitted until both local reviews finish. Compare git diff -- src/api.js src/utils.js with the brief. Add no unrelated features.

  5. Run the existing checks.

npm test

Some tests may still pass because the defects aren't fully covered. Note the output and any missing coverage.

  1. Review the change yourself first. Record your initial verdict in lab/starter/partner-review-checklist.md. Record the two findings that matter most in the triage table with Human as the source, before you open an assisted review. Cite the file or function and the code or test output.

  2. Run the general code review. Start copilot in the working repository:

/review Review the current changes to src/api.js and src/utils.js for
correctness and missing tests. Cite file and line references. Review only;
do not edit files.
  1. Run the security review on the same diff:
/security-review

Both commands review staged and unstaged changes. Committing the patch first removes it from that scope.

  1. Triage both outputs in fix-evaluation-template.md. Leave your human review unchanged. For each finding, record the source, file/line, claimed impact, and reproduction or code reference. Accept, reject, or leave it unresolved with a reason. If a review reports no findings, record that.

The search route builds SQL text but connects to no database, so reject a claim that the lab proves database compromise. Synthetic key-shaped strings aren't a leaked real credential. Keep actual data exposure separate from unsafe patterns and maintainability suggestions.

  1. Open the training PR. Commit only the intended files, push to the private remote, and open a PR:

    git add src/api.js src/utils.js
git commit -m "Add synthetic user-management change for review"
git push -u origin feature/add-user-management
gh pr create --base main --title "Review synthetic user management" \
  --body "Training-only change. Contains intentional defects; do not merge."

    Request Copilot review from the PR page and record at least one comparison with the local results. Don't merge the flawed change.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
• Which findings block approval, and which are suggestions only?
  • Which defects did the existing tests miss?
  • What did /review and /security-review each report?
  • What changed after the assisted review?
  • Which claim rests on actual behavior rather than an assumed backend?

docs.title: Exercise 2: Validate and correct the starter project (35 minutes)
docs.text: Fix the defects with the smallest safe changes, then show the corrected project meets the review criteria.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Prioritize blocking findings. Start with issues that leak sensitive data, allow injection, crash the server, or return incorrect behavior. List each defect, its file, and the check you will run.

  2. Fix input handling in src/api.js. Replace unsafe string interpolation and fragile parsing with validated inputs and safe response shapes. The endpoint should handle empty, missing, malformed, and valid inputs predictably. Show the error responses in tests or manual requests.

  3. Fix sensitive response data. Remove password-like or token-like fields from responses. The JSON should show only fields the API contract needs.

  4. Fix pagination in src/utils.js. Page 1 starts with the first item, and boundary cases return predictable results. A focused test or Node.js check covers page 1, page 2, and empty collections.

  5. Add or update focused tests in tests/api.test.js for the behavior the original suite missed. New tests fail before the fix and pass after it.

  6. Run checks again.

npm test

All tests should pass. If one fails, record the failing assertion and correct only the related implementation or test expectation.

  1. Update the triage rows in fix-evaluation-template.md. Add the fix and regression test to each accepted finding. Record residual risk in its Human decision section.

  2. Review the correction diff before committing. Rerun /review and /security-review on it and compare with the initial findings. Rerun npm test, then commit and push only the reviewed fixes to the same PR. A clean automated review doesn't approve the PR.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
• Every blocking finding maps to a focused fix.
  • New tests cover the missed behavior.
  • npm test passes.
  • The fix evaluation names residual risk.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Resolve a conflict (25 minutes)
docs.text: Resolve a merge conflict so both branches' intended behavior survives.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Read the scenario. Open lab/starter/conflict-scenario/README.md. Two branches modify src/utils.js: one adds date formatting, the other changes price formatting.

  2. Open the conflicting source, lab/starter/conflict-scenario/utils-with-conflict.js. Find the conflicting region and state what each side does.

  3. Write the merged behavior before editing:

Preserve formatDate for date display and preserve formatPrice with an explicit
currency parameter. Existing callers should continue to work or be updated
intentionally.

  1. Resolve the conflict manually. Remove the <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>> markers, keep both valid behaviors, and avoid unrelated formatting changes.

  2. Add focused tests for date formatting, default currency, supplied currency, and unchanged helpers.

  3. Run the project test command and save the output.

  4. Peer review the resolution. Ask a partner to review only the resolution and tests. They should be able to say why both branch goals appear in the result.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
• No conflict markers remain.
  • Both branch goals appear in the resolved behavior.
  • Tests cover date and currency formatting.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Review the code and test results (20 minutes)
docs.text: Use the code and test results to make your final decision. An automated suggestion alone isn't enough.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Select one blocking finding from Exercise 1 (security, correctness, or reliability). It needs a file reference, impact, and acceptance criterion.

  2. Check its triage row. Add any missing before/after behavior, test names, or command output. A reviewer should reproduce the result from your notes.

  3. Classify remaining risk:

Risk type Question Data Did the change expose or process restricted data? Dependency Did the change add or update packages? Permission Did the workflow need a new permission? Security Did validation, error handling, or secrets handling change? Quality Do the tests and review results support the decision?

  1. Complete Human decision in fix-evaluation-template.md. Choose approve, request changes, or pause, and explain why. Someone reading it should understand the decision without seeing your lab conversation.

  2. Compare your initial review with both local outputs and the PR review. Complete the remaining template fields. Keep the original critique, record which source raised each finding, and say why you accepted, revised, or rejected it. The table should show differences, false positives, new code references or test results, and any finding that changed the verdict.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text:
• The decision is approve, request changes, or pause.
  • The rationale cites findings, fixes, and check results.
  • You accepted automated findings only after reviewing them.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
One folder or document containing:

  1. partner-review-checklist.md with the unchanged initial verdict.
  2. fix-evaluation-template.md with the review runs, finding triage, fixes, test results, remaining risk, and final decision.
  3. Initial and correction outputs from /review and /security-review, the private training PR reference, and test output for the corrected project.
  4. The resolved conflict decision and its test results.

Don't merge the training PR.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-04: Code review workflows
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Before teaching
docs.text: Prepare a small synthetic pull request, a reviewer, and a test command. Check that CLI /review and /security-review, Copilot PR review, and a private training remote with the baseline main branch work before the lab.

docs.title: Session objective
docs.text: Show learners how to use automated findings in a review. Learners check the diff, tests, and comments before they decide.

docs.title: Minute-mapped delivery plan (60 minutes)
docs.text:
Time Segment Result 0:00 to 0:08 Review roles Author, automation, checks, and reviewer roles are named. 0:08 to 0:18 PR summaries and review contracts Learners compare generated prose with the diff. 0:18 to 0:28 Local commands and PR review The group tells diff review from PR review. 0:28 to 0:43 Intentional-defect and triage demo Findings connect to behavior. Unsupported exploit claims are rejected. 0:43 to 0:51 Suggested fixes and conflicts Learners preserve intent before editing. 0:51 to 0:58 Limits, adoption, and Q&A Learners decide where people must review. 0:58 to 1:00 Close and lab handoff Reviewer roles are assigned.

The lab allocates 40/35/25/20 minutes to its four exercises.

docs.title: Segment 1: Review is an accountable decision (0:00 to 0:08)
Talking points
docs.text:
1. The author explains intent and supplies the diff and test output.
  2. Automated checks report results.
  3. Assisted review suggests issues to investigate.
  4. A human reviewer weighs intent, results, and risk.
  5. Branch rules and required approvals still apply.
  6. A generated summary, comment, or fix is never proof by itself.

Ask: "Who can explain why this change should merge?" The answer is the author and reviewer, backed by the diff and test output.

docs.title: Segment 2: Review contract and PR description (0:08 to 0:18)
docs.text:
Display:

## Problem
Suspended users must not view invoices.

## Change
Add an explicit suspended-status denial before role and ownership checks.

## Validation
- [ ] suspended administrator is denied
- [ ] suspended owner is denied
- [ ] active administrator is allowed
- [ ] active owner is allowed

## Risk and rollback
Authorization behavior changes only for suspended users; revert the bounded commit if needed.

docs.title: Talking points
docs.text:
• Compare every generated statement with the diff.
  • Don't claim a test ran unless command output exists.
  • Name breaking behavior, dependencies, permissions, and data implications.
  • Keep the PR small enough to reconstruct intent.

docs.title: Mini-exercise
docs.text:
Read: "Improves invoice security and all tests pass."

Ask learners to find the unsupported claims. "Improves" needs defined behavior. "All tests pass" needs named command output.

docs.title: Segment 3: Review request and quality gates (0:18 to 0:28)
docs.text:
Open the small synthetic diff. Prepare the human-only review worksheet before opening assisted review.

Gate Result Ready for independent critique Clear intent, a small diff, and focused checks. Ready for assisted review The learner has written an initial verdict and the findings that matter most. Ready for human review Local and PR findings are classified and checks reported. Ready for approval A human reviewer has checked acceptance criteria and risks. Ready for merge Required approvals and repository protections are satisfied.

Before the assisted prompt, have learners write their initial verdict in lab/starter/partner-review-checklist.md and their two important findings in lab/starter/fix-evaluation-template.md, with Human as the source. Afterward, they compare missed findings, false positives, and anything that changed the final decision.

docs.title: Demonstrate the two local commands
docs.text:
Use a fresh Git repository with a committed baseline. Apply the synthetic changes from code-changes.md and leave them uncommitted.

/review Review the current changes for correctness and missing tests. Cite files
and lines. Review only; do not edit.

Then run:

/security-review

Both commands must see the same staged or unstaged patch. Committing it first removes it from the security command's scope. Keep the output even if there are no findings. Check git diff afterward; review should not change the project.

Use the triage table in fix-evaluation-template.md. Each accepted finding needs a source, a claimed impact, and a reproduction or code reference. The mock search route doesn't execute SQL, and the training strings aren't live credentials, so don't teach them as proven exploits. Show the password exposure defect separately by inspecting the response.

After the local review, commit and push only the training patch, request Copilot PR review, and compare results. Repeat both local commands on the uncommitted correction diff before you commit fixes.

docs.title: Scripted demo: Suspended invoice viewer (0:28 to 0:43)
docs.text: Use synthetic code with a local authorization defect to show the review steps.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Use a disposable JavaScript file:

export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}

Requirement:

Suspended users must never view invoices.
Active administrators and active invoice owners may view an invoice.
Other users may not view it.

Prepare four cases: suspended administrator, suspended owner, active administrator, and unrelated active user.

docs.title: Assisted-review prompt
docs.text:
Review only canViewInvoice against the stated requirement.
Return one file-specific finding with observed behavior, impact, and a test idea.
Do not propose unrelated refactoring.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Read the requirement before the implementation.
  2. Ask learners to predict each case.
  3. Run a prepared test or trace the cases manually.
  4. Request the assisted review of this function only.
  5. Classify the response as valid, uncertain, noise, or out of scope.
  6. Restate the valid finding:
Observed: suspended administrators and owners currently return true.
Required: suspended users must always return false.
Decision: request changes and add regression coverage.
  1. Add or display a failing suspended-administrator test.
  2. Apply the smallest proposed fix:
export function canViewInvoice(user, invoice) {
  if (user.status === "suspended") return false;
  return user.role === "admin" || user.id === invoice.ownerId;
}
  1. Run all four focused cases and inspect the complete diff.
  2. Ask the human reviewer to choose approve, request changes, or pause.

docs.title: Expected outcome
docs.text:
• The suspended cases fail before the fix and return false after it.
  • Active administrator behavior stays true. An unrelated active user stays denied.
  • The diff contains one guard plus focused test changes.
  • The final decision cites the requirement and test results.

docs.title: Questions to ask
docs.text:
• Does the guard run before role and ownership checks?
  • Did any unrelated behavior change?
  • Does the review comment separate observation from assumption?

docs.title: Fallback worksheet
docs.text:
If the assisted review is unavailable or misses the defect, learners complete this table, write a review comment, a minimal patch, and test names. A peer makes the final decision.

User state Role/ownership Before Required Decision Suspended Admin true false Block Suspended Owner true false Block Active Admin true true Preserve Active Neither false false Preserve

If the assisted review invents broader policy, mark the comment uncertain or out of scope. If a suggested fix rewrites unrelated code, reject it and use the guard only.

docs.title: Segment 5: Suggested fixes and conflict intent (0:43 to 0:51)
Before applying a suggested fix
docs.text:
1. Restate the finding yourself.
  2. Reproduce the defect or find the violated criterion.
  3. Inspect the entire patch.
  4. Add a test that fails before the fix when practical.
  5. Run broader checks in proportion to risk.

docs.title: Conflict micro-exercise
docs.text:
Present:

Branch A adds formatDate.
Branch B adds an explicit currency parameter to formatPrice.

Before editing, learners write:

Preserve date formatting and price formatting with explicit currency.
Keep existing callers working or update them intentionally.

Ask for four checks: no conflict markers, a date example, a default currency example, and an explicit currency example.

Learners resolve the lab conflict manually, run tests, and review the result.

docs.title: Segment 6: Limits and adoption (0:51 to 0:58)
docs.text:
Assisted review may find local correctness issues, missing tests, error-handling problems, or convention mismatches.

It may miss unstated product intent, cross-system behavior, subtle authorization issues, operational risk, or plausible but misleading changes.

To adopt it, start with a small set of repositories. Track actionable findings, noise, rework, delays, and escaped defects. Decide who triages and how to pause automatic review.

docs.title: "Can Copilot approve a PR?"
docs.text: No. Required reviewers and branch rules still apply.

docs.title: "Should we apply every suggested fix?"
docs.text: No. Reproduce the issue, inspect the complete patch, add a focused test, and accept only the smallest correct change.

docs.title: "What if human and assisted reviews disagree?"
docs.text: Return to the requirements, diff, and test output. Ask a domain owner if that doesn't settle it.

docs.title: "Can automatic review replace branch protection?"
docs.text: No. Keep required human review.

docs.title: "Why review a generated PR description?"
docs.text: It can invent results, omit risk, or misread intent. Compare every claim with the diff and command output.

docs.title: "Is security review covered by this feature?"
docs.text: /review checks general code issues. /security-review targets high-confidence vulnerabilities in current changes. It's a focused, read-only check. It doesn't replace code scanning, secret scanning, or dependency checks. It's a preview feature, so check access before teaching.

docs.title: "Which repositories should enable automatic review?"
docs.text: Start with a few low-risk repositories. Define exclusions, owners, and a way to turn it off.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Reviewing the summary before the diff Read intent, diff, and checks first. Applying a patch from the highlighted lines only Inspect the entire proposed patch. Approving because checks pass Review coverage, intent, risk, and scope. Choosing "ours" in a conflict without thought Write the merged behavior before editing. Claiming tests passed without output Name and rerun the command.

docs.title: Closing and lab handoff (0:58 to 1:00)
docs.text:
Use automation as a first pass. Check its findings against the intended behavior, diff, and test output. The reviewer decides.

Open lab/README.md and assign author and reviewer roles. Learners use code-changes.md, partner-review-checklist.md, fix-evaluation-template.md, the local review project, and the conflict scenario. The demo worksheet doesn't replace the learner pull-request workflow.

Make sure the private remote has the baseline branch before learners open a PR, and that no learner commits the initial patch before the local reviews.

docs.title: Session M2-05: GitHub Copilot App for developers
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Module 2: Copilot in Practice

Difficulty: Intermediate

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04

Duration: 180 minutes (1 hour trainer content, 2 hour lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Use the GitHub Copilot app for engineering work. Separate exploratory chats from project sessions and choose Interactive, Plan, or Autopilot based on risk. Keep concurrent work in isolated working trees.

Follow one synthetic change through a local inner loop and a GitHub-facing outer loop. Attach files and test output, hand work between sessions, and request an independent critique. Then inspect an issue and pull-request snapshot and define a manual read-only automation that reports PR readiness without changing GitHub.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Choose between a chat and a project session, and between Interactive, Plan, and Autopilot.
  • Start isolated work and check the working-tree boundary.
  • Hand a task to a fresh session through a written handoff.
  • Challenge /plan with /rubber-duck, compare a /spar fork, and run /review on the uncommitted repair.
  • Connect issue intent, pull-request changes, review threads, and checks.
  • Define and run a manual read-only PR-readiness automation.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
GitHub Copilot app access. Each learner must be able to open the app, sign in, connect the local Git training project, and start a working-tree session. Check that /plan, /review, /rubber-duck, /fork, /merge-to-parent, and /spar appear in the command picker. Keep the local sandbox and approval settings as they are.

After this session, use the Session M7-05 developer route to practise supervising independent child sessions. Sessions M7-01 to M7-04 are not prerequisites for that route.

docs.title: Session structure
docs.text: Block Duration Content Trainer content 60 min Slides and trainer guide Lab 120 min App workflow lab

docs.title: Materials
docs.text:
Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab guide lab/README.md Starter project and sample results lab/starter/ Reference solution lab/solution/ Shared glossary ../glossary.md

All issue text, code, pull-request metadata, checks, and review comments are synthetic. Don't replace them with customer data, private repository URLs, secrets, or production logs.

docs.title: Product references
docs.text:
The app is evolving. Recheck command names and preview labels before you teach.

  • About the GitHub Copilot app
  • Get started with the GitHub Copilot app
  • Work with agent sessions
  • Manage issues and pull requests
  • Use automations in the app
  • GitHub Copilot app slash commands

docs.title: GitHub Copilot App for developers
docs.text:
Isolate work, check results, and hand off the next step

Session M2-05 | Module 2 | Intermediate

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time App mental model and engineering surfaces 10 min Chats, sessions, modes, and isolation 15 min Tests, diffs, and handoffs 12 min Issue-to-PR outer loop and critique 13 min Prepared demo and lab handoff 10 min

docs.title: The app has two different work surfaces
docs.text:
Surface Good use Boundary Chat Questions, comparison, early exploration No dedicated branch or working tree Project session Code changes, commands, tests, PR work Runs in a selected project workspace

Decision: Start in chat to understand the task. Start a project session when you need file changes or results tied to a branch.

docs.title: A useful prompt names the files and checks
docs.text:
Weak:

Fix the readiness tool.

Better:

Read issue-brief.md and the failing tests. Explain the current behavior, propose
the smallest change, then run the focused test command. Do not edit unrelated files.

The second prompt names the scope and the checks the agent must return.

docs.title: Choose autonomy from the cost of a wrong move
docs.text:
Mode Use it when Human checkpoint Interactive Scope is unclear or decisions need discussion Frequent steering Plan The task spans files or has review risk Approve the plan before edits Autopilot Scope and checks are clear, and rollback is cheap Review the diff and check results

Mode is a risk control. It is not a ranking of model quality.

docs.title: Isolation has two layers
docs.text:
Project
├── local repository session
├── working-tree session A
└── working-tree session B

A working tree separates branches and files for concurrent sessions.

Local sandboxing restricts filesystem, network, and credential access. A working tree doesn't.

docs.title: Check the workspace before work starts
docs.text:
Ask the session to report:

pwd
git status --short --branch
git worktree list

Then check:

  • the expected project path;
  • the session branch;
  • no unrelated changes;
  • the allowed test command.

If the boundary is wrong, stop before editing.

docs.title: Attach context for the next decision
docs.text:
Use @ references or /attach-files for:

  • the issue brief;
  • the failing test or error output;
  • the implementation file;
  • the session handoff.

Do not attach the whole repository by habit. Unrelated context can obscure the files the task needs.

docs.title: Make the handoff usable in a fresh session
docs.text:
Write a short handoff that includes:

Goal
Accepted scope
Files changed
Checks run and exact result
Open risks
Next decision

Start a fresh session and attach the handoff plus the relevant files. If the new session cannot continue, the handoff is incomplete.

docs.title: Check behavior before editing
docs.text:
Observe failing behavior
  → form a bounded plan
  → change the smallest surface
  → run focused checks
  → inspect the diff

Check the result with a command, diff, test, or reproducible manual check.

docs.title: Check only what supports the decision
docs.text:
Claim Check Result Failed checks block readiness focused unit test pass Unresolved blocking review blocks readiness snapshot fixture + test pass Neutral checks do not hide failures full test output pass

Each claim should point to something another engineer can inspect.

docs.title: Critique the plan before implementation
docs.text:
Use the required command while the plan can still change:

/rubber-duck Critique the plan and tests against issue-brief.md. Look for a false
READY verdict or missing reason-code checks. Do not edit files.

Check each suggestion. Revise the plan or explain why the suggestion was rejected. Record the decision in engineering-review.md.

docs.title: Review the patch after implementation
docs.text:
/review Review the uncommitted repair against issue-brief.md.
Focus on correctness and regression coverage. Cite files and lines. Do not edit.

Triage findings against actual code or tests. Fix supported defects and rerun tests and review. Keep the patch uncommitted until this is complete.

Plan critique and code review answer different questions.

docs.title: Why rubber duck is a second opinion
docs.text:
It's a built-in, read-only critic in the CLI and app. Copilot picks a contrasting model automatically when one is available.

Check the feedback yourself. An extra reasoning pass doesn't approve the change.

Session M2-01 covers the CLI's Proactive invocation opt-in. This lab invokes the critic manually.

docs.title: Fork a plan before writing code
docs.text:
/fork
/spar Challenge the readiness plan with a counterexample.
Use the same brief and tests. Reason only; do not implement.

Check the fork's workspace and the argument. Write only planning-alternative.md, then inspect /merge-to-parent.

Accept only the note. Check that parent source is unchanged before you approve the plan. /spar has no read-only guarantee, so keep permissions restricted.

docs.title: The outer loop starts with issue intent
docs.text:
Issue acceptance criteria
  → branch and diff
  → pull-request summary
  → review threads
  → required checks
  → human readiness decision

A passing local test checks part of the change. Review threads and required checks still affect PR readiness.

docs.title: Read the pull request as a linked record
docs.text:
Surface Question Issue What outcome was requested? Diff What changed, including scope drift? Review Which concerns remain unresolved? Checks Which required jobs passed, failed, or did not run?

The app keeps these surfaces close. The learner still has to connect them.

docs.title: Automate the report, not the decision
docs.text:
The lab defines a manual, read-only automation.

It may:

  • read issue and PR metadata;
  • inspect review and check status;
  • return blockers, unknowns, and a suggested verdict;
  • link each statement to its source.

It must not comment, label, push, approve, merge, or resolve threads.

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
1. Open the starter as a project.
  2. Use chat to explain the issue without editing.
  3. Start a Plan-mode working-tree session.
  4. Attach the brief and focused test.
  5. Critique the plan, revise it, and approve it before implementation.
  6. Run checks, inspect the diff, and run /review.
  7. Show the synthetic PR snapshot and readiness report.

If the live app fails, show the saved session output at the same step.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
You will submit:

  • an implementation with passing tests;
  • a session handoff;
  • engineering-review.md with plan critique and code-review triage;
  • the checked analysis note returned from the /spar fork;
  • a PR-readiness report;
  • a manual read-only automation specification.

Another engineer should be able to check your decision from these files.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text: Check live app access before the lab.

docs.title: Continue with Session M7-05
docs.text:
The developer route uses /orchestrate for independent read-only reviews of:

  • the readiness implementation;
  • regression coverage;
  • the supplied PR snapshot.

Redirect a child and reconcile conflicting readiness claims. Sessions M7-01 to M7-04 aren't required.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M2-05 lab: From isolated session to PR-readiness report
docs.text: Duration: 120 minutes

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Use the GitHub Copilot app to repair a small readiness evaluator. Run focused checks, hand the work to a fresh session, and assess a synthetic pull request. Finish by defining a manual read-only automation that repeats the readiness report without modifying GitHub.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• the GitHub Copilot app, with permission to connect a local training folder;
  • a GitHub account and Copilot plan;
  • Python 3.10 or later;
  • Git with a configured local commit identity.

Open the app and check that you can create a project session. Interactive, Plan, and Autopilot should appear in the mode picker. /plan, /review, /rubber-duck, /fork, /merge-to-parent, and /spar should appear in the command picker. Keep the trainer's filesystem and network restrictions on. A separate worktree isolates files. It isn't a sandbox or a permission grant.

Use only the synthetic assets in this session.

docs.title: Workspace
docs.text:
Copy lab/starter to a writable training folder. If the copy is inside a Git repository, create a clean branch before opening it in the app.

cp -R lab/starter ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-05
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-05
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
git init
printf '__pycache__/\n*.pyc\n' > .gitignore
git add .
git commit -m "Record readiness training baseline"

The starter is intentionally incomplete. Three focused readiness tests should fail. Use a fresh folder if ~/copilot-labs/session-m2-05 already exists. The committed baseline lets /review inspect the repair diff. Keep the repair uncommitted until the review and triage finish.

docs.title: Exercise 1: Choose the surface and establish isolation (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Use chat for discovery, then start a project session with a named workspace and mode.

  1. Open a new Chat in the app.
  2. Attach issue-brief.md and ask:
Explain the requested behavior and identify the evidence needed to prove it.
Do not edit files.
  1. Decide whether Chat was the right surface for discovery.
  2. Add the copied starter as a project.
  3. Start a Plan mode session in a new working tree of the training repository.
  4. Ask the session to run:
Report the current path, branch, worktree list, and concise Git status. Do not
edit anything.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text:
• The chat produced understanding, not edits.
  • The project session has a named workspace boundary.
  • Plan mode matches the task risk.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Challenge the plan, compare an alternative, and repair (55 minutes)
docs.text:
Repair the evaluator with a plan that names the files and tests.

  1. Attach issue-brief.md, readiness_guard/readiness.py, and tests/test_readiness.py.
  2. Ask the session to run:
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
  1. Use /plan to request a plan that maps each failing test to one issue criterion. Reject unrelated refactoring.
  2. Before implementation, run:
/rubber-duck Critique this plan and its test coverage against issue-brief.md.
Look for a way incomplete or contradictory evidence could produce READY.
Check the sorted reason-code requirement too. Do not edit files.
  1. Check the critique against the brief and tests. Ask the planning session to revise the plan for useful findings and explain rejected suggestions. If the critique finds nothing, don't invent a flaw.
  2. Record the initial plan, critique, and revision in engineering-review.md. Inspect the source diff and complete the fork exercise below before approval. Then return here and settle the plan using both critiques. Approve only a plan that names the target file and checks, and leave Plan mode before implementation.
  3. Let the session implement the accepted plan. Run the same test command and inspect every changed line in the diff.
  4. While the repair is still uncommitted, run:
/review Review the current repair diff against issue-brief.md. Focus on
correctness and regression coverage. Cite files and lines. Do not edit files.
  1. Triage findings in engineering-review.md. Link each accepted finding to a test or code reference. Fix supported defects, rerun the focused tests, and rerun /review on any correction. If a review reports no findings, record that.

docs.title: What the critic does
docs.text:
Rubber duck is a built-in, read-only agent in the app and CLI. Copilot picks a contrasting model automatically when one is available. Record the model only if the client shows it. Another answer from the session that wrote the plan isn't a second opinion.

Check the critique before changing the plan. The critic adds model usage and latency, and its conclusion isn't an approval. Session M2-01 covers the CLI's opt-in Proactive invocation setting in /subagents, which persists. This lab invokes the critic manually.

docs.title: Fork a plan and challenge it with /spar
docs.text:
Do this before implementation, while the parent source still matches the committed baseline:

  1. Inspect the parent path, branch, and source diff. Run /fork in the app.
  2. Inspect the fork's path, branch, and files. The command may not copy uncommitted files or create the workspace you intended. Stop if the fork can't be separated safely from the parent.
  3. Attach the same brief and tests. Run:
/spar Challenge the proposed readiness plan. Look for a counterexample where
missing or contradictory inputs would incorrectly produce READY. Stay within
issue-brief.md. Reason only; do not edit files, run commands, or implement.
  1. Check the argument against the tests. /spar is adversarial reasoning. It doesn't share rubber duck's model selection or read-only tool guarantees, so keep permissions restricted and inspect the diff.
  2. Switch the fork to Interactive mode to write only planning-alternative.md, with the counterexample (or no-findings result) and its effect on the plan. Inspect the note and the entire fork diff.
  3. Run /merge-to-parent from the fork. Review the return flow and accept only the analysis note. If it asks for a commit, commit only that note in the fork. Stop on an unexpected source change or merge conflict.
  4. Return to the parent. Check that the note arrived and that readiness_guard/readiness.py and tests/ still match the baseline. Reconcile the two critiques, settle the plan, and approve implementation.

This is a local fork-to-parent operation. It isn't /pr-merge, and it doesn't merge a GitHub pull request.

docs.title: Required behavior
docs.text:
evaluate_readiness(snapshot) must:

  • return NOT_READY when a required check failed;
  • return NOT_READY when a blocking review thread is unresolved;
  • return UNKNOWN when required evidence is absent;
  • return READY only when required checks pass and blocking threads are resolved;
  • return stable, sorted reason codes.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: You can explain the diff from the accepted plan and any revision. Your tests and /review triage support the behavior claims. The plan critique and the patch review stay separate.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Create a handoff and request independent critique (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Check that a fresh session can continue from a concise handoff.

  1. Ask the current session to write a handoff using session-handoff-template.md.
  2. Start a fresh project session.
  3. Attach the handoff, issue brief, changed file, and test output.
  4. Ask the fresh session:
Review this handoff. State what is proven, what remains uncertain, and the next
human decision. Do not edit files.
  1. Attach engineering-review.md and the implementation diff. Ask the fresh reader to separate the plan critique from the code-review findings and name any unresolved concern.
  2. If the fresh reader finds a supported gap, return it to the implementation session, rerun the tests and /review, and update the handoff.

Keep the fresh reader read-only, and don't start a second implementation in another worktree. Session M7-05 teaches coordinating several child sessions.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: A fresh reader can name the goal, changed files, checks, remaining risk, and next decision without the original conversation.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Assess the outer loop and define automation (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Trace the issue's requirements through the PR diff, reviews, and checks. Then create a repeatable read-only readiness report.

  1. Open prepared-evidence/05-pr-snapshot.json.
  2. Trace each issue criterion to changed files and checks.
  3. Inspect review threads. Separate blocking comments from non-blocking notes.
  4. Inspect required check results and their timestamps.
  5. Write pr-readiness-report.md with:
  6. suggested verdict;
  7. blocker reason codes;
  8. references to the snapshot data;
  9. missing or stale data;
  10. the human decision still required.
  11. Open automation-prompt-template.md.
  12. Define a manual trigger and read-only tools.
  13. In the live app, create the automation and run it manually against a synthetic repository. If automation is unavailable or no repository is available, keep it as a saved specification.
  14. Check that the automation can't comment, label, push, approve, merge, or resolve review threads.

The supplied PR snapshot should produce NOT_READY.

docs.title: Checkpoint
docs.text: The report names the failing required check and the unresolved blocking thread. The automation gathers check results and review-thread status without changing repository state.

docs.title: Final deliverables
docs.text:
• the repaired readiness_guard/readiness.py;
  • passing focused test output;
  • engineering-review.md with plan critique, plan revision, and /review triage;
  • planning-alternative.md returned from the /spar fork;
  • session-handoff-template.md completed as a handoff;
  • pr-readiness-report.md;
  • a completed automation-prompt-template.md.
