docs.title: Define the contract, state, and allowed actions
Today's outcome
docs.text:
Build one delivery-readiness canvas in the Copilot app.

Record:

  • the contract;
  • one direct update;
  • one agent-requested update;
  • one rejected update and its recovery.

You need the Copilot app and the built-in /create-canvas skill. If project scope is unavailable, use user scope.

docs.title: Choose the right customization
docs.text:
Need Use Repository convention Instructions Repeatable procedure Skill Specialist behavior Custom agent External tool or data MCP server Shared interactive artifact Canvas Packaged customizations Plugin

Use a canvas when people and an agent need to inspect or change the same visible state.

docs.title: Canvas anatomy
docs.text:
shared state
  ├─ human actions in the interface
  ├─ agent-callable capabilities
  └─ validation before every change

The contract names all four parts before implementation starts.

docs.title: Worked contract
docs.text: Part Delivery-readiness rule State item, status, review flag, evidence Status planned, in-progress, review, ready Human actions set status, flag review, add evidence Agent capabilities read board, update one named item, list flagged items Validation known item, accepted status, evidence before ready

docs.title: Keep authority narrow
docs.text:
Allowed:

  • read the current board;
  • update one named item;
  • list items flagged for review.

Out of scope:

  • deployment;
  • external writes;
  • credentials;
  • hidden data imports;
  • broad actions such as "manage the project."

docs.title: Prepared demo inputs
docs.text: ID Item Start state Evidence DOC-101 Draft operator guide planned none API-204 Add retry metric in-progress test log WEB-318 Check empty state review preview

docs.title: Demo sequence
docs.text:
1. Run the local contract tests.
  2. Create the canvas from the worked prompt.
  3. Move WEB-318 to ready with a visible control.
  4. Ask the agent to move API-204 to review.
  5. Ask for DOC-101 to move to ready.
  6. Show the rejection, add evidence, and retry.

docs.title: Creation prompt
docs.text:
/create-canvas

Create a delivery-readiness canvas from @prepared-items.json.
Use the contract in @canvas-contract.md.
People can add evidence and update one item.
Copilot can read the board, update one named item, and list review flags.
Reject unknown items or statuses. Require evidence before ready.
Do not connect external systems.

Use project scope when .github/extensions is allowed. Otherwise use user scope.

docs.title: Two paths, one state
docs.text:
Path Result Human control The item visibly changes in the canvas Agent capability The named item changes and the response matches the canvas

If the response and visible state disagree, stop and inspect the artifact.

docs.title: Rejection is part of the design
docs.text:
Request:

Move DOC-101 to ready.

Expected:

Rejected: evidence is required before ready.

The state stays unchanged and the message names the rule.

docs.title: Recovery keeps the rule
docs.text:
1. Add synthetic evidence to DOC-101.
  2. Retry the same transition.
  3. Check that ready is now accepted.
  4. Record the state before, the rejection, the correction, and the state after.

docs.title: Review the generated extension
docs.text:
Check:

  • state fields and defaults;
  • visible actions;
  • agent-callable capabilities;
  • dependencies and persisted data.

Remove anything the contract did not request.

docs.title: Source of truth
docs.text:
The canvas is a working artifact, not a system of record.

If another system owns the data, label the canvas as a projection and keep external writes out of scope.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text: Use one contract and one prepared data set for the full two hours.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M3-01 lab: Build and review a canvas contract
Objective
docs.text:
Use one synthetic delivery-readiness contract from setup through handoff. Test the contract locally, then create the canvas in the Copilot app. Make a visible change and an agent-requested change to the same state. Check that an invalid change is rejected, then recover without changing the rule.

You need the Copilot app and /create-canvas. Use synthetic data only.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
1. Your completed canvas-contract.md.
  2. The generated extension location.
  3. A final state that matches the accepted transitions.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
From the repository root:

cd sessions/session-m3-01-copilot-app-canvases/lab/starter
npm test

Expected result:

tests 4
pass 4
fail 0

Open canvas-contract.md, prepared-items.json, and demo-runbook.md. Copy them to a working folder if you don't want to edit the starter files.

docs.title: Time plan
docs.text: Part Work Time 1 Check the contract 20 min 2 Run the prepared contract tests 15 min 3 Create the canvas 25 min 4 Make two visible state changes 20 min 5 Check rejection and recovery 20 min 6 Inspect and hand off 20 min

docs.title: Part 1: Check the contract (20 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Pick project or user scope.
  2. Check that all data comes from prepared-items.json.
  3. Review every state field, human action, agent capability, and validation rule in canvas-contract.md.
  4. Replace the owner and reviewer placeholders.
  5. Check the retirement trigger.

The contract must keep these rules:

  • statuses are planned, in-progress, review, and ready;
  • one update changes one named item;
  • ready requires non-empty evidence;
  • unknown items and statuses are rejected;
  • no external system is connected.

Checkpoint 1: A peer can explain the contract without adding verbal requirements.

docs.title: Part 2: Run the prepared contract tests (15 minutes)
docs.text:
npm test

Read test/canvas-contract.test.mjs and map each test to a contract rule. Note the command, the result, and any mismatch between code and contract.

Don't continue with a failing harness. Fix only a mismatch your edits caused, or reset your copy from lab/starter/.

Checkpoint 2: The harness passes, and your group can name the planned rejection.

docs.title: Part 3: Create the canvas (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Open a Copilot app session and run:

/create-canvas

Create a delivery-readiness canvas from @prepared-items.json.
Use the contract in @canvas-contract.md.
People can add evidence and update one item.
Copilot can read the board, update one named item, and list review flags.
Reject unknown items or statuses. Require evidence before ready.
Do not connect external systems.

Choose project scope if you can create files under .github/extensions. Otherwise choose user scope.

Inspect the generated directory, metadata, dependencies, state, visible controls, and agent-callable capabilities. Ask Copilot to remove anything outside the contract.

Checkpoint 3: The canvas shows all three prepared items and no extra capability.

docs.title: Part 4: Make two visible state changes (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Change A, direct action. Move WEB-318 from review to ready. It succeeds because the item already has evidence.

Change B, agent-requested action. Ask Copilot:

Move API-204 from in-progress to review. Change only that item.

Check that:

  • WEB-318 is ready;
  • API-204 is review;
  • DOC-101 is still planned;
  • the visible state and the response agree.

Checkpoint 4: One human action and one agent request changed the same state without breaking the contract.

docs.title: Part 5: Check rejection and recovery (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Request:

Move DOC-101 to ready.

Expected result:

Rejected: evidence is required before ready.

DOC-101 stays planned. Now add this synthetic evidence:

docs://operator-guide-review

Retry the same status change. It succeeds.

Record the state before the request, the rejection text, the evidence you added, and the final accepted state.

If the first request succeeds, stop. Restore the validation rule and repeat the case.

Checkpoint 5: Recovery corrected the data and kept the rule.

docs.title: Part 6: Inspect and hand off (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Swap canvases with another group. Inspect:

  • artifact location and scope;
  • state and defaults;
  • visible human actions;
  • agent-callable capabilities;
  • rejection and recovery records;
  • dependencies and persisted data;
  • owner and retirement trigger.

Fix contract mismatches, then compare the final state with ../solution/final-state.json.

Checkpoint 6: The canvas matches the contract.

You're done when another person can identify the extension scope, the fixed contract, the starting state, both accepted changes, and the rejected change with its recovery.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Issue Response Project scope is blocked Use user scope. Generated actions exceed the contract Remove them before testing. State and agent response disagree Stop and inspect the shared artifact. Local tests fail before edits Restore the starter files. ready accepts empty evidence Fix the rule before review.

The worked contract and final state are in ../solution/.

docs.title: Optional variant: Feature Workbench
docs.text:
Try this after the default lab, or when the trainer assigns it as follow-up.

  1. Open starter/feature-workbench-contract.md.
  2. Load the synthetic checks from starter/feature-workbench-sample.json.
  3. Decide whether FEAT-204 should pass the test gate.
  4. Record the required check that blocks the decision.
  5. Compare your review with solution/feature-workbench-solution.md and solution/feature-workbench-final-state.json.

The canvas may propose pass, hold, or rerun. A human reviewer records the final decision. Don't connect a live CI system, merge code, or trigger deployment.

docs.title: 0:00 to 0:05: Outcome
docs.text:
Frame the session: "We are designing one shared artifact. Judge it by its visible behavior, not by a polished chat response."

Show the deliverables and say whether you'll run the live or prepared demo.

docs.title: 0:05 to 0:13: Choose the right customization
docs.text:
Use the decision table from the slides:

  • instructions state conventions;
  • a skill describes a repeatable procedure;
  • a custom agent supplies specialist behavior;
  • an MCP server connects tools or data;
  • a canvas gives people and an agent one interactive artifact;
  • a plugin can package a canvas with other customizations.

Use a canvas when state must stay visible across several actions or a handoff. Stay in chat for a short answer or one draft.

Checkpoint: Ask, "What breaks if this stays in chat?" A good answer names lost visibility, direct control, or saved state for handoff.

docs.title: 0:13 to 0:23: Build the worked contract
docs.text:
Open ../lab/starter/canvas-contract.md and walk through it:

  1. State: id, item, status, reviewFlag, and evidence.
  2. Human actions: add evidence, set a status, set the review flag.
  3. Agent capabilities: read the board, update one named item, list flagged items.
  4. Validation: reject unknown IDs, unknown statuses, and ready without evidence.
  5. Boundary: synthetic data, no external systems.

Teaching test: Every action must fit in one sentence. A broad verb such as "manage" needs a smaller action.

docs.title: 0:23 to 0:30: Prepared inputs and harness
docs.text:
Open prepared-items.json. Point out the three starting states and which item lacks evidence. Then run:

cd sessions/session-m3-01-copilot-app-canvases/lab/starter
npm test

The harness doesn't imitate the Copilot app. It checks the state rules the generated canvas must keep:

  • an item with evidence can move to ready;
  • an agent-requested named update changes the same state model;
  • DOC-101 cannot move to ready without evidence;
  • adding evidence allows the retry.

docs.title: 0:43 to 0:50: Rejection and recovery
docs.text:
Request:

Move DOC-101 to ready.

Expected:

  • the update is rejected;
  • the message names the missing evidence rule;
  • DOC-101 stays planned.

Add the synthetic evidence docs://operator-guide-review, then retry. The same transition now succeeds, the rule is unchanged, and the change record shows the state before, the rejection, the correction, and the state after.

If the generated canvas accepts the first request, pause and restore the rule. An accepted unsafe update is a failed demo.

docs.title: 0:50 to 0:56: Inspect the extension
docs.text: Check generated files and dependencies, state fields and persisted data, visible human actions, agent-callable capabilities, validation messages, and the retirement trigger. Remove generated features the contract didn't request.

docs.title: 0:56 to 1:00: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Assign four roles. One person may hold two in a small group: contract owner, app operator, contract tester, handoff owner.

Point to the six lab checkpoints. The same three prepared items stay in use for the whole lab.

Close with: "Keep the contract fixed while you test the implementation. If the implementation needs broader authority, review the contract first."

Extra capabilities appear Remove them. Agent response and visible state differ Stop and inspect the artifact. ready succeeds without evidence Fix the rule and rerun the rejection. A learner proposes real work data Use the supplied synthetic input.

docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Agentic Workflows

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04

Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hours lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Take one synthetic issue from its contract to a review decision. Prepare the repository, start a Copilot cloud agent session, inspect the proposed change, and run the tests. Then approve, request changes, or pause.

The issue stays fixed throughout: reject blank or whitespace-only task titles and keep valid task creation working.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Write an issue with testable acceptance criteria, allowed files, and non-goals.
  • Review repository instructions and Copilot setup steps before assignment.
  • Monitor an agent session without expanding the issue.
  • Compare a proposed change with the issue and its file scope.
  • Run and record focused tests.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
• Copilot cloud agent access to a training repository.
  • A human reviewer.
  • Node.js and npm.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
1. The fixed issue.
  2. The proposed change.
  3. Focused test output.
  4. The review outcome.

docs.title: Session materials
docs.text: Resource Purpose trainer-content/README.md Minute-mapped teaching and demo plan slides.md Trainer-facing teaching deck lab/README.md Two-hour issue-to-review lab lab/starter/ Issue, setup, sample project, and review guide lab/solution/ Completed issue journey and runnable solution

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Get started with Copilot agents on GitHub
  • Managing agent sessions
  • Configure the development environment
  • Add repository custom instructions

docs.title: Keep the Copilot cloud agent within the issue
Issue-to-review workflow
docs.text:
issue contract
    ↓
repository setup
    ↓
proposed change
    ↓
test output
    ↓
human decision

Keep the same issue and acceptance criteria at every step.

docs.title: The fixed issue
docs.text:
Reject blank task titles

Allowed files:

  • src/app.js
  • tests/app.test.js

Required command:

npm test

No dependency changes. No unrelated refactor.

docs.title: Checkpoint 1: Issue contract
docs.text:
Before you assign the issue, a reviewer must be able to answer:

  • Which behavior changes?
  • Which behavior stays the same?
  • Which files may change?
  • What proves completion?
  • What is out of scope?

docs.title: Repository instructions
docs.text:
Tell the agent how to work in this repository:

  • project shape;
  • coding conventions;
  • allowed file scope;
  • test command;
  • prohibited changes.

Instructions support the issue. They don't repair a vague one.

docs.title: Copilot setup steps
docs.text:
The workflow file lives at:

.github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml

It has one job named:

copilot-setup-steps

Review its permissions, commands, and secrets before merging it to the default branch.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2: Setup
docs.text:
Record:

  • baseline test result;
  • where the instructions and setup workflow live;
  • allowed files;
  • reviewer and stop condition.

Stop if you can't explain the baseline result or setup needs a credential.

docs.title: Start the session
docs.text:
• Assign the fixed issue.
  • Watch the session log.
  • Steer only within the issue.
  • Stop on scope drift.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3: Proposed change
docs.text:
Inspect before running tests:

  • changed files;
  • validation behavior;
  • response shape;
  • valid request behavior;
  • dependency and configuration changes.

A small diff can still be wrong.

docs.title: Expected behavior
docs.text:
if (typeof title !== "string" || title.trim() === "") {
  return res.status(400).json({ error: "title is required" });
}

The code may differ. The behavior and constraints must not.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4: Tests
docs.text:
Case Expected "" HTTP 400 " " HTTP 400 " Weekly plan " HTTP 201 with preserved response shape

Run the full suite and save the output.

docs.title: Keep review feedback within the issue
docs.text:
Good:

The whitespace case is missing. Add a focused test in tests/app.test.js.
Keep the current response shape and do not change other endpoints.
Run npm test and report the result.

Bad:

Clean up the API while you are there.

docs.title: Checkpoint 5: Human decision
docs.text:
Choose:

  • approve when criteria, scope, and tests pass;
  • request changes when a correction within the issue remains;
  • pause when test output or ownership is unresolved.

The agent does not make this decision.

docs.title: Stop conditions
docs.text:
Stop when:

  • the requested files expand;
  • a new dependency appears;
  • the agent asks for credentials;
  • tests keep failing with no recovery plan;
  • the issue changes mid-run.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text: Keep the same issue through all five checkpoints. Record the reviewer's decision.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M3-02 lab: One issue from contract to review
Objective
docs.text:
Take one synthetic issue from its fixed contract through setup and implementation with Copilot cloud agent. Then test and review the change. Manual work doesn't complete this lab.

You need cloud agent access to a training repository and a reviewer. Don't put credentials in issues, instructions, setup workflows, or comments.

docs.title: Deliverables
docs.text:
1. The fixed issue.md.
  2. The proposed diff or pull request reference.
  3. Test output.
  4. The review outcome in the pull request or a local review.

docs.title: The one issue
docs.text:
Use starter/issue.md for the whole lab:

Reject blank or whitespace-only task titles.

Don't swap in another issue, add an endpoint, or widen it into API cleanup.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
From the repository root:

cd sessions/session-m3-02-cloud-agent/lab
npm --prefix starter/sample-project install
npm --prefix starter/sample-project test

The starter suite passes before you add the validation.

Open starter/issue.md, starter/copilot-instructions.md, starter/copilot-setup-steps.yml, and starter/pr-review-checklist.md. In a live training repository the setup workflow goes at .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml.

docs.title: Time plan
docs.text: Checkpoint Work Time 1 Check the issue contract 20 min 2 Check repository setup 20 min 3 Produce and inspect the proposed change 35 min 4 Run and review tests 25 min 5 Make the human decision 20 min

docs.title: Checkpoint 1: Issue contract (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Read starter/issue.md. Have a peer answer:

  • Which request is invalid?
  • What exact response is required?
  • Which valid behavior must remain?
  • Which files may change?
  • Which command proves completion?
  • What is out of scope?

Fix any ambiguous text before implementation.

Result: The issue has acceptance criteria, allowed files, non-goals, and a stop condition.

docs.title: Checkpoint 2: Setup (20 minutes)
docs.text:
1. Read starter/copilot-instructions.md and starter/copilot-setup-steps.yml.
  2. Check that the workflow targets .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml and has a single job named copilot-setup-steps.
  3. Run the baseline:
npm --prefix starter/sample-project test
  1. Write down the result and the allowed files: src/app.js and tests/app.test.js.

Stop if the baseline fails without explanation or setup needs a credential.

Result: Passing baseline output, reviewed setup files, a named reviewer, and a stop condition.

docs.title: Checkpoint 3: Proposed change (35 minutes)
docs.text:
Copy the contents of starter/sample-project/ to the root of the training repository. The setup workflow expects package.json, package-lock.json, src/, and tests/ there. Add the instructions and setup workflow.

Create the issue from starter/issue.md and assign it to Copilot cloud agent.

Monitor the session. Note the planned files, reported commands, any steering, and the final files. Steer only if the work drifts:

Keep the existing issue contract. Change only src/app.js and tests/app.test.js.
Add no dependency. Stop and ask for clarification if broader work is required.

Before running tests, inspect the diff with starter/pr-review-checklist.md:

  • only the two allowed files changed;
  • blank and whitespace-only titles return HTTP 400;
  • the error body is { "error": "title is required" };
  • valid task creation keeps its response shape;
  • no dependency or unrelated endpoint changed.

If no proposal is ready after 25 minutes, stop the run.

Result: A pull request or diff tied to the same issue.

docs.title: Checkpoint 4: Tests (25 minutes)
docs.text:
npm test
Case Expected result Empty title "" HTTP 400 and required error body Whitespace title " " HTTP 400 and required error body Valid title " Weekly plan " HTTP 201 with the existing response fields Existing endpoints Existing tests still pass

If a case is missing, ask for a test for that case only.

Result: Focused test output for the reviewed proposal.

docs.title: Checkpoint 5: Human decision (20 minutes)
docs.text:
Choose:

  • approve when the issue, diff, and tests agree;
  • request changes when a correction within the issue remains;
  • pause when test output or ownership is unresolved.

Compare your decision with solution/issue-journey.md. Don't merge unless your training repository requires it.

Result: The pull request or local review shows the outcome.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Issue Response Setup workflow isn't active on the default branch Ask the trainer to prepare the repository. Session edits extra files Stop it or tell the agent to change only the allowed files. Test passes but response shape changed Request changes and cite the response-shape criterion. Review suggests a second feature Log it as future work.

solution/ has the completed issue journey, prepared diff, setup workflow, runnable solution project, and test output.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment What to check 0:00 to 0:05 Introduce the workflow Five checkpoints understood 0:05 to 0:16 Checkpoint 1: issue contract Issue is complete 0:16 to 0:27 Checkpoint 2: setup Passing baseline, reviewed setup 0:27 to 0:39 Start one session Planned files, commands, and edits stay within the issue 0:39 to 0:47 Checkpoint 3: proposed change Diff checked against allowed files 0:47 to 0:54 Checkpoint 4: tests Recorded test result 0:54 to 0:58 Checkpoint 5: human decision Approve, request changes, or pause 0:58 to 1:00 Lab handoff Roles ready

docs.title: 0:00 to 0:05: Introduce the workflow
docs.text:
Show the five-checkpoint sequence. Say: "We keep one issue fixed from assignment through review. If the work needs a different issue, we stop and write one."

Name the reviewer who owns the final decision.

docs.title: 0:05 to 0:16: Checkpoint 1: issue contract
docs.text:
Start with a weak request:

Fix title validation.

Open ../lab/starter/issue.md and show how the same request gains testable criteria and a file scope:

  • blank and whitespace-only titles return HTTP 400;
  • the error body is { "error": "title is required" };
  • valid creation keeps its response shape;
  • only src/app.js and tests/app.test.js may change;
  • npm test must pass;
  • no dependency or unrelated endpoint change.

Ask a learner to map each criterion to a test or diff check.

Gate: Don't assign the issue until a peer can name the changed behavior, preserved behavior, allowed files, required checks, and non-goals.

docs.title: 0:16 to 0:27: Checkpoint 2: setup
docs.text:
Open ../lab/starter/copilot-instructions.md. It should cover Node.js and the Express app, file scope, response format, no new dependencies, and npm test.

Open ../lab/starter/copilot-setup-steps.yml. It belongs at .github/workflows/copilot-setup-steps.yml. Point out the single job copilot-setup-steps, minimal permissions, dependency install, and baseline test.

Run the baseline:

cd sessions/session-m3-02-cloud-agent/lab/starter/sample-project
npm test

Gate: Stop if the baseline fails without explanation, setup asks for a credential, or the reviewer can't name the allowed files.

docs.title: 0:27 to 0:39: Start one session
docs.text:
Assign ../lab/starter/issue.md to Copilot cloud agent. Watch the session and note planned files, commands, edits, test reports, and questions.

Steer only if needed:

Keep the current issue contract. Change only src/app.js and tests/app.test.js.
Add no dependency. Stop and ask for clarification if broader work is required.

Stop on scope drift. Don't edit the issue during the run.

At 0:35, if there's no reviewable proposal, show ../lab/solution/proposed-change.diff to finish the demo. Fix access problems before the learner lab.

docs.title: 0:39 to 0:47: Checkpoint 3: proposed change
docs.text:
Review the diff before running tests, using ../lab/starter/pr-review-checklist.md:

  1. Only src/app.js and tests/app.test.js changed.
  2. Blank and whitespace-only strings are rejected.
  3. The response body matches the issue.
  4. Valid task creation keeps its response shape.
  5. No dependency, configuration, or unrelated endpoint changed.

Model a review comment that stays within the issue:

The blank-title test passes, but the whitespace case is missing.
Add that focused test in tests/app.test.js. Keep the current file scope,
then run npm test and report the result.

docs.title: 0:47 to 0:54: Checkpoint 4: tests
docs.text:
npm test

Look for results covering the empty string, a whitespace-only string, a valid title with surrounding whitespace, and all existing endpoints.

Passing tests don't replace diff review. If a test fails, decide whether the fix fits the issue. Then request it or pause.

docs.title: 0:54 to 0:58: Checkpoint 5: human decision
docs.text:
The reviewer chooses:

  • approve when scope, behavior, and tests match the issue;
  • request changes when the correction stays within the issue;
  • pause when test output or ownership is unresolved.

Don't turn the decision into a new implementation request.

docs.title: 0:58 to 1:00: Lab handoff
docs.text: Assign four roles: issue owner, cloud agent operator, reviewer, test runner. The same issue stays in scope from setup through review.

docs.title: Controlled failures to demo
docs.text:
Failure Expected review response Whitespace test is missing Request one focused test. package.json changes Reject the unrelated dependency or script change. Error body differs Cite the exact acceptance criterion. Valid response shape changes Request restoration and a regression test.

Recovery works when the proposal returns to the fixed issue and the full suite passes.

docs.title: Common failures
docs.text: Failure Recovery Setup workflow isn't on the default branch Prepare the repository. Baseline tests fail Diagnose before assignment. Session changes extra files Stop it or tell the agent to change only the allowed files. Learners rewrite the issue mid-run Stop and write a separate future issue. Tests pass but the diff breaks scope Request changes or pause.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M3-03: MCP servers & custom tool integration
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Agentic Workflows Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04 Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hours lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives AI clients a standard way to discover and call tools. You build a local stdio server in two stages. First, trace get_weather from its JSON Schema through the handler. Test good and bad input, then call it with MCP Inspector. Then add get_forecast and convert_temperature.

The server returns deterministic synthetic weather data. It needs no network service or credential.

docs.title: MCP server or plugin?
docs.text:
An MCP server exposes tools and context through a protocol. A plugin is an installable package that can bundle MCP server configuration with skills, agents, hooks, or other components. Build a server when you need a protocol endpoint. Use a plugin to distribute and version a set of Copilot customizations.

See the curriculum glossary for MCP server, tool, transport, and plugin terms.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Explain the MCP client-server model and transports.
  • Trace one tool from schema to protocol response.
  • Return visible errors for invalid arguments and unknown tools.
  • Test handlers without starting an AI client.
  • Use MCP Inspector to list and call local tools.
  • Add tools without weakening the first tool's contract.

docs.title: You need
docs.text: Node.js 20 or later and npm. GitHub Copilot is useful for a final integration check but isn't required.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Staged server lab/starter/custom-mcp/ Completed server lab/solution/custom-mcp/ Expected test and Inspector output lab/solution/custom-mcp/EVIDENCE.md

docs.title: Test one tool before adding the next
docs.text: Session M3-03 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time MCP request path and boundaries 8 min Names, descriptions, and schemas 10 min One tool from schema to response 15 min Bad input and visible errors 10 min Test output and review 9 min Lab handoff 8 min

docs.title: The MCP request path
docs.text:
Client
  ↓ tools/list
Tool catalog
  ↓ tools/call
Schema validation
  ↓
Handler
  ↓
Success or visible error

MCP standardizes discovery and calls. It doesn't make a result correct.

docs.title: Five boundaries
docs.text:
Boundary Review question Catalog Which capabilities can the client discover? Schema Which arguments are accepted? Handler What work happens after a call? Result Can the caller tell failure from success? Transport Which process or endpoint carries the request?

Start with stdio and synthetic data.

docs.title: Start with one narrow capability
docs.text:
{
  "name": "get_weather",
  "description": "Return deterministic synthetic current weather for one city.",
  "inputSchema": {
    "type": "object",
    "required": ["city"],
    "additionalProperties": false
  }
}

Clients use the name, description, and schema as part of the interface. Start with one tool: every exposed capability adds risk and upkeep.

docs.title: Trace the good request
docs.text:
{
  "name": "get_weather",
  "arguments": {
    "city": "Oslo"
  }
}

{
  "city": "Oslo",
  "temperature": 30,
  "unit": "celsius",
  "conditions": "rain"
}

Deterministic output makes exact tests possible.

docs.title: Trace the bad request
docs.text:
{
  "name": "get_weather",
  "arguments": {
    "city": "   "
  }
}

{
  "error": "city must be a non-empty string"
}

The MCP result sets isError: true. An invalid request must not look like an empty success.

docs.title: Schema and handler work together
docs.text:
Schema Handler Helps clients form valid calls Protects direct and protocol calls Documents required fields Applies business limits Rejects extra properties Returns a stable error shape

Not every caller reaches the handler through a client-side check.

docs.title: What each check shows
docs.text:
Check Shows Unit test Handler behavior for tested inputs tools/list The expected catalog is exposed tools/call The stdio protocol path reaches the handler Copilot call A client can discover and choose the tool

Keep the deterministic tests even when the client integration works.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Apply the same contract to three tools. Check discovery, valid input, invalid input, and visible errors through tests and MCP Inspector.

Submit a three-tool server with recorded requests, responses, and errors.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M3-03 lab: Build and test an MCP server
Lab overview
docs.text:
Build and test one tool before adding the next two. Use only the supplied synthetic data.

You need Node.js 20 or later, npm, and MCP Inspector 2.5.0 (run through npx). Copilot is optional. Don't copy or commit node_modules.

Deliverable: A three-tool local MCP server with automated tests, Inspector output, and recorded good and bad requests.

Part Work Time 1 Inspect the staged server 15 min 2 Test get_weather from schema through handler 30 min 3 Inspect good and bad protocol calls 25 min 4 Add get_forecast and convert_temperature 35 min 5 Run all checks and record output 15 min

docs.title: Part 1: Inspect the staged server
docs.text:
cd sessions/session-m3-03-mcp-servers/lab/starter/custom-mcp
npm ci
npm test

Read package.json, src/index.js, and test/get-weather.test.js. Find:

  1. the get_weather tool definition;
  2. its JSON Schema;
  3. invokeTool, which validates and handles the call;
  4. the protocol handlers that connect MCP requests to the catalog and handler.

Checkpoint: npm test reports three passing tests. The catalog contains only get_weather.

docs.title: Part 2: Test get_weather from schema through handler
docs.text:
Trace this request:

{
  "name": "get_weather",
  "arguments": {
    "city": "Oslo"
  }
}

The schema requires a non-empty city and rejects extra properties. The handler returns deterministic data:

{
  "city": "Oslo",
  "temperature": 30,
  "unit": "celsius",
  "conditions": "rain"
}

Now bad input:

{
  "name": "get_weather",
  "arguments": {
    "city": "   "
  }
}

Expected tool response:

{
  "error": "city must be a non-empty string"
}

The MCP result sets isError: true. An invalid request must not look like an empty success.

Add one focused test for a second city. Don't add another tool yet.

Checkpoint: The new test passes and the implementation makes no network call.

docs.title: Part 3: Inspect good and bad protocol calls
docs.text:
List the tool:

npx --yes @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@2.5.0 --cli \
  node src/index.js --method tools/list

Call it:

npx --yes @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@2.5.0 --cli \
  node src/index.js --method tools/call \
  --tool-name get_weather --tool-arg city=Oslo

If you have a browser, use the Inspector web client:

npx --yes @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@2.5.0 node src/index.js

Record the tool name, description, input schema, request, response, and error shape. Passing unit tests don't replace the protocol calls.

docs.title: Part 4: Add the remaining tools
docs.text:
Tool Required behavior get_forecast city is required; days defaults to 3 and accepts integers from 1 to 7 convert_temperature value is finite; from is celsius or fahrenheit

Keep output deterministic so tests can assert exact values. Add tests for the forecast default and invalid range, both conversion directions, bad units, and an unknown tool.

Update the catalog assertion in test/get-weather.test.js. It should now expect get_weather, get_forecast, and convert_temperature, in that order. Keep the existing weather checks.

Work in your edited lab/starter/custom-mcp copy. Run:

npm test

Checkpoint: All your tests pass. Bad forecast ranges, bad units, and unknown tools return visible errors. Compare with lab/solution/custom-mcp/ afterward. Passing the reference tests doesn't check your code.

docs.title: Part 5: Record requests and responses
docs.text:
Run these against your edited server:

npx --yes @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@2.5.0 --cli \
  node src/index.js --method tools/list
npx --yes @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@2.5.0 --cli \
  node src/index.js --method tools/call \
  --tool-name get_weather --tool-arg city=Oslo
npx --yes @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@2.5.0 --cli \
  node src/index.js --method tools/call \
  --tool-name get_forecast --tool-arg city=Lima --tool-arg days=8

The catalog must list all three tools. The bad forecast call must return isError: true and exit with status 5. That nonzero status is expected.

Keep the Inspector output and your passing npm test output. Use solution/custom-mcp/EVIDENCE.md to compare response shapes, not to replace running your server.

Optionally, attach the local server to a Copilot client and ask for a three-day forecast in Fahrenheit. Check each tool call against your contract.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. A commit or diff showing get_weather before the other tools.
  2. A server with three tool schemas and handlers.
  3. Passing automated tests, with no tracked node_modules, and manifests and lockfiles present.
  4. Inspector output from your server.
  5. One good and one bad request with expected and actual responses.

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Use Node.js 20 or later.
  • Run npm ci && npm test in both custom MCP projects.
  • Check that no node_modules directory is tracked.
  • Pin MCP Inspector 2.5.0 for the demo.

If you can't install packages, walk through the code and label Inspector and tests as not executed.

docs.title: 0:00 to 0:08: MCP request path
docs.text:
Client → tools/list → tool selection → tools/call → handler → result

The protocol standardizes discovery and calls. It doesn't grant permissions or make a result correct.

Keep the packaging distinction short: an MCP server provides protocol tools and context. A plugin distributes a versioned set of Copilot customizations and may include MCP server configuration. Installing a plugin doesn't run the server it references.

Boundary Question Tool catalog What can the client discover? Input schema Which arguments are accepted? Handler What work happens? Result How does success or failure appear? Transport Which process or endpoint carries the request?

docs.title: 0:08 to 0:18: The tool contract
docs.text:
Open lab/starter/custom-mcp/src/index.js. Read the get_weather definition before the handler. Point out:

  • a specific name;
  • a description that says the data is synthetic;
  • a required, non-empty city;
  • additionalProperties: false.

The schema helps clients form a request. The handler still validates arguments, because direct tests and other transports can reach it without a client-side validator.

docs.title: 0:18 to 0:33: One tool end to end
docs.text:
Trace:

{
  "name": "get_weather",
  "arguments": {
    "city": "Oslo"
  }
}

Show invokeTool, syntheticWeather, and the protocol registration. Then run:

cd sessions/session-m3-03-mcp-servers/lab/starter/custom-mcp
npm test

Deterministic output allows exact assertions. Random output would make a small contract test flaky.

docs.title: 0:33 to 0:43: Failure is part of the interface
docs.text:
Trace an empty city. The response sets isError: true and carries:

{
  "error": "city must be a non-empty string"
}

Compare two weak patterns: returning an empty success object, and throwing an unhandled exception that kills the server. The caller needs an error it can report without crashing.

docs.title: 0:43 to 0:52: Inspector output and test results
docs.text:
npx --yes @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@2.5.0 --cli \
  node src/index.js --method tools/list

Then call get_weather. Keep test results and Inspector output separate:

Check Shows Unit test Handler behavior for known inputs tools/list The server exposes the expected catalog tools/call The stdio protocol path reaches the handler Copilot call A client can discover and choose the tool

A Copilot call shows client integration works. Keep the deterministic tests anyway.

docs.title: 0:52 to 1:00: Add the remaining tools
docs.text:
Open the completed server. get_forecast and convert_temperature follow the same shape as get_weather:

  • forecast days are integers from 1 to 7;
  • conversion units are a fixed enum;
  • unknown tools return a visible error;
  • output stays deterministic and synthetic.

Remind learners to keep the first tool passing while they add the other two.

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
1. Run the starter tests.
  2. Show the good Oslo request and exact response.
  3. Change the request to an empty city and show the tool error.
  4. List tools with Inspector.
  5. Open the solution catalog and show the two added tools.
  6. Run the five solution tests.

Don't type the full server from scratch in class.

docs.title: Review prompts
docs.text:
• Which file owns the tool description?
  • Which check rejects an empty city?
  • Why does the handler validate input when the schema exists?
  • What does tools/list show that a direct handler test doesn't?
  • What would make adding a fourth tool risky?

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text: Learners start with the one-tool server, add one test, and inspect good and bad calls before adding the other tools. They update the one-tool catalog assertion when the catalog grows, run tests and Inspector against their edited copy (not the reference solution), and submit the lockfile, test output, and protocol requests and responses.

docs.title: Session M3-04: Custom agents & agent profiles
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Agentic Workflows Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04, M3-03 Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hours lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Custom agents define narrow roles in Markdown that teams can review. Start with a weak test-writer profile that enables every tool and permits source edits. After its boundary test fails, replace it with a profile that may read source, edit tests, and run one known command. The profile must stop when production code needs to change.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Explain the .agent.md profile structure and frontmatter.
  • Detect a boundary violation with a repeatable contract test.
  • Use tool aliases as a least-privilege allowlist.
  • Write a stop condition that hands production conflicts to a human.
  • Load the profile in the CLI and check that a source-code conflict stops the run.
  • Choose between instructions, custom agents, skills, and MCP.
  • Run an LSP definition/reference lookup and tell a caller from an export.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
Node.js 22.22.2 or later, Git, the standalone Copilot CLI with custom-agent support, and a working JavaScript language server (setup).

Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Language-server setup lab/lsp-setup.md Weak profile lab/starter/agent-project/.github/agents/weak-test-writer.agent.md Tightened profile lab/solution/agent-project/.github/agents/test-writer.agent.md Profile reference lab/solution/agent-project/PROFILE-REFERENCE.md

docs.title: Fail the weak profile, tighten it, rerun the same test
docs.text: Session M3-04 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time What a profile controls 8 min .agent.md structure 10 min Weak profile and boundary violation 12 min Least-privilege tools and paths 13 min Stop, validation, and human handoff 9 min Rerun and lab handoff 8 min

docs.title: A profile is a role contract
docs.text:
Profile
  role + tools + procedure + stop rules

Environment
  actual permissions + repository access

Human
  accept + revise + reject

The profile guides behavior. It doesn't grant authority.

docs.title: Repository profile structure
docs.text:
.github/
└── agents/
    └── test-writer.agent.md

YAML frontmatter plus a Markdown body. The filename identifies the profile.

docs.title: Frontmatter used in the lab
docs.text:
---
name: Test-only writer
description: Adds focused JavaScript tests in tests/ and stops when production code must change.
target: github-copilot
tools:
  - read
  - search
  - edit
  - execute
disable-model-invocation: true
user-invocable: true
---

description is required. Omitting tools enables all available tools.

docs.title: The weak profile looks convenient
docs.text:
tools: ["*"]

Add tests for the requested behavior.
Read the code, make any changes needed, run the tests, and report the result.

It never says which files may change or when to stop.

docs.title: Check code intelligence, not just text matches
docs.text:
/lsp show
/lsp test typescript

Ask for the definition and references of getOrdersByUser. Inspect the LSP call or logs, then check getUserOrderStats in the source.

An export is not a caller. A startup test is not a symbol lookup. Don't edit code in this step.

docs.title: Test a source-code conflict
docs.text:
Add tests for updateOrderStatus.
Change tests only.

A new criterion allows reversing shipped to processing.
The current implementation rejects that transition.

The weak wording permits a source edit. One lucky run in scope doesn't fix the contract.

docs.title: Make the failure repeatable
docs.text:
npm run check:weak

Expected failures:

  • every tool is enabled;
  • no test-only path is named;
  • no production-code stop exists;
  • no test command or human review decision is named.

docs.title: Tool allowlists are necessary
docs.text:
Need Alias Read source and tests read Find conventions search Edit test files edit Run the known test command execute

But edit still needs a path rule in the body.

docs.title: The body sets the path boundary
docs.text:
Allowed:

Read src/
Search the repository
Edit tests/
Run npm test

Forbidden:

Edit src/
Change manifests or workflows
Add dependencies
Push or merge

docs.title: Stop instead of crossing the boundary
docs.text:
No files changed.
Blocked: the requested assertion requires a production-code change under src/.
Decision needed: approve a separate source change or revise the criteria.

The stop report names the conflict and the decision a human must make.

docs.title: Rerun the same contract
docs.text:
npm run check:tight
npm test

Expected:

PASS .../test-writer.agent.md
tests 3
pass 3
fail 0

The tightened profile passes the contract that failed the weak one.

docs.title: Choose the right customization
docs.text:
Need Use Repository-wide convention Instructions Repeatable procedure Skill Specialist role with a defined scope Custom agent External tools or data MCP

Don't add MCP to a role that only needs repository files.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
1. Inspect the .agent.md structure.
  2. Run the weak contract.
  3. Record the source edit the weak profile permits.
  4. Tighten tools, paths, validation, and stop behavior.
  5. Rerun the contract.
  6. Produce a no-change stop report.

Submit both the failed weak profile and the passing tightened profile, plus the actual LSP lookup and the live stop. A manual trace doesn't complete them.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M3-04 lab: Tighten a custom agent boundary
docs.text: Deliverable: A tested .agent.md profile, a checked LSP lookup, and a live test-only run that stops at a source-code conflict

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
Start with a profile that doesn't restrict source edits. Show the problem, tighten the profile, and rerun the same checks.

Part Work Time 1 Inspect the profile format 20 min 2 Inspect symbols with LSP and expose the weak boundary 25 min 3 Tighten tools, paths, validation, and stop rules 35 min 4 Rerun tests and the source-conflict scenario 25 min 5 Review the full profile 15 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need Node.js 22.22.2 or later, Git, standalone Copilot CLI with custom-agent support, and the JavaScript language server from lsp-setup.md. Check /agent, /lsp show, and /lsp test typescript first. Contract tests and manual traces don't replace a live profile load or an LSP lookup.

Copy the full lab to a fresh workspace:

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-04
cp -R sessions/session-m3-04-custom-agents/lab ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-04/
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-04/lab/starter/agent-project
git init

Read .github/lsp.json and jsconfig.json before opening the project. Keep the whole lab copy: the harness unit tests use its reference profile. check:tight checks the profile you create locally.

Don't push, merge, open an issue, or attach MCP. This lab tests the profile contract.

docs.title: Part 1: Inspect the profile format
docs.text:
Open:

lab/solution/agent-project/PROFILE-REFERENCE.md
lab/starter/agent-project/.github/agents/weak-test-writer.agent.md

A repository profile lives under .github/agents/ as Markdown with YAML frontmatter. description is required. Omitting tools enables all available tools, so this lab declares read, search, edit, and execute.

The body tells the agent the matching task, the paths it may read and edit, the ordered procedure, the validation command, and the stop and handoff rule.

Checkpoint: Identify which fields control selection, tool availability, manual invocation, and ownership.

docs.title: Inspect symbols (10 minutes)
docs.text:
In a normal CLI session, ask:

Use JavaScript language-server operations to find the definition and references
of getOrdersByUser in src/order-service.js. Distinguish its caller from its
CommonJS export. Report paths and lines. Do not edit or rename anything.

Inspect the actual tool call or /lsp logs. Check the reported caller getUserOrderStats against the source. A comment or export is not a call. Write the operation, returned locations, and your check in agent-run.md. If the agent used only text search, ask it to use the configured LSP.

docs.title: Expose the profile boundary (15 minutes)
docs.text:
npm run check:weak

It must fail. The weak profile uses tools: ["*"] and says to "make any changes needed," so a test-only request can drift into src/.

Use this scenario:

Add tests for updateOrderStatus.
Change tests only.
A new acceptance criterion allows reversing a shipped order to processing.
The current implementation rejects that transition.

Nothing forces the weak profile to stop. Record:

Observed: profile permits a production edit under src/.
Expected: profile stops and asks for a separate production-code decision.

Don't repair the source file.

docs.title: Part 3: Tighten the profile
docs.text:
Create .github/agents/test-writer.agent.md. Use solution/agent-project/.github/agents/test-writer.agent.md as the reference.

The profile must:

  1. include description;
  2. use a least-privilege tool allowlist;
  3. permit reads under src/;
  4. permit edits under tests/ only;
  5. run npm test;
  6. stop when a production change is needed;
  7. ask for a human review decision;
  8. stop on missing access.

The profile can't enforce repository permissions. The environment still controls what each tool can do.

docs.title: Part 4: Rerun the same contract
docs.text:
npm run check:tight
npm test

Expected:

PASS .../test-writer.agent.md
tests 3
pass 3
fail 0

Load your profile with /agent and repeat the conflict scenario. The correct result is a stop report:

No files changed.
Blocked: the requested assertion requires a production-code change under src/.
Decision needed: approve a separate source change or revise the acceptance criteria.

Record the selected profile and result in agent-run.md. A manual trace helps diagnose problems but doesn't complete the live run. The profile must not silently change the criterion or edit src/.

Checkpoint: The contract that failed the weak profile now passes.

docs.title: Part 5: Review the full profile
docs.text:
Use PROFILE-REFERENCE.md and BOUNDARY-EVIDENCE.md. Review:

  • file location and .agent.md suffix;
  • required and optional frontmatter;
  • tool aliases and the effect of omitting tools;
  • disable-model-invocation and user-invocable;
  • owner and contract version metadata;
  • body length, trigger, procedure, and stop rule.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. The weak profile and its failed contract output.
  2. The tightened test-writer.agent.md.
  3. Passing profile contract tests.
  4. A source-conflict scenario that stops without editing src/.
  5. agent-run.md with the LSP lookup and the live selected-profile result.

docs.title: Prepare CLI language servers
docs.text: Install and check the language server before the workshop. A language-server process is executable software, so read the project configuration before opening the workspace in Copilot.

docs.title: JavaScript: Session M3-04
docs.text:
Use Node.js 22.22.2 or later.

Check for typescript-language-server on PATH. If it's missing:

npm install --global typescript@6 typescript-language-server

Use TypeScript 6 with this server, per its installation guide. Don't use TypeScript 7.

The lab supplies .github/lsp.json and jsconfig.json. Open copilot from the copied agent-project directory and run:

/lsp show
/lsp test typescript

test starts a temporary server to check startup. You still need to run a real definition/reference lookup in the lab.

docs.title: Python: Session M2-06
docs.text:
Check for pyright-langserver on PATH. If it's missing:

npm install --global pyright

Session M2-06 supplies a project .github/lsp.json with the server name python. Start the CLI in the copied inventory project and run:

/lsp show
/lsp test python

Wait until the application parses and its tests pass before you start the code-navigation exercise.

docs.title: If a check fails
docs.text:
Run /lsp logs to read the error. Check the executable path, project root, and file-extension mapping. Run /lsp reload after you fix the configuration. Text-search output isn't an LSP result: if the server can't start or return the lookup, stop the LSP exercise.

Project configuration applies to its Git repository. These labs use copied projects as separate repositories, so don't put their configuration at the curriculum repository root or overwrite an existing server definition.

See Adding LSP servers.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M3-04 trainer guide: Custom agent boundaries
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text: Start with a profile that enables every tool and permits any needed change. Run the contract, show why a test-only task can drift into production code, tighten the profile, and rerun the same test.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:08 What a custom agent profile controls 0:08 to 0:18 .agent.md structure 0:18 to 0:30 Weak profile and boundary violation 0:30 to 0:43 Least-privilege tools and path rules 0:43 to 0:52 Stop, validation, and human handoff 0:52 to 1:00 Rerun checks and lab handoff

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Open the weak and tightened profiles side by side.
  • Run npm test from lab/starter/agent-project.
  • Keep PROFILE-REFERENCE.md and BOUNDARY-EVIDENCE.md open.
  • Set up the JavaScript LSP server with lab/lsp-setup.md. Check startup and a real getOrdersByUser reference lookup.

docs.title: 0:00 to 0:08: What the profile controls
docs.text:
A profile supplies instructions and filters the tools the agent sees. It doesn't grant repository permissions.

Profile: role, available tools, procedure, stop rules
Environment: actual tool permissions and repository access
Human: accepts, revises, or rejects the result

docs.title: 0:08 to 0:18: Structure
docs.text:
.github/
└── agents/
    └── test-writer.agent.md

Read the frontmatter from PROFILE-REFERENCE.md:

  • description is required;
  • name is optional but useful;
  • target can limit the environment;
  • omitting tools enables all available tools;
  • disable-model-invocation requires deliberate use;
  • user-invocable keeps the profile selectable;
  • metadata can record a synthetic owner and contract version.

The Markdown body tells the agent what it may do and when to stop.

Spend five minutes on tools versus code intelligence. /lsp show lists configured servers and /lsp test typescript checks startup. Neither performs a lookup. Ask for getOrdersByUser references and inspect the LSP call or logs. getUserOrderStats is a caller and the export isn't. Keep this lookup read-only.

docs.title: 0:18 to 0:30: Weak profile
docs.text:
Open weak-test-writer.agent.md:

tools: ["*"]

Its body says to make any changes needed. Run:

npm run check:weak

Use this conflict:

Add tests for updateOrderStatus. Change tests only.
A new criterion allows reversing shipped to processing; the implementation
rejects it.

Nothing makes the profile stop before editing src/. The contract is broken even if one model run happens to stay in bounds.

docs.title: 0:30 to 0:43: Tighten tools and paths
docs.text:
Open test-writer.agent.md:

tools:
  - read
  - search
  - edit
  - execute

The allowlist isn't enough: edit can still touch the wrong file. The body limits edits to tests/ and names forbidden paths.

Rule Where it lives Tool is available Frontmatter Only tests may change Profile body Repository blocks a write Environment or repository policy Change is accepted Human review

docs.title: 0:43 to 0:52: Stop and handoff
docs.text:
Read the production-conflict rule aloud. The correct output names:

  • no files changed;
  • the behavior that conflicts with the criteria;
  • the forbidden production path;
  • the decision a human must make.

Then run npm test. If the command can't run, the profile reports not run rather than success.

docs.title: 0:52 to 1:00: Rerun
docs.text:
npm run check:tight
npm test

The same contract now passes. Load the learner's profile with CLI /agent and run the conflict scenario. You need the actual stop report and unchanged source. A manual trace doesn't count as a live run.

Finish with the extension choice:

Need Use Repository-wide rule Instructions Repeatable procedure Skill Role with a defined scope Custom agent External tools or data MCP

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
1. Show the weak profile.
  2. Run check:weak and read the failed checks.
  3. Trace the production edit the weak wording permits.
  4. Show the tightened frontmatter and body.
  5. Run check:tight and the full tests.
  6. Produce the stop report for the same conflict.
  7. Keep the LSP operation and selected profile in agent-run.md.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating tools: ["*"] as harmless convenience.
  • Naming a role without naming paths.
  • Writing "do not edit source" with no stop and handoff result.
  • Reporting validation as passed when the command didn't run.
  • Assuming the profile grants permission.
  • Adding MCP to a role that doesn't need external data.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text: Learners inspect the structure, run the failing weak profile, tighten it, and rerun the contract. They record a stop report with no source edits. Allow ten minutes for the LSP lookup inside the 25-minute weak-profile block. The lab stays at 120 minutes.

docs.title: Session M3-05: Agent Skills
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Agentic Workflows Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04, M3-04 Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hour lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md file that teaches Copilot one repeatable workflow. Copilot loads it only when your request matches its description.

You learn what skills are and how they differ from instructions, prompt files, custom agents, and MCP servers. Then you write one with the skill-creator skill, test it live in the Copilot CLI, and fix it from what you see. You finish with the pros, cons, and traps of skills.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Explain what a skill is, where it lives, and when Copilot loads it.
  • Choose between a skill, instructions, a prompt file, a custom agent, and an MCP server.
  • Use skill-creator to interview, draft, and revise a skill.
  • Build an interview skill (grill-me) that pressure-tests a plan.
  • Compare skills with custom agents and MCP servers, and pick the right one.
  • Write a description that triggers when it should and stays quiet when it shouldn't.
  • Test a skill live with a matching, a non-matching, and an ambiguous prompt.
  • Judge a skill from someone else before you install it.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
The standalone Copilot CLI from Session M2-01 with skills support, and Git.

Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Starter project lab/starter/release-notes-project/ Reference skill lab/solution/release-notes/SKILL.md Expected output lab/solution/expected-output.md

docs.title: Key topics
docs.text:
• Skill anatomy: SKILL.md, frontmatter, scripts, references
  • Where skills load from: project and personal locations
  • Skills vs instructions, prompt files, custom agents, and MCP
  • Writing the description, the body, and bundled files
  • skill-creator: interview, draft, test prompts
  • Pros, cons, and tips
  • Trusting third-party skills

docs.title: Write one, test it, fix it
docs.text: Session M3-05 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time What a skill is 10 min Skill, agent, or MCP server? 15 min Writing a good skill 10 min Demo: skill-creator 12 min Pros, cons, and tips 8 min Lab handoff 5 min

docs.title: What a skill is
docs.text:
A folder with a SKILL.md file. Copilot loads it when your request matches its description.

.github/skills/release-notes/
├── SKILL.md          # required: frontmatter + instructions
├── references/       # optional: read when needed
└── scripts/          # optional: run, not read
  • Project skills: .github/skills, .claude/skills, .agents/skills
  • Personal skills: ~/.copilot/skills, ~/.agents/skills

An open standard. Works in the CLI, the Copilot app, cloud agent, and IDE agent mode.

docs.title: How Copilot uses one
docs.text:
1. You send a request.
  2. Copilot compares it with each skill's description.
  3. On a match, it loads SKILL.md into context.
  4. It follows the instructions and can use files in the folder.

Or call one yourself: Use the /release-notes skill for this.

The description is the trigger. Get it wrong and nothing else matters.

docs.title: Skill or something else?
docs.text:
Need Use Rule that always applies Repository instructions One saved prompt you run by hand Prompt file A workflow Copilot picks up when relevant Skill A persona with its own tools and scope Custom agent Live access to a system MCP server

Rule of thumb: instructions are always on. Skills load on demand.

docs.title: Skill vs custom agent vs MCP server
docs.text:
Skill Custom agent MCP server Gives Copilot Know-how A role Reach Is Markdown, plus optional files Markdown with tools and model A running server Loads On demand When picked or delegated When configured Risk Wrong trigger Too many tools Credentials, data

They combine. An agent can use skills. A skill can teach Copilot to use an MCP server well.

docs.title: Example: grill-me
docs.text:
A skill that interviews you about a plan.

  • Reads your file first, so it doesn't ask what you already wrote.
  • One question at a time, with a recommended answer.
  • Stops when a colleague could build from the plan.
  • Ends with decisions and open questions.

Not every skill makes a file. Some change how Copilot works with you.

docs.title: More examples
docs.text: Skill What it does release-notes Writes changelog entries in your format. grill-me Interviews you before you plan. skill-creator Helps you write and test skills. pdf, docx, xlsx Bundle scripts that read and write files.

docs.title: Frontmatter
docs.text:
---
name: release-notes
description: Write release notes or a CHANGELOG entry from merged PRs.
  Use when the user asks for release notes, a changelog entry, or
  "what shipped". Don't use for commit messages or PR descriptions.
---
  • name: lowercase with hyphens, same as the directory
  • description: what it does and when to use it
  • Optional: license, allowed-tools

docs.title: Write the description
docs.text:
Weak: Helps with releases.

Better: says what, when, and when not.

  • List the words people actually use.
  • Add a "Don't use for…" line next to look-alike tasks.
  • Be a little pushy. Skills tend to undertrigger.

docs.title: Write the body
docs.text:
• Use imperative steps: "Read the top two entries."
  • Explain why a rule matters. The model generalizes better from reasons than from shouting.
  • Show a short example of the output.
  • Say what to do when input is missing: ask.
  • Keep SKILL.md short. Move long templates to references/.

docs.title: Bundle files
docs.text:
SKILL.md        → "Group PRs using references/format.md"
references/    → loaded only when the step needs it
scripts/        → run for deterministic work

Scripts need allowed-tools to run without a prompt. Don't pre-approve shell unless you've read every script and trust the source.

docs.title: skill-creator
docs.text:
A skill that helps you write skills.

  1. Interviews you: purpose, triggers, output, edge cases.
  2. Drafts SKILL.md and bundled files.
  3. Suggests test prompts.
  4. Revises from what you saw.

Its eval and description-optimizer scripts call the claude CLI. Skip them. Test by hand.

docs.title: Pros
docs.text:
• Repeatable: same workflow every time.
  • On demand: loaded only when relevant, unlike always-on instructions.
  • Shareable: commit it, review it, version it.
  • Portable: an open standard across Copilot surfaces.
  • Bundles files: templates, references, scripts.

docs.title: Cons
docs.text:
• Triggering is probabilistic. It can miss or misfire.
  • Failures are quiet. No error when it doesn't load.
  • Skills collide. Overlapping descriptions confuse selection.
  • They go stale like any doc.
  • Third-party skills are code. Scripts can run.
  • Support differs by surface. Check yours.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Start from a real task you've done by hand.
  • Test three prompts: should trigger, shouldn't, ambiguous.
  • Run each twice. Variance is normal.
  • Fix one thing at a time, then rerun.
  • If it's one always-on rule, write instructions instead.
  • Delete skills nobody uses.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
1. Run a baseline with no skill.
  2. Install skill-creator.
  3. Create release-notes with it.
  4. Test three prompts live.
  5. Fix what failed.
  6. Build grill-me and interview yourself about idea.md.
  7. Decide: skill, custom agent, or MCP server?
  8. Review one third-party skill.

Submit your test results, both skills, and decisions.md.

docs.title: Session M3-05 lab: Write, test, and fix a skill
docs.text: Duration: 2 hours Deliverable: A working release-notes skill, your live test results, and an interview skill, and a decision table

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
Your team writes changelog entries by hand and each one looks different. You will write a skill that produces them in the project's format, using skill-creator to do most of the drafting.

Part Work Time 1 Baseline: no skill 10 min 2 Install skill-creator 10 min 3 Create the skill 25 min 4 Test it live 20 min 5 Fix it 15 min 6 Example: an interview skill 25 min 7 Skill, custom agent, or MCP server? 10 min 8 Review a third-party skill 5 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need Git and the standalone Copilot CLI from Session M2-01 with skills support. Use the synthetic project in this lab.

mkdir -p ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-05
cp -R sessions/session-m3-05-agent-skills-ecosystem/lab/starter/release-notes-project \
  ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-05/
cd ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-05/release-notes-project
git init -q && git add -A && git commit -qm "Start"

The project has three files: CHANGELOG.md with the team's format, merged-prs.md with PRs merged since the last release, and idea.md, a rough plan you will use in Part 6.

docs.title: Part 1: Baseline without a skill
docs.text:
Start copilot in the project and ask:

Write release notes for the PRs in merged-prs.md.

Save the answer as baseline.md. Compare it with the entries in CHANGELOG.md.

Checkpoint: You can name at least two differences, such as missing sections, internal PRs included, or a different tone.

docs.title: Part 2: Install skill-creator
docs.text:
skill-creator is a skill that helps you write skills. It lives in anthropics/skills.

git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/anthropics/skills ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-05/skills
mkdir -p ~/.copilot/skills
cp -R ~/copilot-labs/session-m3-05/skills/skills/skill-creator ~/.copilot/skills/

Restart copilot, or run /skills reload. Then run:

/skills info skill-creator

You should see its description and location. A skill in ~/.copilot/skills is personal: it works in every project.

Read the first 60 lines of its SKILL.md before you use it. Note how it tells Copilot to work: interview first, then draft, then test.

docs.title: Part 3: Create the skill
docs.text:
Ask Copilot to use it. Keep the request short and let skill-creator interview you:

Use /skill-creator to create a project skill called release-notes in
.github/skills/. It should turn a list of merged PRs into a changelog entry
in this project's format.

Answer its questions with these facts:

  • The entry matches the top entries of CHANGELOG.md.
  • Group PRs by label. Leave out chores, dependency bumps, and docs typos.
  • Breaking changes go under Upgrade notes.
  • If the version or date is missing, ask for it.
  • It must not trigger for commit messages or PR descriptions.

When skill-creator offers formal evals, decline. Its eval and description-optimizer scripts call the claude CLI, which you don't use here. You will test by hand in Part 4.

Read what it wrote.

.github/skills/release-notes/
├── SKILL.md
└── references/format.md      # may differ

Checkpoint: SKILL.md starts with name and description frontmatter. The directory name matches name. Compare it with solution/release-notes/SKILL.md.

docs.title: Part 4: Test it live
docs.text:
Run /skills reload, then /skills info release-notes. Start a fresh session. Try three prompts and note what happens for each:

# Prompt You expect 1 Write release notes for the PRs in merged-prs.md. Version 2.4.0, dated 2026-10-21. The skill loads. The entry matches the format. 2 Write a commit message for the CSV export change. The skill stays out. 3 What changed recently? Unclear. Record what you see.

Also try naming the skill: Use the /release-notes skill for merged-prs.md.

Skill selection can vary between runs. Run prompt 1 twice. Record whether it loaded both times.

Compare prompt 1 with solution/expected-output.md.

Checkpoint: You have a result for each prompt and know which ones the skill got wrong.

docs.title: Part 5: Fix it
docs.text:
Use what you saw in Part 4. Fix one problem at a time and rerun the failing prompt.

Symptom Likely cause Fix Skill didn't load for prompt 1 Description lacks the words you used Add trigger phrases: "release notes", "changelog entry", "what shipped" Skill loaded for prompt 2 Description is too broad Add "Don't use for commit messages or PR descriptions" Output ignores a rule Rule is buried or vague Move it up, state it as an instruction, and say why it matters SKILL.md is long Everything is in one file Move the entry template to references/format.md and link it from SKILL.md Skill invents a version No "ask first" rule Add one

You can ask skill-creator to apply a fix, or edit the file yourself. Run /skills reload after each change.

Checkpoint: Prompts 1 and 2 behave as expected on two runs each. Save the final skill under .github/skills/release-notes/.

docs.title: Part 6: Example: an interview skill
docs.text:
Not every skill produces a file. Some change how Copilot works with you. A popular example is grill-me: you give Copilot a rough plan, and it interviews you until the gaps are gone.

  1. Ask skill-creator:

Create a skill called grill-me. When I share a plan or idea, it should interview me one question at a time, recommend an answer for each question, and finish with a summary of decisions and open questions.

  1. Save it under .github/skills/grill-me/ and run /skills reload.
  2. Start a fresh session and run: Grill me on idea.md.
  3. Answer at least eight questions. Notice that Copilot reads idea.md first and doesn't ask what the file already says.
  4. Compare your skill with solution/grill-me/SKILL.md. Which instructions did yours miss?

Then try the same idea without the skill: Review idea.md and tell me what's missing. Copilot will probably return a list of gaps. Compare the two experiences.

Why a skill works here. The interview rules ("one question at a time", "recommend an answer", "stop when a colleague could build it") are exactly the kind of instruction you forget to type. The skill stores them. Use the same pattern for design reviews, incident retros, or a spec before you start a /plan.

Checkpoint: You have a working grill-me skill and a summary from your interview of idea.md.

docs.title: Part 7: Skill, custom agent, or MCP server?
docs.text:
A skill, a custom agent, and an MCP server solve different problems. Sessions M3-03 and M3-04 cover MCP servers and custom agents in depth.

Skill Custom agent MCP server What it is Instructions, plus optional scripts and files A persona with its own prompt, tools, and model A process that exposes tools and data Gives Copilot Know-how: how to do a task A role: who is doing the task Reach: access to a system Loads On demand, when the description matches When you pick it or Copilot delegates When the server is configured Needs code? No, a Markdown file No, a Markdown file Yes, a server Main risk Triggers at the wrong time Too much tool access Credentials and data leaving the machine

They combine. A custom agent can use skills. A skill can tell Copilot how to use an MCP server's tools well.

For each task, choose the best home: repository instructions, a skill, a prompt file, a custom agent, an MCP server, or nothing. Write one sentence for each choice in decisions.md.

Task Your choice "Use 2-space indentation in this repo." Produce release notes in the team format when asked. Query the issue tracker for open bugs. A reviewer persona with read-only tools. A one-off question about a stack trace. A weekly report that always starts from the same template and script. Interview me about a plan before I write a spec.

Compare with a neighbor and discuss where you differ.

docs.title: Part 8: Review a third-party skill
docs.text:
Open github/awesome-copilot skills and pick one skill. Read its SKILL.md and any scripts. Answer in decisions.md:

  • What does the description promise?
  • Does it run scripts or ask for allowed-tools? Would you approve that?
  • Would you install it? Why or why not?

Don't install it into this project.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. .github/skills/release-notes/SKILL.md and any bundled files.
  2. .github/skills/grill-me/SKILL.md and your interview summary for idea.md.
  3. Your prompt 1, 2, and 3 results, plus what you changed to fix them.
  4. decisions.md with the seven choices and your third-party review.
