docs.title: Session M3-05 trainer guide: Agent Skills
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Teaching goal
docs.text: Learners leave knowing what a skill is, when to write one, how to write one with skill-creator, and what can go wrong.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:10 What a skill is 0:10 to 0:25 Skill, agent, or MCP server? 0:25 to 0:35 Writing a good skill 0:35 to 0:47 Demo: skill-creator 0:47 to 0:55 Pros, cons, and tips 0:55 to 1:00 Lab handoff

docs.title: Preparation
docs.text:
• Install skill-creator in ~/.copilot/skills (see lab Part 2) and run /skills info skill-creator.
  • Copy the starter project to a scratch folder and run the lab once. Keep the reference skill in lab/solution/release-notes/ open for comparison.
  • Pick a second demo task you can finish in 10 minutes (a commit-message or PR-template skill works).

docs.title: What a skill is (0:00 to 0:10)
docs.text:
• A skill is a folder. SKILL.md is required and must be named exactly that.
  • Frontmatter needs name and description. name is lowercase with hyphens and matches the directory.
  • Project skills live in .github/skills, .claude/skills, or .agents/skills. Personal skills live in ~/.copilot/skills or ~/.agents/skills.
  • Copilot picks a skill from the description. It then loads SKILL.md and can use other files in the folder. You can also name it: Use the /name skill.
  • It's an open standard used by several tools. Support differs by surface. Check the docs for the one you teach on.

Show: /skills list, /skills info <name>, /skills reload.

docs.title: Skill, agent, or MCP server? (0:10 to 0:25)
docs.text:
Ask the room to sort five tasks, then reveal the table.

Need Use Rule that always applies Repository instructions One saved prompt you run by hand Prompt file Workflow Copilot should pick up when relevant Skill Persona with its own tools and scope Custom agent Live access to a system MCP server

Key line: instructions are always on, skills load on demand.

Skill vs custom agent vs MCP server. Use one sentence each: a skill gives Copilot know-how, a custom agent gives it a role, an MCP server gives it reach. Link back to M3-03 (MCP) and M3-04 (custom agents) rather than re-teaching them. Stress that they combine: an agent can load skills, and a skill can describe how to use an MCP server's tools.

Example: grill-me. Show the slide, then run it live on idea.md: Grill me on idea.md. Let it ask three questions, answer them, and stop. Point out that it reads the file first and recommends an answer. The takeaway: skills can shape how you work with Copilot, not only what it produces. The finished skill is in lab/solution/grill-me/SKILL.md.

Answer key for lab Part 7:

Task Best home 2-space indentation Instructions: always applies Release notes in team format Skill Query issue tracker for open bugs MCP server Read-only reviewer persona Custom agent One-off stack trace question Nothing Weekly report from template and script Skill, with the script bundled Interview me about a plan Skill (grill-me). A custom agent also works if you want a fixed persona with restricted tools.

Accept other answers if the reasoning holds. Prompt file is a fair answer for the release notes if the team runs it by hand every time.

docs.title: Writing a good skill (0:20 to 0:32)
docs.text:
Description. It decides whether the skill loads. - Say what it does and when to use it. - List the words people actually say. - Add "Don't use for…" for look-alike tasks. - Skills tend to undertrigger, so lean specific and a bit pushy.

Show a weak and a better description side by side.

Body. - Imperative steps. - A reason for each non-obvious rule. - A short output example. - An "ask if missing" rule instead of guessing. - Keep it short. Move long templates to references/ and link them.

Scripts and tools. Files in the skill folder are available to Copilot. allowed-tools pre-approves tools. Warn that pre-approving shell removes the confirmation step, so only do it after reading every script and trusting its source.

docs.title: Demo: skill-creator (0:32 to 0:44)
docs.text:
Build your second demo skill live. Narrate the loop.

  1. Prompt: Use /skill-creator to create a project skill called <name> in .github/skills/.
  2. Let it interview you. Answer in one line each.
  3. Decline formal evals. Its eval and description-optimizer scripts call the claude CLI.
  4. Read the draft out loud. Point at the description.
  5. /skills reload, then test one matching and one non-matching prompt.
  6. If it misfires, change the description and retest.

Say what you'd edit by hand. The tool drafts; you own the result.

docs.title: Pros, cons, and tips (0:44 to 0:54)
docs.text:
Pros: repeatable, loaded on demand, shareable through git, portable across surfaces, can bundle templates and scripts.

Cons: - Triggering is probabilistic and can miss or misfire. - Failures are quiet. Nothing errors when it doesn't load. - Overlapping descriptions collide. - Skills go stale. - Third-party skills can run scripts. - Support differs by surface.

Tips: - Start from a task you've done by hand. - Test three prompts: should trigger, shouldn't, ambiguous. Run each twice. - Fix one thing at a time. - If it's one always-on rule, write instructions instead. - Delete skills nobody uses.

docs.title: Lab handoff (0:54 to 1:00)
docs.text: Open lab/README.md. Walk through the seven parts. Tell learners to run the baseline first so they can see what the skill changes.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text: Mistake Fix Directory name differs from name Make them match File is skill.md or Skill.md Rename to SKILL.md Skill doesn't show up /skills reload, then /skills info <name> Description is "helps with X" Add triggers and a "don't use for" line Everything in one long SKILL.md Move templates to references/ Learner tries the skill-creator eval scripts Skip them. Test by hand

docs.title: Session M4-01: GitHub Actions & workflow generation
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: DevOps & Infrastructure with Copilot Difficulty: Intermediate Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-02 Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content + 2 hours lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You use one Node.js application, copilot-webapp, for four workflow tasks: create CI, design a staged deployment, repair broken workflow files, and validate a local JavaScript action. Every decision traces back to the same scripts, tests, build output, and health endpoint.

Submit your workflow files. At each checkpoint, record the command, the result, and the file that changed.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Generate CI from repository facts and check it with local commands.
  • Design staging and production jobs without a live deployment.
  • Repair workflow syntax and behavior from exact failures.
  • Validate a JavaScript action against the application with pass and fail cases.
  • Review triggers, permissions, secrets, artifacts, and deployment gates.

docs.title: You need
docs.text:
Node.js 20 or later and GitHub Copilot. Repository and GitHub Actions access are optional: the lab runs on local tests and YAML parsing.

Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Application starter lab/starter/webapp/ Reference workflows and action lab/solution/

docs.title: DevOps & infrastructure | Intermediate
docs.text: Session M4-01 | 3 hours

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Time Topic 0:00 to 0:08 Baseline and Actions model 0:08 to 0:18 Generate CI 0:18 to 0:28 Design deployment 0:28 to 0:40 Repair workflow failures 0:40 to 0:52 Validate a JavaScript action 0:52 to 1:00 Review and lab handoff

docs.title: Start with repository facts
docs.text:
copilot-webapp already defines the contract:

npm ci
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
test -f dist/app.js

The workflow calls these commands. It doesn't invent another build, artifact path, or runtime.

docs.title: A workflow is code with an execution boundary
docs.text: Review Question Trigger Who can cause this code to run? Runner Which tools and trust boundary apply? Permissions What can the token read or change? Commands Do they exist in the repository? Artifacts Which files leave the job? Environment Which approval gate applies?

docs.title: Generate CI from the application
docs.text:
Read package.json, tests, and scripts/build.js. Create ci.yml for pull requests
and pushes to main. Use Node.js 20, npm ci, existing lint, test, and build scripts,
npm caching, contents: read, and a seven-day dist artifact.

Then check YAML syntax and application behavior:

ruby -e 'require "yaml"; Psych.parse_stream(File.read(ARGV[0]))' ci.yml
npm test && npm run lint && npm run build

docs.title: Deployment stays a design exercise
docs.text:
build → staging → production

The workflow references environments and secrets. Production reviewers are set in repository settings. Placeholder commands must not imply a deployment ran.

docs.title: Syntax and behavior fail differently
docs.text:
broken-ci.yml doesn't parse.

broken-deploy.yml parses but has a stale runner, a bad Git ref, a wrong secret name, and no checkout.

Get the failed-step output before the repair.

docs.title: Tie each repair to a failure
docs.text:
Observation: the parser fails near Setup Node.js.
Change: align the step indentation.
Proof: parse the file again.

For behavior faults, cite the deployment spec or repository facts, then check the repair.

docs.title: Validate both action outcomes
docs.text:
env INPUT_THRESHOLD=0 ... node src/main.js
env INPUT_THRESHOLD=101 ... node src/main.js

The first run passes and writes a summary. The second exits with code 1.

One successful run doesn't show the action enforces the threshold.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Create CI, design deployment, repair failures, and validate the action against copilot-webapp.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M4-01 lab: One application, four workflow tasks
docs.text: Deliverable: Workflows, command output, and review notes for copilot-webapp

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You use the same application for every part.

Part Work Time 1 Check the application baseline and create CI 30 min 2 Design staged deployment jobs 25 min 3 Repair two supplied workflow failures 30 min 4 Validate a JavaScript action 25 min 5 Collect command results and review notes 10 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need GitHub Copilot and Node.js 20 or later. Repository access is optional. Unless the instructor says otherwise, don't push, run Actions, install an external action, or use a deployment target. Everything here runs locally. Use no real credentials or deployment endpoints.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Run commands from this session directory unless a command changes directory.

node --version
cd lab/starter/webapp
npm ci
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
test -f dist/app.js
cd ../../..

Expected: Node 20 or later, seven passing tests, lint and build succeed, and dist/app.js exists.

Create lab/evidence.md from this table:

Checkpoint Command or review Result Changed files Reviewer Baseline CI Deployment design Workflow repair Custom action

docs.title: Part 1: Create CI
docs.text:
Ask Copilot to read lab/starter/webapp/package.json, the tests, and the build script. Create lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/ci.yml with:

  • pushes to main and pull requests;
  • ubuntu-latest and Node.js 20;
  • npm ci, lint, tests, and build;
  • npm caching;
  • permissions: contents: read;
  • the dist/ build artifact with seven-day retention.

Rerun the application checks:

cd lab/starter/webapp
npm ci
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
test -f dist/app.js
cd ../../..

Validate the workflow syntax:

ruby -e 'require "yaml"; Psych.parse_stream(File.read(ARGV[0]))' \
  lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/ci.yml

Review the generated commands against package.json. Compare with lab/solution/webapp/.github/workflows/ci.yml.

Checkpoint: Record both results and explain why the workflow uploads dist/ and not a path the assistant invented.

docs.title: Part 2: Design deployment
docs.text:
Read lab/starter/deployment-spec.md. Create lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/cd.yml. It must build the same application, deploy to staging before production, reference GitHub Environments and secrets, run two health checks, and describe rollback without calling a real endpoint.

ruby -e 'require "yaml"; Psych.parse_stream(File.read(ARGV[0]))' \
  lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/cd.yml
grep -nE 'environment: (staging|production)|needs:|permissions:' \
  lab/starter/webapp/.github/workflows/cd.yml

Expected: the YAML parses, and the output shows both environments, job ordering, and a permissions block.

Compare with lab/solution/workflows/cd.yml. Repository settings configure production reviewers. The workflow only references the production environment.

Checkpoint: Record the secret names, the production gate, the health-check behavior, and the rollback steps. No deployment occurred.

docs.title: Part 3: Repair workflow failures
docs.text:
Both broken workflows target copilot-webapp.

Run the parser on the CI file:

ruby -e 'require "yaml"; Psych.parse_stream(File.read(ARGV[0]))' \
  lab/starter/broken-workflows/broken-ci.yml

Expected failure: an indentation error near Setup Node.js. Fix the indentation, update the checkout action, add least-privilege permissions, and use the package command meant for CI. Parse again and compare with lab/solution/fixed-workflows/fixed-ci.yml.

The deployment workflow parses, but its behavior is wrong:

ruby -e 'require "yaml"; Psych.parse_stream(File.read(ARGV[0]))' \
  lab/starter/broken-workflows/broken-deploy.yml
grep -nE 'ubuntu-18.04|refs/head/main|DEPLOY_KEY|checkout' \
  lab/starter/broken-workflows/broken-deploy.yml

Parsing succeeds. The grep exposes the stale runner, bad ref, wrong secret name, and missing checkout step. Repair them, parse again, and compare with the solution.

Checkpoint: For each change, cite the failure or repository fact behind it. Reject a broad rewrite unless each change answers a recorded failure.

docs.title: Part 4: Validate the custom action
docs.text:
Complete the metadata and implementation in lab/starter/custom-action/. The action scans the same application.

Copy the dependency manifests into your action directory, install, and check against the application:

cp lab/solution/custom-action/package.json \
  lab/solution/custom-action/package-lock.json lab/starter/custom-action/
npm ci --prefix lab/starter/custom-action
cd lab/starter/webapp
: > ../custom-action/summary.md
env INPUT_THRESHOLD=0 'INPUT_REPORT-FORMAT=markdown' \
  GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY="$PWD/../custom-action/summary.md" \
  node ../custom-action/src/main.js
test -s ../custom-action/summary.md
cd ../../..

Expected: passed: true, exit code 0, and a written summary.

Now the intentional failure:

cd lab/starter/webapp
action_status=0
env INPUT_THRESHOLD=101 'INPUT_REPORT-FORMAT=json' \
  node ../custom-action/src/main.js || action_status=$?
printf 'Action exit code: %s\n' "$action_status"
test "$action_status" -eq 1
cd ../../..

Expected: the action reports a score below 101 and exits with code 1. The threshold changes the result.

After your checks pass, compare with lab/solution/custom-action/. If act is installed, you can run this reference-only demo. It doesn't validate your action:

act -W lab/solution/custom-action/.github/workflows/quality-check.yml -j quality-check

Checkpoint: Record the pass and fail exit codes, score, scanned path, outputs, and summary location.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. CI and deployment workflow files for copilot-webapp.
  2. Both repaired workflow files, with explanations tied to the recorded failures.
  3. The completed JavaScript action.
  4. lab/evidence.md with commands, results, changed files, and reviewer decisions.

Local syntax checks don't show that a production deployment is safe.

docs.text:
Time Segment 0:00 to 0:08 Application baseline and Actions model 0:08 to 0:18 Generate CI from repository facts 0:18 to 0:28 Design staging and production jobs 0:28 to 0:40 Diagnose workflow failures 0:40 to 0:52 Validate a JavaScript action 0:52 to 1:00 Security review and lab handoff

The timings match slides.md. Stop a live tool response at the end of its segment and use the prepared solution.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
• Run the application tests, lint, and build.
  • Keep the supplied broken workflows unchanged.
  • Install the solution action dependencies.
  • Prepare one passing threshold and the threshold-101 failure.
  • Don't configure a deployment target.

docs.title: 0:00 to 0:08: Baseline and model
docs.text:
cd lab/starter/webapp
npm ci
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
test -f dist/app.js

Tie each workflow step to a repository fact. npm test, npm run lint, and npm run build exist because package.json defines them. dist/ is valid because the build creates it.

docs.title: 0:08 to 0:18: Generate CI
docs.text:
Read package.json, tests, and scripts/build.js in copilot-webapp. Create ci.yml
for pull requests and pushes to main. Use Node.js 20, npm ci, the existing lint,
test, and build scripts, npm caching, contents: read, and a seven-day dist artifact.
Do not add dependencies or deployment steps.

Parse the YAML, then rerun the local checks. A valid workflow can still call a missing script or upload a path that doesn't exist.

docs.title: 0:18 to 0:28: Deployment design
docs.text:
Open lab/starter/deployment-spec.md. Ask learners to find the trigger, environments, secret names, health checks, and rollback rule before generating YAML.

Review the design without deploying it. Repository settings enforce production reviewers, and the endpoints are placeholders.

docs.title: 0:28 to 0:40: Diagnose failures
docs.text:
Run the YAML parser against broken-ci.yml and let it reveal the first fault. After learners fix it, inspect action versions, permissions, and package commands.

broken-deploy.yml parses. Use the lab's grep command to separate syntax from behavior. Each repair needs a source: platform support, the deployment spec, the Git ref format, or the checkout requirement.

docs.title: 0:40 to 0:52: Validate the action
docs.text:
A custom action needs two outcomes. A passing run shows it can scan the application and emit outputs. The threshold-101 run shows it can fail the job.

Run the lab's commands. Show the step summary and exit code. A repository workflow run alone isn't enough.

docs.title: 0:52 to 1:00: Review and handoff
docs.text:
Review:

  • triggers and token permissions;
  • action references;
  • secret references and environment gates;
  • artifact contents and retention.

Point learners to lab/evidence.md. Their workflow files and action should agree with the command results.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Valid YAML only proves the file parses. Run the application commands and review what the workflow does.

Why one application? Learners use the same repository facts for each decision instead of rebuilding a project per exercise.

Why test an action failure? An action that always exits successfully hasn't shown it enforces the threshold.

docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: DevOps & Infrastructure with Copilot Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-02, M4-01 Duration: 2 hours 30 minutes (1 hour trainer content + 1 hour 30 minutes lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
You use Terraform to build one modular infrastructure project. Connect the network, compute, and database modules and validate each stage. Then repair a supplied configuration that fails the local security gate.

Bicep is a trainer comparison and optional extension, not a learner deliverable.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Generate Terraform modules from fixed architecture constraints.
  • Connect module inputs and outputs without copying values between layers.
  • Run formatting, initialization, validation, and a local security gate in order.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need GitHub Copilot and Terraform 1.5 or later with the provider source. No cloud account, credentials, state backend, plan, or apply.

terraform version
terraform fmt -check -recursive lab/starter/terraform

docs.title: Part 1: Read the module contract
docs.text:
Open lab/starter/terraform/. Keep the supplied architecture:

  • VPC 10.0.0.0/16;
  • two public, two private application, and two private database subnets;
  • an internet-facing load balancer;
  • private application instances;
  • an encrypted, private PostgreSQL database;
  • database ingress only from the application security group.

Checkpoint: List the root inputs and the outputs that connect network to compute and compute to database.

docs.title: Part 2: Build and connect the modules
docs.text:
Create the missing module files:

modules/network/
modules/compute/
modules/database/

Use typed variables and narrow outputs. Keep the database password sensitive. Compare with lab/solution/terraform/ only after your first draft.

terraform fmt -check -recursive lab/starter/terraform

The supplied files pass. If your generated files fail, run terraform fmt -recursive lab/starter/terraform and check again.

Checkpoint: Record the format result and any files Terraform changed.

docs.title: Part 3: Initialize and validate
docs.text:
terraform -chdir=lab/starter/terraform init -backend=false
terraform -chdir=lab/starter/terraform validate

Expected: initialization downloads the provider and validation reports Success! The configuration is valid.

If validation fails, fix the first reported module contract error and rerun. Don't add provider credentials to make it pass.

Checkpoint: Record the provider version, the validation result, and any contract error you repaired.

docs.title: Part 4: Investigate the intentional security failure
docs.text:
bash lab/starter/check-security.sh lab/starter/insecure-iac/main.tf

Expected failure: exit code 1, with findings such as public access, a hardcoded password, wildcard IAM access, missing database encryption, or missing load-balancer logging.

Repair lab/starter/insecure-iac/main.tf before opening the solution. Use the architecture to address the findings, then check:

bash lab/starter/check-security.sh lab/starter/insecure-iac/main.tf
terraform fmt lab/starter/insecure-iac/main.tf
terraform fmt -check lab/starter/insecure-iac/main.tf
terraform -chdir=lab/starter/insecure-iac init -backend=false
terraform -chdir=lab/starter/insecure-iac validate

Expected: the security gate and Terraform validation pass. Then compare with lab/solution/secure-iac/main.tf.

Checkpoint: Record the failing exit code, each cited line, the repaired file, and the passing rerun. Passing this gate doesn't mean the configuration is safe to deploy.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
• Run terraform fmt -check -recursive on the solution.
  • Initialize it with -backend=false and run terraform validate.
  • Run the security gate once against the insecure file and once against the fix.

docs.title: Architecture and module contracts
docs.text:
Use the supplied three-tier design. Trace address space and subnets through the network module. Show how compute uses subnet IDs and exposes the application security group, then how the database uses that group and its private subnets.

Ask learners to state each boundary before generating code. A module pays off when callers depend on a small, stable interface.

docs.title: Root composition
docs.text:
Read the Terraform root module and architecture constraints. Complete the network,
compute, and database module contracts. Pass values through typed variables and
outputs. Keep the database password sensitive. Do not add credentials, a backend,
plan, or apply command.

Inspect every added input and output. Reject duplicated CIDRs or values copied between modules when an output should carry them.

docs.title: Staged validation
docs.text:
terraform fmt -check -recursive
terraform init -backend=false
terraform validate

Formatting catches style drift. Initialization resolves providers and modules. Validation checks the configuration against the installed provider schema. None of them compares the configuration with a cloud environment.

Skip terraform plan in this session. A plan needs an identity, a target environment, a backend decision, and human review.

docs.title: Intentional security failure
docs.text:
bash lab/starter/check-security.sh lab/starter/insecure-iac/main.tf

Let learners read the output before you show the solution. The gate fails. Each repair must connect a reported pattern to the architecture or a security rule.

Rerun the gate and terraform validate on the repaired file, then compare with lab/solution/secure-iac/main.tf.

docs.title: Bicep comparison
docs.text: Spend six minutes on the prepared Bicep module calls, the @secure() parameter, and outputs. Learners don't build a second project.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text: Learners have 90 minutes to complete the modules, run the staged checks, and investigate the security failure. They submit command output.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Why no plan? There's no cloud target or identity. Local validation covers the learning goal.

Why keep Bicep a comparison? It shows the module and validation ideas transfer without doubling the work.

Does the security script replace policy tooling? No. It's a deterministic training gate for the supplied failure.

docs.text:
You debug CI/CD failures from workflow files, failed-step output, and local checks. Record an observation and a hypothesis before you open a reference fix. One case has a second failure that appears only after the first repair.

The security exercise uses a deliberately vulnerable training app. Review the smallest patch locally.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Separate observations, hypotheses, repairs, and check results.
  • Reproduce pipeline commands locally.
  • Handle a second-stage failure without stacking speculative fixes.
  • Review a security patch for scope and focused protection.

docs.text:
Observation:
Local proof:
Hypothesis:
Smallest repair:

Keep the root-cause answer out of the observation field.

docs.title: Check the application first
docs.text:
npm ci
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
test -f dist/index.js

If these pass locally, the workflow may still use the wrong runtime, directory, environment, or job order.

docs.title: Give Copilot the workflow and failed-step output
docs.text:
Read this workflow and failed-step output. Separate observations from hypotheses.
Use the local command as additional evidence. Propose the smallest repair and one
proof command. Do not change unrelated jobs.

Check every claim against the files.

docs.title: Investigate before you open the answer
docs.text:
1. Read the failed step.
  2. Record the exact log output.
  3. Reproduce the relevant command.
  4. State one hypothesis.
  5. Repair one cause.
  6. Check the rerun.
  7. Open the reference fix.

docs.title: One failure can hide another
docs.text:
first failed stage
        ↓ repair
next workflow run
        ↓
new failed stage

Diagnose the next failure from the new log. Keep the repair you already checked and avoid speculative changes.

docs.title: Check the affected code path
docs.text:
For each finding, identify:

  • input source;
  • dangerous sink;
  • expected protection;
  • focused test results.

No scanner findings isn't enough.

docs.title: Session M4-03 lab: Debug pipelines from logs and local checks
docs.text: Deliverable: Three investigation records, fixed workflows, and a reviewed security patch

docs.title: Lab overview
docs.text:
You investigate three pipeline failures, review a security repair, and speed up feedback without removing checks.

Part Work Time 0 Check the local application baseline 10 min 1 Investigate three pipeline cases 50 min 2 Review a security remediation 30 min 3 Improve feedback speed 20 min 4 Collect investigation records 10 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need GitHub Copilot and Node.js 20.x. Use only the supplied application, logs, and workflow files. Remote workflow runs and security products are optional.

Don't open lab/solution/fixed-pipelines/ until a checkpoint says to compare. For Case 3, don't open error-log-3-stage-2.txt until the first repair is done.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Run commands from this session directory unless a command changes directory.

cd lab/starter/pipeline-app
npm ci
npm test
npm run lint
npm run build
test -f dist/index.js
cd ../../..

Expected: install, tests, lint, and build pass.

Create one investigation record per case:

Field Record Failed job and step Exact observation Local proof command Hypothesis Smallest repair Proof after repair

docs.title: Part 1: Investigate the pipeline cases
docs.text:
For every case:

  1. Read the workflow and failed-step output.
  2. Record observations without naming a root cause.
  3. Run the local command and record its result.
  4. State one hypothesis.
  5. Ask Copilot to challenge the hypothesis and propose the smallest repair.
  6. Validate the repaired YAML.
  7. Compare with the solution only after the checkpoint.
Read this workflow and failed-step output. Separate observations from hypotheses.
Use the supplied local command as additional evidence. Propose the smallest repair
and one proof command. Do not change unrelated jobs.

docs.title: Case 1
docs.text:
Open pipeline-1.yml and error-log-1.txt.

node --version
cd lab/starter/pipeline-app
npm pkg get engines.node
npm test
cd ../../..

Record what the log and package metadata say. Edit only after your hypothesis explains both. After the repair:

ruby -e 'require "yaml"; Psych.parse_stream(File.read(ARGV[0]))' \
  lab/starter/failing-pipelines/pipeline-1.yml

Checkpoint: Record the parser result, then compare with lab/solution/fixed-pipelines/pipeline-1.yml.

docs.title: Case 2
docs.text:
Open pipeline-2.yml and error-log-2.txt. Run the failing command from the workflow location:

npm ci

Expected failure: npm can't find the project package metadata in the session root. Now run it in the application directory:

npm --prefix lab/starter/pipeline-app ci
npm --prefix lab/starter/pipeline-app test

After the repair, parse the YAML and compare with the solution.

Checkpoint: Explain why changing dependency resolution wouldn't fix the observed path failure.

docs.title: Case 3: multi-stage failure
docs.text:
Open pipeline-3.yml and error-log-3.txt. Investigate only the first failed stage.

cd lab/starter/pipeline-app
npm pkg get engines.node
npm ci
npm test
cd ../../..

Repair the first failure and parse the workflow. Then open error-log-3-stage-2.txt, the next run after the first repair.

Use the new log. Don't undo the first change or add unrelated fixes. After the second repair:

ruby -e 'require "yaml"; Psych.parse_stream(File.read(ARGV[0]))' \
  lab/starter/failing-pipelines/pipeline-3.yml
npm --prefix lab/starter/pipeline-app run build
test -f lab/starter/pipeline-app/dist/index.js

Checkpoint: Record two observations, two repairs, and separate check results for each stage. Then compare with lab/solution/fixed-pipelines/pipeline-3.yml.

docs.title: Part 2: Review a security remediation
docs.text:
Open lab/starter/vulnerable-app/src/app.js and check its syntax:

node --check lab/starter/vulnerable-app/src/app.js

Complete the CodeQL workflow template. If you have a remote scan, inspect its findings. Otherwise use the source as the finding context.

Investigate these sinks without opening the secure solution:

  • SQL query construction;
  • HTML response construction;
  • file path resolution.

Ask for one repair at a time in lab/starter/vulnerable-app/src/app.js and review each diff. Copy only the test harness and dependency manifests, not the solution source:

mkdir -p lab/starter/vulnerable-app/test
cp lab/solution/secure-app/package.json lab/solution/secure-app/package-lock.json \
  lab/starter/vulnerable-app/
cp lab/solution/secure-app/test/security.test.js \
  lab/starter/vulnerable-app/test/
node --check lab/starter/vulnerable-app/src/app.js
npm ci --prefix lab/starter/vulnerable-app
npm test --prefix lab/starter/vulnerable-app

Explain how each repair protects its path: parameterized queries for SQL, output encoding for HTML, and resolved-path containment for file access. The three tests must pass. Then compare with lab/solution/secure-app/src/app.js.

docs.title: Part 3: Improve feedback speed
docs.text:
Review lab/starter/slow-pipeline/workflow.yml. Keep its checks and add lockfile caching, parallel lint and test jobs, shallow checkout, and a main-push deployment condition.

ruby -e 'require "yaml"; Psych.parse_stream(File.read(ARGV[0]))' \
  lab/starter/slow-pipeline/workflow.yml
grep -nE "cache: 'npm'|needs: \\[lint, test\\]|fetch-depth: 1|github.event_name" \
  lab/starter/slow-pipeline/workflow.yml

Then compare with lab/solution/optimized-pipeline/workflow.yml.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. Three fixed workflows.
  2. Three investigation records, two stages for Case 3.
  3. A reviewed security patch and syntax-check output.
  4. The optimized workflow review.

Write the root-cause statement after the observation and local check results. Keep the original logs with your records.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment 0:00 to 0:08 Observation, hypothesis, and check results 0:08 to 0:18 Local application baseline 0:18 to 0:34 Prepared pipeline investigation 0:34 to 0:44 Multi-stage failure 0:44 to 0:54 Security remediation review 0:54 to 1:00 Lab handoff

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
• Run the pipeline application tests, lint, and build.
  • Keep the solution directory closed.
  • Hold error-log-3-stage-2.txt until the first Case 3 repair.
  • Put the vulnerable and secure source side by side.

docs.title: Debugging sequence
docs.text:
Observation:
Local proof:
Hypothesis:
Smallest repair:
Proof after repair:

An observation quotes a file, command, or log. A hypothesis explains those facts. Don't let learners write the root cause before they've checked the files and logs.

docs.title: Prepared investigation
docs.text:
Start with Case 2, because the tempting dependency fix is wrong. Show the failed npm ci step and workflow. Run npm ci from the session root, then again with --prefix lab/starter/pipeline-app.

Pause for hypotheses. Reveal the reference fix once the room can explain why the project location matters.

docs.title: Multi-stage failure
docs.text:
For Case 3:

  1. Show error-log-3.txt.
  2. Record the first observation and local package metadata.
  3. Apply only the first repair.
  4. Say that the next run reached another stage.
  5. Reveal error-log-3-stage-2.txt and repeat the investigation.
  6. Compare with the solution after both checks pass.

The first failure can hide another. Update the diagnosis from the new log and keep each repair focused.

docs.title: Security review
docs.text:
Open one vulnerable route at a time. Ask learners to name the source, sink, and expected protection before you show the secure file.

Run the local syntax checks. A clean scan doesn't show the repair preserves behavior or covers the intended path.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text: Learners keep solutions closed until each checkpoint. Case 3 needs two investigation records in sequence. They submit the records and the fixed files.

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Reveal after the matching investigation:

  • Case 1 uses a runtime below the application's declared engine.
  • Case 2 runs npm from the wrong directory.
  • Case 3 first includes an unsupported runtime, then reaches a build job that runs outside the application directory.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Can Copilot name the cause first? Ask it to separate observations from hypotheses. Learners still need local command results before changing the workflow.

Why hold back the second log? The first failure stops the later stage from running. Showing both logs early gives away the sequence.

Accept a different repair if it explains the observed output, stays small, and passes the same checks.

docs.title: Session M5-01: Brady's Squad: Human-led AI teams
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Specification-Driven Frameworks

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04 and M3-02 to M3-05

Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content, 2 hours lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Use Brady's Squad to assign roles, route work, and keep a shared decision record. You carry one input-validation issue from assignment through tests and lead review.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Define a coordinator, specialized roles, and clear charters.
  • Design shared decision records and role-specific history.
  • Route independent work without overlapping ownership.
  • Use GitHub Issues as reviewable work contracts.
  • Decide when orchestration is worth its cost.

docs.title: You need
docs.text: Node.js 20 or later, Git, a GitHub training repository, GitHub Copilot, and Squad.

docs.title: Deliverable
docs.text: One review packet for the input-validation issue: assignment, implementation, test results, lead decision, and decision record. The reference solution includes a .squad/ result and a trainer walkthrough.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/ Lab lab/ Starter files lab/starter/ Reference solution lab/solution/

docs.title: Module 5: Specification-driven frameworks | Advanced
docs.text:
Session M5-01 | 3 hours | Optional

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04 and M3-02 to M3-05

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time Coordination trade-offs 7 min Roles, routing, and memory 20 min Issues and monitored work 8 min Prepared team demonstration 12 min Decision framework and lab handoff 13 min Lab 2 hours

docs.title: Coordination has a cost
docs.text:
Use a team when work has separate owners, clear interfaces, and a decision record to share. An individual agent is better for a small, well-understood change.

More agents create more state, review work, and cost.

docs.title: Parallelism only helps with real independence
docs.text:
Work can run in parallel when each stream has its own inputs, a clear output, and no hidden dependency on another stream's decision.

Work item Parallel? Reason Review separate test files Often Each reviewer can return findings Choose a shared domain model No Every implementation depends on the decision Update unrelated documentation Often Output boundaries are clear

Splitting an ambiguous task across agents spreads the ambiguity.

docs.title: The coordinator owns the integration risk
docs.text:
A coordinator needs to know:

  1. Which decision makes the workstreams compatible.
  2. Which files or systems only one role may change.
  3. Which results each role must return.
  4. When a conflict should stop the workflow rather than be merged automatically.

The coordinator stays human-led even when agents do the initial work.

docs.title: Return a result summary
docs.text:
Use:

Scope completed:
Evidence:
Files or records changed:
Checks run:
Open questions:
Recommendation:

The parent can compare these summaries without reading each agent's full conversation. Report missing results.

docs.title: Coordinator pattern
docs.text:
Issue with acceptance criteria
        ↓
Coordinator selects a bounded role
        ↓
Role writes a proposal or change
        ↓
Focused checks and human review
        ↓
Decision record, merge, follow-up, or pause

The coordinator assigns work with a defined scope. Clarify an ambiguous request before implementation.

docs.title: Team boundaries
docs.text:
Role Responsibility Lead Scope, decisions, review gate Implementer A defined product area or file set Tester Focused checks and reported gaps Scribe Shared decisions and history Work monitor Flag ready, approved work

Agents need charters that state inputs, outputs, and limits. Avoid concurrent writes to the same files.

docs.title: Shared memory
docs.text:
Commit decision records with the choice, supporting results, owner, and date. Keep temporary drafts separate.

Agents can write individual proposals. A designated owner reviews and merges the shared record. Git history keeps the trail.

docs.title: Issues and monitored work
docs.text:
An issue is a work contract. It needs acceptance criteria, non-goals, constraints, checks, and a reviewer.

Ready issue → assignment → bounded change → focused checks →
human review → merge or follow-up issue

Treat Ralph as a monitored queue. Stop when ownership, test status, or scope is unclear.

docs.title: When orchestration helps
docs.text: Situation Path One small repair Individual agent or manual work Separate work with defined interfaces Coordinated team Overlapping ownership or unclear design Plan before implementation No tool access Manual workflow

docs.title: One issue, one review trail
docs.text:
The worked issue adds validation to POST /api/users.

Issue contract
  → lead assignment
  → backend implementation
  → tester evidence
  → lead review
  → durable decision

Keep the same acceptance criteria through every step. A role may add test results but must not expand the issue.

docs.title: Reference .squad/ result
docs.text:
.squad/
├── team.md
├── routing.md
├── decisions.md
├── agents/{lead,backend,tester,scribe}/
├── decisions/inbox/issue-001-proposal.md
├── orchestration-log/issue-001.md
└── reviews/issue-001-review.md

The reference project also includes the implemented route and passing tests.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Copy the starter project and check Squad access.

Submit:

  • one issue assignment;
  • the input-validation implementation;
  • passing focused tests;
  • a lead review and decision record.

Use lab/solution/squad-project/ to check the expected result.

docs.title: Session M5-01 lab: Carry one issue through a Squad
docs.text:
Duration: 2 hours

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04 and M3-02 to M3-05

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Use synthetic data only. You need Node.js 20 or later, Git, authenticated gh, GitHub Copilot, Squad, and a training repository you can push to.

Exercise Work Time 1 Prepare the project and team 25 min 2 Assign Issue 001 20 min 3 Implement and test 45 min 4 Review, decide, and monitor 30 min

docs.title: Exercise 1: Prepare the project and team (25 min)
docs.text:
Copy lab/starter/squad-project/ into a training repository. Run the baseline:

npm install
npm test

The starter suite should pass. You will add Issue 001's validation cases later.

Check the installation:

squad --version

Read lab/starter/squad-init-guide.md, then initialize or inspect the team:

Initialize a Squad team for this Node.js Express API. Define role limits
for lead review, backend implementation, test results, and decision recording.
Keep one owner for the shared decision record.

Review .squad/team.md, .squad/routing.md, .squad/decisions.md, and every charter. The backend role may edit src/routes/api.js. The tester may edit tests/api.test.js. The lead reviews the result. The scribe is the only role that updates the shared decision record.

tree .squad/ -L 3
Check Expected result Team Lead, backend, tester, and scribe have charters and history files. Routing Implementation, test results, review, and decision updates have one owner each. Decisions The shared record names the scribe as its editor. Stop rule Overlapping ownership, failed tests, scope growth, or an unclear data boundary pauses work.

Checkpoint: Check the role boundaries against lab/starter/work-assignments.md before you assign Issue 001.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Assign Issue 001 (20 min)
docs.text:
Open Issue 001 in lab/starter/sample-issues.md. It is the only issue you implement in the required lab.

As the lead, assign it with this work order:

Assign Issue 001 to the backend role.

Implement validation for POST /api/users in src/routes/api.js.
Accept a non-empty string name up to 100 characters and a valid email shape.
Return status 400 with a descriptive error for invalid input.
Do not add dependencies, change the response envelope, or edit unrelated routes.
The tester owns focused evidence in tests/api.test.js.
The lead reviews the final packet.

Record the assignment in the live .squad/ log. It must include the issue, owner, permitted files, non-goals, tests, reviewer, and stop conditions.

Checkpoint: A partner compares the assignment with Issue 001. Fix any added scope before implementation starts.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Implement and test (45 min)
docs.text:
Have the backend role update src/routes/api.js. Keep validation inline and add no package.

Have the tester add focused cases to tests/api.test.js for:

  • a trimmed non-empty name;
  • an empty or non-string name;
  • a name longer than 100 characters;
  • a malformed email;
  • a valid request that still returns 201.

Run:

npm test

Record the command, result, and changed files. If a test fails, return the packet to the owning role. Do not weaken the issue or delete a failing case to get a green run.

Checkpoint: All focused and existing tests pass. Compare the result with lab/solution/squad-project/src/routes/api.js and lab/solution/squad-project/tests/api.test.js.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Review, decide, and monitor (30 min)
docs.text:
As the lead, check the implementation against every acceptance criterion. Record one outcome: approve, request changes, or pause.

The review packet must include:

  • issue and assignment;
  • changed files;
  • test command and result;
  • acceptance-criteria checks;
  • lead decision;
  • committed decision-record entry.

Use lab/starter/ralph-guide.md to simulate the monitor after review. The monitor may mark Issue 001 as ready to close only after the lead approves it. A human still closes or merges the work.

The items in lab/starter/backlog-items.md are optional discussion prompts. Do not implement them during the required lab.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
Submit one folder or pull request containing:

  1. the reviewed Squad team structure;
  2. the Issue 001 assignment;
  3. the code and test changes for Issue 001;
  4. passing npm test output;
  5. the lead review and recorded decision.

docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M5-01 trainer guide: Brady's Squad
docs.text:
00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide Enable timer shortcut (T)

Module: 5: Specification-Driven Frameworks

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04 and M3-02 to M3-05

Duration: 1 hour trainer content + 2 hours lab

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Squad is an optional open-source example: bradygaster/squad. Use it to teach coordination, role limits, shared decisions, and review. Learners decide whether a task needs an agent team and assign owners without conflicting changes.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text: Time Segment Outcome 0:00 to 0:07 Why coordinate agents Learners can name the cost and benefit of orchestration. 0:07 to 0:17 Roles and routing Learners can define a coordinator, agent limits, and a reviewer. 0:17 to 0:27 Shared memory Learners can separate committed decisions from temporary work. 0:27 to 0:35 Work monitoring and issues Learners can map an issue to assignment, review, and closure. 0:35 to 0:47 Prepared demo Initialize or inspect a small team and assign Issue 001. 0:47 to 0:55 Decision framework Learners choose one agent or a team. 0:55 to 1:00 Lab handoff Learners start the lab.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
• Install Node.js 20 or later, the Squad CLI, and sign in to GitHub.
  • Prepare a small repository with several independent issues. Label only the issues used in the demo.
  • Have an exported .squad/ example or recording ready in case the live run stalls.

docs.title: 1. Why coordinate agents (0:00 to 0:07)
docs.text:
Start with a task one agent can finish alone. Contrast it with work that needs several specialties and shared decisions beyond one conversation.

Coordination adds state, review work, and cost. Someone still owns scope and the final decision.

Individual agent Coordinated team One focused change Several independent work items Context stays in one conversation Decisions and assignments must be shared Human routes the work A coordinator routes the work Low overhead Extra review and state-management cost

A team for a typo or a one-file repair is slower and harder to review.

docs.title: 2. Roles and routing (0:07 to 0:17)
docs.text:
The coordinator receives a request, picks the role, and gathers the result. It should not turn an ambiguous request into a broad implementation.

Role Owns Lead Scope, technical decisions, and review gate Frontend or backend implementer A defined part of the product Tester Test plan, focused checks, and reported gaps Scribe or decision owner Committed decisions and change history Work monitor Triage of ready work

A charter states a role's responsibilities, inputs, outputs, and boundaries. Assign file ownership or dependency order before running tasks in parallel. Two agents editing the same route or dependency manifest cause conflicts.

Use an issue as the work contract: acceptance criteria, non-goals, constraints, required tests, and a reviewer. The coordinator then picks a single agent, fans out read-only research, or defers the work.

docs.title: 3. Saved team decisions (0:17 to 0:27)
docs.text:
A committed decision log holds the chosen architecture, the rejected option, the owner, supporting results, and the date. Personal history can record role-specific lessons. Inboxes, drafts, and task output stay out.

To avoid conflicting writes:

  1. Each agent writes its proposal to its own file.
  2. The lead or scribe reviews the proposals.
  3. One owner updates the shared decision record.

Git history is the audit trail.

docs.title: 4. Ralph, issues, and review (0:27 to 0:35)
docs.text:
Ralph is a work monitor. It inspects ready issues, picks work that meets its rules, and presents the result for review. A human approves delivery.

Issue with acceptance criteria → assignment → bounded change →
focused checks → human review → merge or follow-up issue

Stop when ownership is unclear, a test fails, an unexpected dependency appears, or the task grows beyond its issue.

docs.title: 5. Prepared demonstration (0:35 to 0:47)
docs.text:
Use Issue 001, Add input validation to POST /api/users, from lab/starter/sample-issues.md. Keep it on screen.

  1. 0:35 to 0:37: Read the contract. Point to the acceptance criteria, non-goals, permitted files, required tests, and reviewer.
  2. 0:37 to 0:39: Show the team. Open the reference .squad/team.md, .squad/routing.md, and the backend charter. The backend role owns the implementation. The tester returns test results without editing source.
  3. 0:39 to 0:41: Assign the issue. Open .squad/decisions/inbox/issue-001-proposal.md and .squad/orchestration-log/issue-001.md. The assignment must keep the issue limits.
  4. 0:41 to 0:44: Inspect implementation and tests. Compare the starter and solution versions of src/routes/api.js and tests/api.test.js. Run npm test from the solution.
  5. 0:44 to 0:46: Review the result. Open .squad/reviews/issue-001-review.md. Check each acceptance criterion against code and test results.
  6. 0:46 to 0:47: Record the decision. Open .squad/decisions.md.

Work order for the live run:

Assign the approved input-validation issue to one role.
Do not edit files outside the issue, add dependencies, or start parallel implementation.
Record the proposal, focused-check evidence, and a lead review decision.
Stop if ownership or the data boundary is unclear.

If the live run has not produced the assignment by 0:41, switch to the reference .squad/ example. If implementation or tests are still blocked at 0:44, switch to the tabletop packet.

docs.title: 6. When a team helps (0:47 to 0:55)
docs.text:
Situation Recommended path One small, well-understood change Individual agent or manual work Separate frontend, backend, and test work with defined interfaces Coordinated team Ambiguous architecture or overlapping file ownership Plan first; do not fan out implementation No tool access Manual workflow with prepared artifacts Repeated operational work with stable acceptance checks A monitored team may help

Judge the team by the changes it completes and reviews, not its agent count.

docs.title: Lab handoff (0:55 to 1:00)
docs.text:
Point learners to lab/README.md.

  1. Learners run the starter tests.
  2. They check Squad access.
  3. They carry Issue 001 through assignment, implementation, tests, and review.
  4. They compare their packet with lab/solution/squad-project/.

The deliverable: one reviewed issue with a matching committed decision record.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Does Squad replace GitHub Copilot? No. It coordinates Copilot-powered agents.

How do we control cost? Limit active tasks, require acceptance criteria, and stop at a set threshold.

What happens when two agents disagree? The decision owner resolves it from test results and review findings. Don't merge competing changes by accident.
