docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M5-02: Spec Kit: Specification-driven development
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Specification-Driven Frameworks

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04, M3-01 to M3-05

Duration: 3 hours 30 minutes (1 hour trainer content, 2 hours 30 minutes lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Use Spec Kit to turn one feature request into tested code. You initialize an existing Python project, create the Spec Kit artifacts, implement an archive operation, and run convergence review. A later restore requirement prompts you to update the living specification and repeat the workflow.

The lab uses Spec Kit's real project model:

  • .specify/memory/constitution.md stores project principles.
  • specs/<feature>/spec.md stores requirements and user stories.
  • plan.md, supporting design files, and tasks.md drive implementation.
  • /speckit-analyze checks artifact consistency.
  • /speckit-converge compares the implementation with the accepted artifacts.
  • /speckit-taskstoissues converts the generated task list into GitHub Issues.

Spec Kit generates its Copilot skills during specify init.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Initialize Spec Kit in an existing repository and inspect the generated files.
  • Write testable requirements before choosing an implementation.
  • Turn the accepted specification into a plan and dependency-ordered tasks.
  • Convert generated tasks into GitHub Issues.
  • Implement the change in stages and use convergence to find missing work.
  • Evolve a living specification and update the plan, tasks, and code to match.
  • Explain which files come from Spec Kit and which records belong to the team.

docs.title: You need
docs.text: A GitHub training repository where you can create issues, Python 3.10 or later, Git, uv, and GitHub Copilot. For disconnected environments, prepare the official air-gapped package before the session.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
export SPECKIT_TAG='<release-tag>'
uv tool install specify-cli --force \
  --from "git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git@${SPECKIT_TAG}"
specify version

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/ Slides slides.md Lab lab/ Starter project lab/starter/archive-task/ Reference result lab/solution/archive-task/

docs.title: Make the work clear before asking an agent to build it
docs.text: Session M5-02 | 3 hours 30 minutes

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time Why specification-driven development 8 min Spec Kit project and artifact model 10 min Requirements and clarification 12 min Planning, checklists, tasks, and analysis 12 min Implementation and convergence 10 min Installation, demonstration, and lab handoff 8 min

docs.title: A feature request is a starting point
docs.text:
Users need to remove completed tasks from their normal working list without deleting task history.

This sounds clear until implementation starts:

  • Does "remove" mean hide, archive, or delete?
  • What happens when the same task is archived twice?
  • Can callers still retrieve archived tasks?
  • What result should an unknown task ID produce?

Code should not be where these decisions first appear.

docs.title: Resolve decisions before implementation
docs.text: Code-first path Specification-driven path The agent fills gaps while coding The team resolves gaps before planning Tests inherit hidden assumptions Acceptance scenarios state expected behavior Scope additions appear as code Non-goals make additions visible Review starts with implementation details Review starts with requirements and test results

docs.title: What Spec Kit provides
docs.text:
Layer Purpose CLI scaffolding Initializes templates, scripts, memory, and an agent integration Agent skills Guide constitution, specification, planning, implementation, and review Feature artifacts Keep requirements, design decisions, tasks, and checks reviewable

The tool supplies a workflow. The team still owns each product and technical decision.

docs.title: Initialize an existing project
docs.text:
specify init --here --force --integration copilot

Review the generated diff before using the workflow:

.specify/
├── memory/constitution.md
├── scripts/
└── templates/

.github/skills/
└── speckit-*/

--force allows initialization in a non-empty directory. It is not permission to accept every generated change without review.

docs.title: Two artifact scopes
docs.text:
Project-wide Feature-specific .specify/memory/constitution.md specs/<feature>/spec.md Shared scripts and templates plan.md and design files Agent integration files checklists/ and tasks.md

The constitution applies across features. Each feature gets its own specification, design, tasks, and review trail.

docs.title: The full workflow
docs.text:
Constitution
    ↓
Specify → Clarify
    ↓
Plan → Checklist → Tasks
    ↓
Analyze
    ↓
Implement ⇄ Converge

Clarify, checklist, and analyze are review gates. Use them when ambiguity or risk justifies the review.

docs.title: Constitution: rules for how the project works
docs.text:
/speckit-constitution

A useful principle is testable:

Weak principle Reviewable principle Write high-quality code Every accepted behavior has a focused automated test Keep things simple Use the Python standard library unless the plan records an approved exception Avoid regressions Existing create and list tests must remain in the suite

If a principle cannot affect a plan or review, delete it.

docs.title: Specify behavior, not implementation
docs.text:
/speckit-specify

spec.md should answer:

  • Who needs the behavior?
  • What outcome do they need?
  • Which scenarios test the behavior?
  • What is outside scope?
  • Which requirements are measurable?

Avoid class names, database choices, package names, and file paths at this stage.

docs.title: Write scenarios a reviewer can challenge
docs.text:
Given an active task
When the caller archives its ID
Then the task keeps its ID and title
And the default list no longer returns it

Given an unknown task ID
When the caller archives it
Then the store returns a clear not-found result

Good scenarios expose decisions. "Archive works correctly" does not.

docs.title: Clarify before choosing a design
docs.text:
/speckit-clarify

For the archive feature, clarification must settle:

Question Accepted decision Archive twice? Return the same archived task Unknown ID? Raise TaskNotFoundError Default list? Exclude archived tasks Historical access? Support include_archived=True Title during archive? Preserve it unchanged

Record clarification decisions in the specification so future readers have one place to check the agreed behavior.

docs.title: Plan: decide how the feature will work
docs.text:
/speckit-plan

The plan can now choose implementation details:

  • Python 3.10 or later;
  • standard library only;
  • in-memory dictionary storage;
  • an archived Boolean on each task;
  • changes limited to src/task_store.py and its tests.

The specification owns behavior. The plan owns the technical approach.

docs.title: Supporting design files have a purpose
docs.text:
Artifact Question it answers research.md Which choices were made, and which alternatives were rejected? data-model.md Which entities, fields, rules, and state transitions exist? contracts/ Which external interfaces must consumers follow? quickstart.md How can a reviewer check the planned behavior?

Not every feature needs every optional artifact. Keep the files that help someone implement or review the change.

docs.title: A checklist reviews requirement quality
docs.text:
/speckit-checklist

A requirements checklist asks questions such as:

  • Is repeated archive behavior defined?
  • Is the default list behavior defined?
  • Does the specification define an unknown-ID result?
  • Are existing behaviors protected?

Checking an item means a reviewer found the requirement clear. It does not mean the code has been implemented or tested.

docs.title: Tasks turn design into executable work
docs.text:
/speckit-tasks

Each task needs a place in the dependency order, a source requirement, and an exact file:

T001 [US1] Add archive state to new tasks in src/task_store.py
T002 [US1] Implement archive_task(task_id) in src/task_store.py
T003 [US1] Test default list filtering in tests/test_task_store.py
T004 [US2] Test repeated archive requests in tests/test_task_store.py

"Implement the feature" is not a task breakdown.

docs.title: Analyze artifacts before implementation
docs.text:
/speckit-analyze

Analysis looks across spec.md, plan.md, and tasks.md for:

  • a requirement with no implementation task;
  • a task with no source requirement;
  • a plan choice that contradicts accepted behavior;
  • ambiguous or inconsistent terminology;
  • missing coverage for a user story.

The command is read-only. Fix each issue in the artifact that owns the decision, then analyze again.

docs.title: Implementation follows the accepted tasks
docs.text:
/speckit-implement

Before implementation:

  1. Review and approve the requirements checklist.
  2. Resolve material analysis findings.
  3. Commit the accepted artifacts.
  4. Check the implementation scope.

During implementation, connect tests and source code to the accepted user stories and requirements. The original prompt alone is not enough.

docs.title: Compare implementation with accepted artifacts
docs.text:
/speckit-converge

Implementation
      ↓
Compare code, tests, spec, plan, and tasks
      ↓
Converged ───────────────→ Review or pull request
      ↓ gaps found
Append tasks → Implement → Test → Converge again

Convergence does not rewrite requirements to match the code. It identifies the work needed to make the implementation and accepted artifacts agree.

docs.title: specify check is not compliance validation
docs.text:
specify check

Use it to inspect the local Spec Kit environment and available tools.

It does not check whether the implementation meets the specification. Use tests, review, /speckit-analyze, and /speckit-converge to compare the accepted artifacts and implementation.

docs.title: Living specifications evolve accepted behavior
docs.text:
When requirements change, update the current feature artifacts in order:

spec.md
  ↓
plan.md
  ↓
tasks.md
  ↓
/speckit-analyze
  ↓
/speckit-implement
  ↓
/speckit-converge

Do not leave a restore requirement only in code or an issue if spec.md remains the contract.

docs.title: Convert tasks into GitHub Issues
docs.text:
/speckit-taskstoissues

The generated issues should preserve:

  • task IDs and user-story references;
  • dependencies and parallel markers;
  • exact file paths and expected work;
  • the boundaries already accepted in spec.md.

Issues distribute the work. They are not a second requirements source.

docs.title: Install Spec Kit
docs.text:
Install from a pinned release:

export SPECKIT_TAG='<release-tag>'
uv tool install specify-cli --force \
  --from "git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git@${SPECKIT_TAG}"
specify version

Disconnected environments need the official air-gapped package prepared on a connected machine.

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
Show one deliberate gap:

  1. Implement archive filtering.
  2. Omit the include_archived=True test.
  3. Run the existing unit tests.
  4. Run /speckit-converge.
  5. Inspect the task it appends.
  6. Add the missing test and converge again.

This shows that passing tests and satisfying the specification are different.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
You will:

  1. Run the starter tests.
  2. Initialize Spec Kit in the Python project.
  3. Specify and clarify task archiving.
  4. Create the plan, checklist, and tasks.
  5. Analyze before implementation.
  6. Convert tasks into GitHub Issues.
  7. Implement in stages and run the unit tests.
  8. Converge until the artifacts and code agree.
  9. Evolve the living specification to add restore behavior.

The lab ends with evolved artifacts, working code, passing tests, GitHub Issues, and a final convergence result.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M5-02 lab: Implement and evolve a feature with Spec Kit
docs.text:
Duration: 2 hours 30 minutes

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04, M3-01 to M3-05

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Add task archiving to a small Python project. You implement it in stages and use convergence review to find missing work. Then you add a restore requirement through the living-spec workflow, updating the artifacts and implementation together.

Part Work Time 1 Prepare and initialize the project 15 min 2 Specify and clarify archive behavior 25 min 3 Plan, check, create tasks, and analyze 25 min 4 Convert tasks to GitHub Issues 15 min 5 Implement in stages and run tests 25 min 6 Converge the archive implementation 15 min 7 Evolve the living specification 30 min

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text: You need Python 3.10 or later, Git, GitHub Copilot, uv, and a GitHub training repository where you can create issues. For a disconnected environment, the instructor prepares the official Spec Kit air-gapped package beforehand.

docs.title: Part 1: Prepare and initialize the project (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Copy the starter into the instructor-provided GitHub training repository:

cp -R sessions/session-m5-02-spec-kit/lab/starter/archive-task/. <training-repository>/
cd <training-repository>
git add .
git commit -m "Start Spec Kit archive-task lab"
python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

The two starter tests should pass. Read feature-request.md, but do not open change-request.md yet.

Install the Spec Kit release the instructor gave you:

export SPECKIT_TAG='<release-tag>'
uv tool install specify-cli --force \
  --from "git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git@${SPECKIT_TAG}"
specify version

Initialize the current repository:

specify init --here --force --integration copilot

Review the generated files:

git status --short
find .specify -maxdepth 3 -type f | sort
find .github -maxdepth 3 -type f | sort

Checkpoint: .specify/memory/constitution.md, templates, scripts, and Copilot integration files exist.

docs.title: Part 2: Specify and clarify archive behavior (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Create the project constitution:

/speckit-constitution

Create principles for this training project:
- preserve existing create and list behavior;
- use only the Python standard library;
- require tests for every accepted behavior;
- keep requirements separate from implementation choices.

Open .specify/memory/constitution.md. Check that you can use each principle to judge a plan, implementation, or review.

Create the feature specification:

/speckit-specify

Use feature-request.md as the source. Add task archiving without changing create
or list behavior. Keep the specification technology-neutral.

Inspect specs/<feature>/spec.md. Check that it contains prioritized, independently testable user stories and measurable acceptance scenarios.

Clarify the missing decisions:

/speckit-clarify

Focus on repeated archive requests, unknown task IDs, whether archived tasks stay
in the default list, and whether task titles may change during archive.

The specification should settle these decisions:

  • archiving an active task succeeds;
  • archiving an already archived task is idempotent;
  • an unknown task ID produces a clear not-found result;
  • the default list excludes archived tasks;
  • callers can request archived tasks explicitly;
  • archiving does not change the title.

Checkpoint: spec.md defines behavior without choosing classes, file names, or storage structures.

docs.title: Part 3: Plan, check, create tasks, and analyze (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Create the implementation plan:

/speckit-plan

Use Python 3.10+ and the standard library. Extend src/task_store.py and
tests/test_task_store.py. Keep storage in memory. Do not add packages.

Review plan.md, research.md, data-model.md, and quickstart.md. Remove any dependency, service, or infrastructure that the accepted feature does not need.

Generate and review a requirements-quality checklist:

/speckit-checklist

Check archive state transitions, list filtering, not-found behavior, and
regression protection for existing create and list behavior.

Mark an item complete only when its requirement is clear in spec.md. A checked requirements item does not mean the implementation exists.

Create tasks and analyze the artifacts:

/speckit-tasks
/speckit-analyze

Fix each material finding in the artifact that owns the decision. Run /speckit-analyze again until the specification, plan, and tasks agree.

Checkpoint: each implementation task names an exact file and traces to an accepted user story.

docs.title: Part 4: Convert tasks to GitHub Issues (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Commit and push the accepted artifacts:

git add .specify .github specs
git commit -m "Specify task archive behavior"
git push

Convert the generated task list into GitHub Issues:

/speckit-taskstoissues

Create issues from the unchecked tasks in tasks.md. Preserve task IDs, user-story
references, dependencies, and file paths.

Open the created issues and check:

  • each issue maps to a task ID;
  • dependency order remains visible;
  • parallel tasks are distinguishable;
  • the issue does not add requirements absent from spec.md.

docs.title: Part 5: Implement in stages and run tests (25 minutes)
docs.text:
Use Spec Kit to implement one set of tasks at a time. Do not implement everything in one agent run.

First implement the primary archive behavior:

/speckit-implement

Implement only the tasks for the primary archive user story. Stop before repeated
archive and unknown-ID behavior.

Run the tests:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

Then implement the remaining archive tasks:

/speckit-implement

Implement the remaining archive tasks, including repeated requests, unknown IDs,
and final verification.

Run the full suite again. Existing create and list tests must still pass.

docs.title: Part 6: Converge the archive implementation (15 minutes)
docs.text:
Run convergence review:

/speckit-converge

If convergence appends a new phase to tasks.md:

  1. inspect each appended task and its source reference;
  2. run /speckit-implement for the appended convergence tasks;
  3. rerun the unit tests;
  4. run /speckit-converge again.

Repeat until Spec Kit reports Converged. When it finds no remaining work, it leaves tasks.md unchanged.

docs.title: Part 7: Evolve the living specification (30 minutes)
docs.text:
Open change-request.md. Add restoring archived tasks to the accepted behavior.

Use the documented living-spec sequence:

  1. Update the specification:
/speckit-clarify

Update the current feature for change-request.md. Define restore success,
repeated restore, unknown IDs, and default-list behavior after restore.
  1. Update the technical plan:
/speckit-plan

Revise the current plan for restore behavior. Keep the existing Python,
standard-library, in-memory design.
  1. Regenerate the task list and analyze it:
/speckit-tasks
/speckit-analyze
  1. Convert only the new unchecked restore tasks into issues:
/speckit-taskstoissues

Create issues only for new restore tasks that do not already have an issue.
Preserve their task IDs and dependencies.
  1. Implement, test, and converge:
/speckit-implement
/speckit-converge

The final suite should check that:

  • archive and restore preserve the task ID and title;
  • repeated archive and restore requests are idempotent;
  • unknown IDs produce TaskNotFoundError;
  • restored tasks return to the default list;
  • existing behavior remains intact.

If convergence appends work, repeat the implement and converge loop.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
1. A project constitution and an evolved feature specification.
  2. Plans, supporting design files, reviewed checklists, and dependency-ordered tasks for archive and restore behavior.
  3. GitHub Issues created from the Spec Kit task list.
  4. Working archive and restore behavior with passing tests.
  5. A final Converged result.

docs.title: Trainer Guide
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M5-02 trainer guide: Spec Kit
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Show the complete Spec Kit loop on one small change: request, specification, plan, tasks, implementation, tests, and convergence. Learners should know which files Spec Kit creates and which decisions the team still owns. The lab then adds restore behavior through the living-spec workflow.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text:
Time Segment 0:00 to 0:08 Why specification-driven development 0:08 to 0:18 Spec Kit project and artifact model 0:18 to 0:30 Requirements and clarification 0:30 to 0:42 Planning, checklists, tasks, and analysis 0:42 to 0:52 Implementation and convergence 0:52 to 1:00 Installation, demonstration, and lab handoff

The timings match the agenda in slides.md. Keep the first five segments moving so the demonstration and lab handoff get the last eight minutes.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
• Pick the Spec Kit release tag and install it.
  • Prepare an initialized copy of the archive-task starter. Run its tests first so learners see the baseline.
  • Check that the training repository allows issue creation.

docs.title: 0:00 to 0:08: Why specification-driven development
docs.text:
Slides: Spec Kit: Specification-Driven Development, Agenda, A feature request is a starting point, and Resolve decisions before implementation

  1. Read the archive request aloud. Ask learners how many decisions hide inside the word "remove." Use the four questions on the slide. Don't answer them yet.
  2. Compare the two paths. Specification-driven development moves decisions earlier. It doesn't add documents for their own sake.

docs.title: 0:08 to 0:18: Spec Kit project and artifact model
docs.text:
Slides: What Spec Kit provides, Initialize an existing project, Two artifact scopes, and The full workflow

  1. Separate the three layers. The CLI creates the project structure, the generated skills guide the workflow, and the feature artifacts hold the work.
  2. Show initialization as a reviewed change. Explain --here, --force, and --integration copilot, then show the generated diff. --force allows initialization in a non-empty directory. It doesn't accept every generated file.
  3. Distinguish scopes. The constitution applies to the project. The specification, plan, design files, checklists, and tasks belong to one feature.
  4. Walk through the workflow once. Clarification, checklist review, and analysis are optional gates for ambiguity or risk.

Check: Learners can say where project principles live and where feature behavior lives.

docs.title: 0:18 to 0:30: Requirements and clarification
docs.text:
Slides: Constitution: rules for how the project works, Specify behavior, not implementation, Write scenarios a reviewer can challenge, and Clarify before choosing a design

  1. Make constitution principles testable. A useful principle changes planning, implementation, or review.
  2. Keep spec.md technology-neutral. It defines the user, outcome, scenarios, non-goals, and measurable requirements. Class names, storage, packages, and paths belong later.
  3. Use scenarios to test decisions. Walk through the active-task and unknown-ID examples. Each Given/When/Then statement lets a reviewer challenge one behavior.
  4. Resolve the archive questions. Reveal the accepted decisions after learners see the ambiguity. Clarification updates spec.md.

docs.title: 0:30 to 0:42: Planning, checklists, tasks, and analysis
docs.text:
Slides: Plan: decide how the feature will work, Supporting design files have a purpose, A checklist reviews requirement quality, Tasks turn design into executable work, and Analyze artifacts before implementation

  1. Move technical choices into the plan. Python version, storage, fields, and file paths belong in plan.md, not spec.md.
  2. Explain each supporting file by the question it answers. Not every feature needs every optional artifact.
  3. Separate requirement review from implementation status. A checked checklist item means the requirement is clear. It doesn't mean the code exists.
  4. Read the sample tasks as a dependency sequence. Point out the task ID, user-story reference, action, and exact file. "Implement the feature" is too broad to assign.
  5. Explain analysis as a read-only check. Fix a finding in the artifact that owns the decision, then analyze again. Don't edit code to hide a spec contradiction.

Check: Ask which artifact owns an ambiguous behavior, a storage choice, and a missing implementation step. Answers: spec.md, plan.md, tasks.md.

docs.title: 0:42 to 0:52: Implementation and convergence
docs.text:
Slides: Implementation follows the accepted tasks, Compare implementation with accepted artifacts, specify check is not compliance validation, Living specifications evolve accepted behavior, and Convert tasks into GitHub Issues

  1. Set the implementation gate. The checklist is reviewed, material analysis findings are resolved, and accepted artifacts are committed.
  2. Explain convergence. It compares implementation, tests, specification, plan, and tasks. When it finds a gap, it adds work. It doesn't rewrite accepted requirements to match the code.
  3. Correct the specify check misconception. It checks the local Spec Kit environment, not implementation compliance, security, performance, or coverage.
  4. Show how accepted behavior changes. Restore behavior starts in spec.md. Analysis, implementation, and convergence then bring plan, tasks, code, and tests back in line.
  5. Show task-to-issue conversion. GitHub Issues keep the accepted task IDs, dependencies, parallel markers, file paths, and scope. They are not a second requirements source.

docs.title: 0:52 to 1:00: Installation, demonstration, and lab handoff
docs.text:
Slides: Install Spec Kit, Prepared demonstration, and Lab handoff

  1. Install from a pinned release. A disconnected environment needs the official air-gapped package prepared beforehand.
  2. Run the convergence demo. Prepare an implementation that hides archived tasks by default but has no test for include_archived=True. Run the existing tests, then /speckit-converge. Inspect the appended task, add the missing test, rerun the suite, and converge again.
  3. Hand off. Learners initialize the project, define archive behavior, plan, create issues, implement in stages, converge, then add restore behavior. Reveal change-request.md to show how restore flows through the workflow.

Final message: Passing tests and satisfying the accepted specification are different things.

docs.title: Generated files and commands
docs.text:
After specify init, show the generated files before running any agent command:

.specify/
  memory/constitution.md
  scripts/
  templates/
.github/
  skills/speckit-*/

Copilot skill names generated by the current integration:

/speckit-constitution
/speckit-specify
/speckit-clarify
/speckit-plan
/speckit-checklist
/speckit-tasks
/speckit-analyze
/speckit-implement
/speckit-converge
/speckit-taskstoissues

Another integration may use different invocation syntax. Teach the workflow and let the generated files define the syntax.

docs.title: Common questions
docs.text:
Why not ask an agent to build it immediately? A specification exposes missing decisions while they are cheap to change.

Can the tool define the process? No. The team owns the process and reviews its outputs.

docs.title: Session M5-03: HVE Core: Evidence-led delivery with RPI
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Specification-Driven Frameworks

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04 and M3-04, or equivalent Copilot and custom-agent experience

Duration: 4 hours (1 hour trainer content, 3 hours lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Use Hypervelocity Engineering (HVE), a structured engineering framework for GitHub Copilot, to take a feature from research to reviewed code. You start with its file-based Research, Plan, Implement, Review (RPI) workflow. Then you add repository instructions, targeted coding standards, and a custom review agent.

Product Manager Advisor tests the value and scope of an Engineering Decision API feature. Agile Coach turns the result into an outcome-oriented story with acceptance criteria. You feed those artifacts back into the HVE plan before implementation and review.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Explain HVE's agents, prompts, instructions, and file-as-interface model.
  • Run direct HVE Research, Plan, Implement, and Review phases and inspect each .copilot-tracking/ handoff.
  • Compare direct RPI phase prompts with the combined /rpi orchestrator and its Follow-up phase.
  • Add project context, targeted JavaScript/API standards, and a custom agent with a defined scope.
  • Use Product Manager Advisor and Agile Coach to refine value, scope, user story, and acceptance criteria.
  • Deliver and review one containerized API slice through the customized HVE workflow.

docs.title: HVE Core requirement
docs.text: The hands-on challenge requires HVE Core (the extension or Copilot CLI plugin). Without it, learners can inspect trainer-provided artifacts but can't complete the challenge. Keep .copilot-tracking/ local and ignored by Git. The challenge handoff lists the four phase artifacts, the final decision, unresolved risks, and the next action.

docs.title: HVE references
docs.text:
HVE commands and generated artifacts change between versions.

  • HVE Core repository and framework overview
  • Install HVE Core
  • RPI workflow overview
  • RPI commands
  • Why RPI works

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/ Slides slides.md Lab lab/ Starter brief and project lab/starter/ Trainer reference solution lab/solution/ HVE artifact reference lab/solution/hve-artifacts.md

docs.title: HVE Core challenge
docs.text: From product intent to reviewed code

docs.title: What HVE is
docs.text:
Hypervelocity Engineering is a structured engineering framework for GitHub Copilot.

It gives agent work defined roles, standards, human review gates, and saved phase artifacts.

docs.title: Four component types
docs.text: Component Job Agents Own roles and multi-step protocols Prompts Start repeatable workflows Instructions Apply standards by file pattern Tracking artifacts Carry state between phases

docs.title: HVE uses files as interfaces
docs.text:
Research artifact
  → Plan + critique
  → Changes log
  → Review findings and decision

Reviewers can inspect and diff each handoff, then resume work from it.

docs.title: Research before code
docs.text:
Research answers:

  • Which files own the behavior?
  • What constraints already exist?
  • Which alternatives were rejected?
  • What check could disprove the approach?

Output: .copilot-tracking/research/

docs.title: Plan before implementation
docs.text:
Plan maps criteria to files, checks, dependencies, and human gates.

Output:

.copilot-tracking/plans/

docs.title: Implement and Review
docs.text:
Implement follows the approved plan and writes a changes log.

Review checks whether the result meets the request, code quality standards, tests, and instructions.

The human still decides: approve, request changes, or pause.

docs.title: Direct and combined RPI
docs.text:
Mode Entry points Use it when Direct prompts /rpi-research, /rpi-plan, /rpi-implement, /rpi-review Learning, demos, explicit approvals Combined /rpi task="..." The team understands and trusts the handoffs

Combined RPI uses Follow-up after Review to route defects or missing evidence.

docs.title: HVE customization is additive
docs.text:
.github/copilot-instructions.md
.github/instructions/*.instructions.md
.github/agents/*.agent.md

Project context reaches all agents. Coding practices activate by applyTo glob. Custom agents add repository-owned roles and output contracts.

docs.title: Show that instructions were used
docs.text:
Creating an instruction file doesn't show that HVE used it.

Show:

  1. a matching path;
  2. the rule that activated;
  3. the plan, code, or review decision it changed.

docs.title: HVE starts before engineering
docs.text:
Business idea
  → BRD Builder / Product Manager Advisor / PRD Builder
  → Agile Coach
  → RPI
  → reviewed code

Product agents test value and assumptions. Agile Coach turns intent into an outcome-oriented story and acceptance criteria.

docs.title: Challenge sequence
docs.text:
1. Run direct Research and Plan prompts.
  2. Add repository context, coding practices, and a custom reviewer.
  3. Use Product Manager Advisor and Agile Coach.
  4. Update the plan, then run Implement and Review.
  5. Compare the result with combined /rpi.

docs.title: Build the endpoint
docs.text:
Deliver POST /api/decisions within the supplied product intent and API contract.

Scope control is part of the score.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
Input Rule title Required non-empty string; duplicate check ignores case context Required non-empty string decision Required non-empty string status proposed, accepted, or superseded

Generate an ID and UTC timestamp. Keep state in memory.

Package tested source in a non-root runtime image with production dependencies and a health check.

docs.title: Fast checks that find weak work
docs.text:
1. Send a required field as whitespace or a number.
  2. Create the same trimmed title with different case.
  3. Send malformed JSON.
  4. Inspect the exact error envelope.
  5. Check which stage supplies source to the runtime image.

These checks test invalid inputs and container build boundaries.

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
Area Weight Grade from HVE RPI artifact chain 40% Four HVE phase artifacts HVE customization and activation 25% Repository files and cited activation Product and Agile agent handoff 20% Platform output cited by Plan Feature and container validation 15% Output cited by Implement or Review

A manual implementation does not complete an HVE challenge.

docs.title: Keep the handoff short
docs.text:
challenge-handoff.md contains only:

  • links or paths to the four HVE artifacts;
  • the final human decision;
  • unresolved risks and the next action.

Do not copy phase narratives, criteria, command output, or proposed Git text into the handoff.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M5-03 lab: HVE from product intent to reviewed code
docs.text:
Duration: 3 hours

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: HVE Core installed; Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04 and M3-04 or equivalent experience

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Use HVE Core to take one Engineering Decision API feature through direct RPI phases, repository customization, product and Agile refinement, implementation, and review. The handoff is an index of the HVE artifacts and the final decision.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need Node.js 20 or later, GitHub Copilot, and the HVE Core extension or Copilot CLI plugin. Use synthetic decision records.

  1. Check that /rpi-research, /rpi-plan, /rpi-implement, /rpi-review, /rpi, @Product Manager Advisor, and @Agile Coach are available.
  2. Check that .copilot-tracking/ is ignored by Git.
  3. Run npm test (run npm ci first if dependencies are missing).
  4. Read starter/product-intent.md, starter/challenge-brief.md, and the artifact index in starter/challenge-handoff.md.
  5. Reserve the last 20 to 30 minutes for Review, your decision, and the handoff.

The baseline is one passing health test and no POST /api/decisions. If one HVE invocation fails, use starter/hve-phase-recovery.md and continue with the next HVE agent.

docs.title: Pacing
docs.text:
Agent latency varies. Move on when you have the artifacts listed for the stage.

Stage Range Required results HVE preflight and artifact model 10 to 15 min Required agents are visible; tracking paths are understood Research and Plan 30 to 40 min Research, plan, critique, and human approval exist HVE customization 20 to 25 min The artifacts show how each of the three customization layers affected the work Product and Agile refinement 20 to 25 min Advisor decision, story, criteria, and exclusions exist Implement and validate 35 to 45 min Changes log, code, test results, and container results exist Review and combined-RPI comparison 20 to 30 min Review artifact, human decision, and comparison are recorded

docs.title: Exercise 1: Understand HVE and run Research
docs.text:
Before changing code, identify HVE's four component types:

  • agents define roles and multi-step protocols;
  • prompts provide slash-command entry points;
  • instructions apply standards by file pattern;
  • .copilot-tracking/ files save state between phases.

Run:

/rpi-research "Add POST /api/decisions to the starter API using the supplied product intent and feature contract"

Open the research artifact under .copilot-tracking/research/. Check that it records the scope, a rejected alternative, a constraint, and the next phase.

Clear the chat, attach the research artifact, then run /rpi-plan. Inspect the plan and critique. Approve the plan only when every acceptance criterion maps to an owning file and a focused check.

docs.title: Exercise 2: Customize HVE for the repository
docs.text:
Create three repository-owned customization layers:

  1. .github/copilot-instructions.md with the service context, architecture, data boundary, and dependency rule.
  2. .github/instructions/javascript-api.instructions.md with description and applyTo frontmatter for src/**/*.js and tests/**/*.test.js. Require stable envelopes, app-instance state, and HTTP-level tests.
  3. .github/agents/decision-api-reviewer.agent.md with a narrow review mission, read/search tools only, and a response format that maps findings to criteria.

Record an activation check for each layer. Then ask HVE to review the current plan again and note one concrete change caused by the repository context, coding instruction, or custom agent. Creating a file alone doesn't show HVE used it.

docs.title: Exercise 3: Explore HVE product and Agile agents
docs.text:
Give starter/product-intent.md to @Product Manager Advisor. Ask it to test the feature's value, users, assumptions, priority, and non-goals. Keep its output in the platform record and cite it from the Plan artifact.

Give the advisor output and challenge brief to @Agile Coach. Ask it to produce one outcome-oriented user story, acceptance criteria, and named exclusions. Compare those criteria with the HVE plan. Update the plan when the product or Agile artifact exposes a gap, and record that effect in the Plan artifact. Do not copy the agent outputs into the handoff. Do not create live work items in this lab.

Use the agent picker to locate @BRD Builder and @PRD Builder. Record when the team would start with each agent instead of the supplied product intent.

docs.title: Exercise 4: Implement and review with HVE
docs.text:
Attach the approved plan and product/Agile artifact, then run /rpi-implement. The finished behavior must:

  • require non-empty string values for title, context, and decision;
  • accept proposed, accepted, or superseded as status;
  • default status to proposed;
  • reject a stored title after trimmed, case-insensitive comparison;
  • generate a unique string ID and UTC createdAt value;
  • return stable success and error envelopes;
  • keep the health route test passing;
  • run tests in a container build stage;
  • ship only production dependencies and tested source in the runtime stage;
  • run as a non-root user with a health check for GET /health.

Inspect .copilot-tracking/changes/, then run /rpi-review. Review every criterion as pass, fail, deferred, or not run. Check that errors reveal no stack traces, app instances do not share records, and the runtime image excludes development dependencies and root execution.

If the platform produces commit or pull-request text, leave it in the platform output. Don't commit, push, merge, or create a remote pull request.

Finally, explain how /rpi task="..." would orchestrate the same phases and use Follow-up to route defects or missing evidence back to the responsible phase. Don't start another implementation cycle.

docs.title: Scenario-to-task map
docs.text:
HVE capability Required task What to show Direct RPI phases Run Research, Plan, Implement, and Review in order Tracking artifact from each phase Combined RPI Explain /rpi orchestration and Follow-up Direct-to-combined comparison Repository context Add .github/copilot-instructions.md Later phase cites a project rule Coding practice Add a targeted API instruction Matching source or test file follows the rule Agent customization Add a review agent with a defined scope Agent output uses the required criterion map Product planning Use Product Manager Advisor Value, assumptions, priority, and human question Agile refinement Use Agile Coach User story, acceptance criteria, and exclusions

Stretch work starts after the review decision.

docs.title: Final deliverable
docs.text:
Submit or demonstrate:

  • Research, Plan, Implement, and Review artifacts from HVE
  • challenge-handoff.md with links or paths to those four artifacts, the final human decision, unresolved risks, and the next action
  • Repository context, a targeted JavaScript/API instruction, and a custom reviewer agent
  • Product Manager Advisor and Agile Coach outputs
  • The implemented endpoint, focused tests, and production container definition
  • Exact test and container results in the HVE artifacts or platform output

docs.title: Scoring
docs.text:
Area Points Grade from HVE RPI artifacts 40 Research, Plan, Implement, and Review artifacts HVE customization 25 Repository files plus examples of their use in the HVE artifacts Product and Agile agents 20 Platform outputs cited by the Plan artifact Feature validation 15 Test and container output cited by Implement or Review

A trainer-provided recovery artifact can unblock one failed phase, but that phase earns no execution points. A manual submission doesn't pass this challenge.

docs.title: Session M5-03 trainer guide: HVE from product intent to reviewed code
docs.text: 00:00 Start timer Reset timer Print guide      Enable timer shortcut (T)

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Use the API challenge to teach how HVE works. Learners move from product intent to reviewed code using HVE agents, prompts, instructions, and saved tracking artifacts.

docs.title: Pacing
docs.text:
Model response time and questions change the pace. Shorten demonstrations before you cut artifact review.

Segment Range What learners should show What HVE is and why it exists 5 to 10 min They can distinguish agents, prompts, instructions, and tracking artifacts Direct RPI phases and their handoffs 15 to 20 min Each phase has an owner, artifact, and gate Combined /rpi, Follow-up, and checkpoints 5 to 10 min They can choose direct prompts or combined mode Additive instructions and custom agents 8 to 12 min They can explain how an instruction or custom agent changed the work Product and Agile agent flow 8 to 12 min They can place Advisor, Coach, BRD, and PRD before RPI Challenge gates and scoring 4 to 6 min They know what completion requires

If an agent response is slow, switch to the reference artifact and keep talking.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
• Install Node.js 20 or later and the HVE Core extension or Copilot CLI plugin. Open Copilot Chat and check the RPI prompts and agents appear.
  • A clean copy of the starter.
  • Reference RPI artifacts and product and Agile outputs.
  • Captured test output and container-build result.
  • One trainer-provided artifact per RPI phase, in case an invocation fails.

Generic agent mode doesn't replace an HVE phase. Without HVE, run an instructor walkthrough. Learners can inspect the artifacts but can't complete the challenge.

docs.title: Teach HVE first
docs.text:
HVE is a structured engineering framework for GitHub Copilot. Learners must distinguish four parts:

  • agents own roles and protocols;
  • prompts provide repeatable workflow entry points;
  • instructions apply standards when file patterns match;
  • .copilot-tracking/ stores local handoff files between phases and stays ignored by Git.

Open the file Research writes for Plan. Show how a person inspects it, reviews a diff, attaches it to the next phase, and approves it.

docs.title: Demonstrate direct RPI phases
docs.text:
Use the starter product intent and run the first two phases live:

/rpi-research "Add POST /api/decisions using the supplied product intent and feature contract"
/rpi-plan

Pause on the artifacts, not the chat narration.

Phase Question Output Research What do we know, what limits apply, and what is uncertain? Research findings and alternatives Plan What will change, in what order, and which checks will catch mistakes? Plan and critique Implement Did the changes follow the approved plan? Code, tests, and changes log Review Does the result satisfy the request and quality bar? Findings, criterion verdicts, decision

Then show the combined form without running a second feature:

/rpi task="<bounded task>"

Combined RPI orchestrates the same phases and uses Follow-up to route new defects or missing evidence back to the responsible phase. Use direct phase prompts to learn and approve phase by phase. Use combined mode once the team trusts the workflow.

docs.title: Demonstrate customization
docs.text:
Show these files in the reference project:

.github/copilot-instructions.md
.github/instructions/javascript-api.instructions.md
.github/agents/decision-api-reviewer.agent.md

HVE is additive. Repository context reaches every agent. Targeted instructions activate only for matching files. A custom agent adds a role with its own mission, tools, protocol, and output contract.

Ask learners which path matched and what changed in Research, Plan, code, or Review. Creating an instruction file doesn't show it activated.

docs.title: Demonstrate the product-to-engineering handoff
docs.text:
Business idea
  → @BRD Builder or supplied product intent
  → @Product Manager Advisor
  → @PRD Builder when a full product specification is needed
  → @Agile Coach
  → approved HVE plan
  → Implement and Review

Learners start with supplied intent, use Product Manager Advisor to test value and assumptions, then use Agile Coach to produce one story and acceptance criteria. They update the HVE plan when those outputs expose a gap. The Plan artifact cites the outputs. Learners don't copy them into the handoff. No live backlog writes.

docs.title: Reference demonstration
docs.text: Show one valid create request, a duplicate whose title uses different case, and a malformed JSON response. Then show the test and runtime stages in the Dockerfile. Keep the RPI artifact chain open beside the code so learners can trace the implementation back to product and Agile decisions.

docs.title: Coaching prompts
docs.text:
• Which file controls the behavior you need to change?
  • Which HVE phase owns that decision?
  • What check could disprove your plan fastest?
  • Which acceptance criterion lacks test results?
  • Does the image build test the exact source copied into the runtime stage?
  • Did an instruction change the review, or did you only create the file?
  • Did Product Manager Advisor or Agile Coach change the plan?
  • What would make you pause rather than approve?

docs.title: Grading
docs.text:
Use the 100-point rubric in lab/solution/reference-evidence.md. Grade Research, Plan, Implement, and Review at their generated paths. Grade the handoff for its artifact index and final human decision, not for duplicated phase records.

The learner ends with a decision: approve, request changes, or pause. Missing artifacts lower the score even when the endpoint works. A trainer-provided recovery artifact keeps the lab moving but earns no execution credit for that phase.

docs.title: Session M6-01: Build reliable agent applications with the GitHub Copilot SDK
docs.text:
Open slides Slides in new tab Download PDF Close slides

Module: Module 6: Advanced Topics & Capstone

Difficulty: Advanced

Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04, M3-01 to M3-05

Duration: 3 hours (1 hour trainer content, 2 hour lab)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Build a TypeScript CLI around an agent to assess whether a synthetic software change is ready to proceed.

You write the reliability controls in application code. The CLI manages the client and session lifecycle, streams progress, and limits tool use. It also shows denied actions, records failures, and closes resources. Tests check that control path. An OpenTelemetry Collector sends traces to Jaeger so you can inspect the same run outside the terminal.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• manage CopilotClient and session startup, use, and shutdown;
  • subscribe to streaming session events without printing duplicate final output;
  • define a typed custom tool over deterministic synthetic data;
  • separate tool availability, permission handling, and pre-tool policy;
  • use pre-tool, failed-tool, error, and session-end hooks;
  • make a denied action visible to the user and trace;
  • test the allowed, denied, failed, and cleanup paths;
  • send SDK traces through an OpenTelemetry Collector to Jaeger.

docs.title: Required access
docs.text: Learners need authenticated GitHub Copilot SDK access, Node.js and npm, Docker with Docker Compose, and a terminal.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
The application is a change readiness assistant. It reads deterministic synthetic change records, asks Copilot to assess the selected change, and returns ready or needs-review with the supporting gaps.

One request targets a restricted synthetic record. The application denies that lookup before execution and shows the reason.

docs.title: Session structure
docs.text: Block Duration Content Trainer content 60 min Slides, concepts, and prepared demo Lab 120 min Build and check the CLI

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab guide lab/README.md Starter project lab/starter/sdk-readiness-assistant/ Reference solution lab/solution/sdk-readiness-assistant/

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
The lab covers:

  • local CopilotClient and session lifecycle;
  • TypeScript streaming event handlers;
  • one application-owned readiness tool;
  • recorded permission decisions;
  • pre-tool, post-tool-failure, error, and session-end hooks;
  • a visible denied action;
  • focused automated tests;
  • OTLP export through an OpenTelemetry Collector;
  • trace inspection in Jaeger.

The session doesn't cover dynamic workflows, fleet, cloud or remote sessions, BYOK, plugin packaging, production deployment, external business systems, or other languages.

docs.title: Build reliable agent applications with the GitHub Copilot SDK
docs.text:
Own the lifecycle, policy, run records, and failure path

Session M6-01 | Module 6 | Advanced

docs.title: Agenda
docs.text: Segment Time The application reliability boundary 8 min Client, session, and streaming lifecycle 12 min Tools, permissions, and hooks 17 min Tests and traces 10 min Prepared demo and lab handoff 13 min

docs.title: The application owns the control path
docs.text:
The SDK provides an agent session. Your application still owns:

  • startup and shutdown;
  • the data boundary;
  • which tools exist;
  • which calls may run;
  • what the user sees when work fails;
  • the records kept after the session ends.

A useful answer with an unsafe control path is still a broken application.

docs.title: The scenario is deliberately small
docs.text:
Synthetic change record
        ↓
TypeScript CLI
        ↓
Copilot session
        ↓
Change request lookup tool
        ↓
ready or needs-review

The data is fixed. You build the controls around the model.

docs.title: Manage startup and cleanup
docs.text:
import { CopilotClient } from "@github/copilot-sdk";

const client = new CopilotClient({
  telemetry: { otlpEndpoint: "http://localhost:4318" },
});

await client.start();
let session;

try {
  session = await client.createSession(config);
  await session.sendAndWait({ prompt });
} finally {
  await session?.disconnect();
  await client.stop();
}

Cleanup belongs in finally.

docs.title: One client can own several sessions
docs.text:
Object Owns Close when CopilotClient Runtime connection and client options The application exits Session Conversation state, tools, hooks, and events The task is complete Event subscription UI updates from that session The session is no longer observed Collector connection Trace export path The local trace stack stops

Keep session state scoped by session ID. Remove it in the session-end path.

docs.title: Streaming improves feedback and creates edge cases
docs.text:
session.on("assistant.message_delta", (event) => {
  if (!event.agentId) {
    process.stdout.write(event.data.deltaContent);
  }
});

session.on("session.idle", () => {
  process.stdout.write("\n");
});

The final assistant.message still arrives. Decide whether the CLI renders deltas, the final message, or both in different places. Printing both produces duplicates.

docs.title: Events do not decide readiness
docs.text:
Session events can show:

  • text deltas;
  • tool requests and results;
  • permission requests;
  • session state changes;
  • usage records.

The readiness verdict must still come from the application's deterministic data and rules. Do not infer readiness from a fluent answer.

docs.title: A custom tool limits what the agent can do
docs.text:
import { defineTool } from "@github/copilot-sdk";

const lookupTool = defineTool("lookup_change_request", {
  description: "Read one synthetic change and calculate readiness gaps",
  parameters: {
    type: "object",
    properties: { requestId: { type: "string" } },
    required: ["requestId"],
    additionalProperties: false,
  },
  handler: async (args) => lookupChangeRequest(changes, args),
});

The schema narrows the input. The handler still validates the request ID before it reads the fixture.

docs.title: Tool availability and permission answer different questions
docs.text:
Control Question Registered tools Can the model choose this capability? onPermissionRequest May this requested execution proceed? onPreToolUse Does application policy allow these exact arguments now? Tool handler Are the input and data valid at execution time?

Use all four where the risk justifies them. One broad approval does not replace argument-level policy.

docs.title: Deny the action before the handler runs
docs.text:
hooks: {
  onPreToolUse: async (input) => {
    if (
      input.toolName === "lookup_change_request" &&
      input.toolArgs?.requestId?.startsWith("RESTRICTED-")
    ) {
      return {
        permissionDecision: "deny",
        permissionDecisionReason:
          "Restricted change requests cannot be read by this assistant.",
      };
    }

    return { permissionDecision: "allow" };
  },
}

The denial reason should appear in the CLI and trace. Silent denial is hard to debug and easy to misread.

docs.title: Keep permission handling narrow
docs.text:
onPermissionRequest: async (request) => {
  if ("managedApprovalRequired" in request &&
      request.managedApprovalRequired === true) {
    return { kind: "no-result" };
  }

  if ("toolName" in request &&
      request.toolName === "lookup_change_request") {
    return { kind: "approve-once" };
  }

  return {
    kind: "reject",
    feedback: "Only the synthetic readiness tool is allowed.",
  };
},

Deny unknown request kinds. Review new capabilities before approving them so they do not inherit permission by accident.

docs.title: Hooks record and control the lifecycle
docs.text:
Session starts
  → request streams
  → tool call reaches pre-tool policy
  → permission decision
  → handler succeeds or fails
  → failure or error hook records the outcome
  → session ends and state is cleared

Hooks run inline. Keep them fast and deterministic.

docs.title: Failure and error are different paths
docs.text:
Path Example Application response Denied call Restricted synthetic ID violates policy Show the reason, record denial Application result Malformed or missing synthetic ID Return a fixed result without invention Tool execution failure Handler throws or returns a failed execution Record the failed tool event SDK error Runtime or model call fails Notify the user, retry only when safe Session end Complete, abort, timeout, or error Flush state and record reason

Do not turn every failure into a retry. Some failures are policy decisions.

docs.title: Use the failed-tool hook for agent guidance
docs.text:
onPostToolUseFailure: async (input) => {
  audit.failedTools.push({
    toolName: input.toolName,
    result: input.toolResult,
  });

  return {
    additionalContext:
      "Do not invent a change record. Report the failed tool result.",
  };
},

This hook sees tool results marked as failures. It does not replace onErrorOccurred.

docs.title: Use the error hook for SDK recovery policy
docs.text:
onErrorOccurred: async (input) => {
  audit.errors.push(input.error);

  return {
    errorHandling: input.recoverable ? "retry" : "abort",
    retryCount: input.recoverable ? 1 : 0,
    userNotification: "The readiness session could not continue.",
  };
},

Retry once only when the error says recovery is possible. Keep the original error in the audit record.

docs.title: End every session with a record
docs.text:
onSessionEnd: async (input, invocation) => {
  audit.endReason = input.reason;
  audit.endedAt = new Date().toISOString();
  sessionState.delete(invocation.sessionId);

  return {
    sessionSummary: `Readiness session ended: ${input.reason}`,
  };
},

Cleanup should be safe to run more than once. A process crash may skip the hook, so the outer finally block still matters.

docs.title: Test the control path, not model phrasing
docs.text:
Test Stable assertion CR-1042 Tool returns ready with no gaps CR-2087 Tool returns needs-review with fixed gaps Restricted ID Pre-tool hook returns deny with the required reason Failed tool event Failed-tool hook records the failure SDK error Error hook chooses the expected recovery action Session completion End hook clears state and records the reason Streaming Deltas render once and final output is not duplicated

Mock the SDK boundary. Keep synthetic data fixed.

docs.title: Trace the same run outside the terminal
docs.text:
CLI process
   │ OTLP/HTTP :4318
   ▼
OpenTelemetry Collector
   │ OTLP
   ▼
Jaeger :16686

const client = new CopilotClient({
  telemetry: {
    otlpEndpoint: "http://localhost:4318",
  },
});

The trace should show session work, tool activity, the denied action, and the end reason for one run.

docs.title: Inspect the run in Jaeger
docs.text:
Use Jaeger to check:

  • which span contained the tool request;
  • whether the denied action reached the handler;
  • how long the model and tool steps took;
  • where a failed run stopped;
  • whether one CLI invocation produced one connected trace.

Trace data can contain prompts and tool details. Keep this lab synthetic.

docs.title: Reliability has tradeoffs
docs.text:
Choice Benefit Cost Stream deltas Faster visible feedback More rendering state Deny by default Smaller execution boundary More permission code Hooks for audit One lifecycle view Inline latency if hooks do too much Deterministic tool data Stable tests and demos Less realism Local tracing stack Traces you can inspect Docker setup and local resource use

Choose controls that show what failed and why.

docs.title: Prepared demonstration
docs.text:
1. Run the passing tests.
  2. Start the Collector and Jaeger.
  3. Assess a known synthetic change.
  4. Watch the response stream.
  5. Request the restricted synthetic record.
  6. Show the denial in the terminal.
  7. Open the same run in Jaeger.
  8. Trigger an unknown ID and show the failure path.

docs.title: Lab handoff
docs.text:
Build the CLI in lab/starter/sdk-readiness-assistant/.

You will complete the lifecycle, streaming, readiness tool, permissions, hooks, tests, and OTLP export. Then you will run the known, denied, and failed paths and inspect the trace in Jaeger.

docs.title: Lab
docs.text: Overview Lab Trainer Guide

docs.title: Session M6-01 lab: Build a traced change readiness assistant
docs.text: Duration: 120 minutes Difficulty: Advanced Prerequisites: Sessions M1-01 to M1-03, M2-01 to M2-04, M3-01 to M3-05 and the Session M6-01 trainer content

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Complete a TypeScript CLI that uses the GitHub Copilot SDK to assess deterministic synthetic change records. Your application must stream its response and call one tool limited to readiness lookups. It must also deny a restricted lookup, record failures, pass focused tests, and export traces through an OpenTelemetry Collector to Jaeger.

docs.title: Final deliverables
docs.text:
Submit or demonstrate:

  1. a working CLI under sdk-readiness-assistant/;
  2. client and session cleanup on every exit path;
  3. streamed parent-agent output without duplicate final text;
  4. the typed readiness tool over the supplied synthetic data;
  5. permission handling plus a pre-tool policy that visibly denies RESTRICTED-0001;
  6. failed-tool, error, and session-end hook records;
  7. passing tests and type checks;
  8. one Jaeger trace for a permitted assessment;
  9. one Jaeger trace or trace event showing the denied action;
  10. terminal output for the unknown-change failure path.

docs.title: Time plan
docs.text: Part Work Time 1 Setup and baseline 15 min 2 Client, session, and streaming 20 min 3 Readiness tool and policy 30 min 4 Failure hooks and cleanup 20 min 5 Tests 15 min 6 Collector, Jaeger, and final checks 20 min

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Work from:

sessions/session-m6-01-copilot-sdk/lab/starter/sdk-readiness-assistant/

You need authenticated GitHub Copilot SDK access, Node.js and npm at the versions in package.json, Docker with Docker Compose, and free local ports for the Compose file. Use Copilot authentication, not BYOK or another provider.

Run the local checks:

node --version
npm --version
docker version
docker compose version
npm ci
npm run check
npm test

Some focused tests should fail until you complete the reliability controls. The project must compile far enough to show those gaps. Run the authentication check in src/live-demo.ts before the live exercises.

docs.title: Project map
docs.text:
The expected layout:

sdk-readiness-assistant/
├── package.json
├── compose.yaml
├── otel-collector-config.yaml
├── fixtures/
│   └── change-requests.json
├── src/
│   ├── live-demo.ts
│   ├── change-store.ts
│   ├── permission-policy.ts
│   ├── hook-decisions.ts
│   └── types.ts
└── tests/
    ├── change-store.test.ts
    ├── permission-policy.test.ts
    └── hook-decisions.test.ts

Do not add external data sources or new runtime dependencies.

docs.title: Part 1: Establish lifecycle and streaming (20 minutes)
Goal
docs.text: Start the client, create one local session, stream parent-agent output, and close the client on every exit path.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the application entry point and lifecycle module.
  2. Create CopilotClient with the supplied telemetry endpoint.
  3. Start the client before creating the session.
  4. Create one session with streaming enabled.
  5. Subscribe to assistant.message_delta.
  6. Print only parent-agent deltas.
  7. Keep final message events for audit or tests. Do not print the same response again.
  8. Put client shutdown in finally.
  9. Keep per-session state keyed by the session ID.

Use this lifecycle shape:

const client = new CopilotClient(clientOptions);
await client.start();
let session;

try {
  session = await client.createSession(sessionConfig);
  subscribeToOutput(session);
  await session.sendAndWait({ prompt });
} finally {
  await session?.disconnect();
  await client.stop();
}

Run:

npm run check
npm test

docs.title: Checkpoint 1
docs.text:
• The client starts before session creation.
  • The session disconnects after success and thrown errors.
  • The client stops after success and thrown errors.
  • Parent text streams once.
  • Per-session state is not global shared state.

docs.title: Part 2: Complete the readiness tool and policy (30 minutes)
Goal
docs.text: Expose deterministic readiness data through one typed tool. Permit normal lookups and deny the restricted synthetic record before the handler runs.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Open the supplied change records in fixtures/change-requests.json.
  2. Do not edit the record IDs or expected verdicts.
  3. Complete the lookup_change_request tool with its supplied JSON Schema.
  4. Validate the change ID inside the handler.
  5. Return the matching evidence, gaps, and verdict.
  6. Return the fixed invalid-input or not-found result for bad IDs.
  7. Add onPermissionRequest.
  8. Approve only the supplied readiness tool request.
  9. Reject unknown request kinds and unrelated tools.
  10. Add onPreToolUse.

  11. Deny IDs beginning with RESTRICTED- with this reason:

    Restricted change requests cannot be read by this assistant.

  12. Record whether the handler ran. The denial test must check that it did not.

Do not use an approve-all helper. You need to show that unrelated requests are rejected while the readiness lookup is permitted.

Run the focused tool and policy tests:

npm test

docs.title: Checkpoint 2
docs.text:
Demonstrate:

  • CR-1042 returns ready with no gaps;
  • CR-2087 returns needs-review with fixed gaps;
  • malformed or unknown IDs return fixed results without invention;
  • a normal lookup is permitted;
  • RESTRICTED-0001 is denied with a visible reason;
  • the denied request never enters the tool handler.

docs.title: Part 3: Add failure, error, and end hooks (20 minutes)
Goal
docs.text: Record the expected failure paths and clear session state at the end.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Complete onPostToolUseFailure.
  2. Record the tool name and failed result.
  3. Add context that tells the agent to report unknown data instead of inventing a change record.
  4. Complete onErrorOccurred.
  5. Store the original error.
  6. Retry once only when the SDK marks the error recoverable.
  7. Abort unrecoverable errors and show a short user notification.
  8. Complete onSessionEnd.
  9. Record the end reason and timestamp.
  10. Delete state for the ended session.
  11. Keep cleanup safe if called more than once.

Do not treat a denied tool call as an SDK error. It is a policy result.

Run:

npm test
npm run check

docs.title: Checkpoint 3
docs.text:
The audit record distinguishes:

  • policy denial;
  • failed tool result;
  • recoverable or unrecoverable SDK error;
  • normal or abnormal session end.

Session state is empty after the end hook.

docs.title: Part 4: Finish the automated tests (15 minutes)
Goal
docs.text:
Test the control path without depending on model wording or a live trace backend.

Complete or repair tests for:

  • a known ready change;
  • a known blocked change;
  • malformed and unknown change IDs;
  • denied RESTRICTED-0001 lookup;
  • handler non-execution after denial;
  • one retry for a recoverable error;
  • abort for an unrecoverable error;
  • session state cleanup;
  • streamed deltas rendered once;
  • client shutdown after an exception.

Mock the SDK at the boundaries the starter provides. Do not call a live model from unit tests.

Run:

npm test
npm run check

If package.json defines linting, run:

npm run lint

docs.title: Checkpoint 4
docs.text: All tests pass twice without data or snapshot changes.

docs.title: Part 5: Start tracing and run the application (20 minutes)
Goal
docs.text: Export one connected trace through the local Collector and inspect it in Jaeger.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. Review compose.yaml and otel-collector-config.yaml.
  2. Check the SDK OTLP HTTP endpoint is:
http://localhost:4318
  1. Start the local stack:
docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d
docker compose -f compose.yaml ps
  1. Wait until the Collector and Jaeger services are healthy.
  2. Run npm run demo.
  3. Check that CR-1042 streams a ready assessment.
  4. Check that bad-id returns the fixed invalid-input result.
  5. Check that RESTRICTED-0001 prints the denial reason.
  6. Check that the session disconnects and the client stops.
  7. Open the Jaeger UI at http://localhost:16686.
  8. Select the service name configured by the project.
  9. Find the three most recent runs.
  10. Open the denied run and check that no lookup handler work follows the policy denial.
  11. Locate the permitted and invalid-input paths.

Stop the local stack when the trainer tells you to:

docker compose -f compose.yaml down

docs.title: Checkpoint 5
docs.text:
Show the trainer:

  • the permitted terminal run;
  • the visible denied action;
  • the invalid-input result;
  • one connected Jaeger trace;
  • the session end reason;
  • passing tests and type checks.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Problem Fix client.getAuthStatus() reports unauthenticated Check the GitHub Copilot sign-in and network path. CopilotClient starts but session creation fails Check the package lock, the Node.js version, and your GitHub Copilot access. Output is duplicated Print assistant.message_delta as live output and keep the final message for records only. Restricted data reaches the handler Match the exact tool name and inspect parsed toolArgs.requestId in onPreToolUse. Unknown IDs produce an invented answer Return a failed tool result and add failure-hook context that forbids invention. Tests call the live model Mock the SDK session boundary and assert deterministic events or decisions. Collector cannot bind port 4318 Stop the conflicting process, or change the local configuration consistently. Jaeger is empty Check container health, the Collector export pipeline, service name, and Jaeger time range. Session state remains after completion Delete the session ID in onSessionEnd and keep outer cleanup in finally.

docs.title: Solution reference
docs.text:
After all checkpoints, compare your work with sessions/session-m6-01-copilot-sdk/lab/solution/sdk-readiness-assistant/:

  1. src/live-demo.ts: client, session, streaming, and hooks;
  2. src/change-store.ts: the deterministic lookup;
  3. src/permission-policy.ts: permission decisions;
  4. src/hook-decisions.ts: prompt and pre-tool policy;
  5. tests/: control-path assertions;
  6. compose.yaml and otel-collector-config.yaml: trace routing.

Duration: 60 minutes Format: Concept teaching, prepared live demo, lab briefing

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: Show where the model's work ends and application code takes over. The model produces an assessment. TypeScript code manages the lifecycle, limits tools, makes permission decisions, handles failures, and records traces.

docs.title: One-hour plan
docs.text:
Time Segment What learners should show 0:00 to 0:08 Application reliability boundary They can name what the application owns 0:08 to 0:20 Client, session, and streaming They can draw the startup and cleanup path 0:20 to 0:37 Tool, permissions, and hooks They can explain where a call is denied 0:37 to 0:47 Tests and traces They can name a stable assertion for each path 0:47 to 0:57 Prepared live demo The denied action is visible in the CLI and Jaeger 0:57 to 1:00 Lab transition Every learner has the tools installed

Use slides.md for the teaching sequence.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
1. Install Node.js and npm at the versions the project declares.
  2. Check that Docker Compose starts the supplied local stack.
  3. Sign in to GitHub Copilot with the account learners will use.
  4. In the reference solution, run npm ci, the tests, and the type check.
  5. Start the OpenTelemetry Collector and Jaeger.
  6. Run one successful assessment and find its trace in Jaeger.
  7. Run the denied action and check the reason appears in the terminal and the trace.
  8. Keep the solution project open at the demo files.

docs.title: The application owns the boundary
docs.text:
Open with the synthetic change record. Ask which parts need model reasoning and which should stay deterministic.

The readiness tool returns fixed lookup results. The model can explain them, but it can't create a record or change the policy. That separation makes the lab testable.

  • register only lookup_change_request;
  • inspect exact tool arguments before execution;
  • deny unrecognized permission requests;
  • show policy denial to the user;
  • clean up even when the session fails.

docs.title: Client and session lifecycle
docs.text:
construct client → start client → create session → subscribe →
send request → await completion → close session state → stop client

The session-end hook records what the agent runtime reports. The outer finally block handles process-level cleanup. You need both.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text:
Show assistant.message_delta and the final assistant.message as separate event types. A CLI that prints both as primary output repeats the response.

The application streams parent-agent text deltas and uses complete events for records and tests. It ignores sub-agent output.

docs.title: Tool and permission layers
docs.text:
Registration, permission requests, pre-tool policy, and handler validation are separate controls. Use the table from the slides.

The lookup tool accepts one synthetic request ID. Normal CR-#### values reach the handler. IDs beginning with RESTRICTED- test the denial path. The pre-tool hook blocks them before the handler runs.

docs.title: Failure and error hooks
docs.text:
• malformed input returns a fixed validation result;
  • a failed tool execution enters onPostToolUseFailure;
  • a runtime or model error enters onErrorOccurred.

A policy denial is not an error. The application did what it was designed to do.

docs.title: Tests and traces
docs.text:
The tests assert control decisions and deterministic results, not the model's prose.

Jaeger shows the timing and sequence of a run: whether the restricted call reached the handler and where a failed run stopped. Trace payloads can expose prompts and tool arguments, so the lab uses synthetic data.

docs.title: Demo: trace a denied change request
docs.text:
Level: L300 Time: 10 minutes

Show the denied lookup for RESTRICTED-0001 in the terminal. Then open Jaeger and point to the same blocked tool call in the connected trace.

  1. Show the starting state. Open lab/solution/sdk-readiness-assistant/. Point to fixtures/change-requests.json, src/live-demo.ts, src/permission-policy.ts, src/hook-decisions.ts, the tests, and the telemetry configuration.

"The model doesn't own this data or policy. TypeScript decides which capability exists and whether the exact call may run."

  1. Run the baseline.
npm test
npm run check

"I want the control path green before I involve a live model. These tests cover known data, denial, failure handling, streaming, and cleanup. They don't compare natural-language answers."

  1. Start the trace stack.
docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d
docker compose -f compose.yaml ps

The SDK exports OTLP data to the Collector on port 4318. The Collector forwards traces to Jaeger.

  1. Run a permitted assessment. Run npm run demo. The first request assesses CR-1042. Let the response stream. The renderer doesn't print the final event a second time.

  2. Watch the restricted lookup. The third prepared prompt requests RESTRICTED-0001. The tool is known, so the request reaches policy. The pre-tool hook checks the request ID and denies it before the handler runs.

  3. Point to the visible denial. Read the denial reason from the terminal and show the audit entry.

  4. Open Jaeger. Select the service name from the project and find the latest trace. It shows the session work and the blocked tool call, with no handler span after the denial.

  5. Show invalid input and the failed-tool policy. Point to the bad-id run, then the failed-tool hook test and the session-end hook test. Invalid input returns a fixed validation result. A failed tool execution uses its own hook.

  6. Close the demo. Stop the application. Leave the trace stack running for the lab if the machine is shared.

docs.title: Demo troubleshooting
docs.text:
Problem Response SDK authentication fails Stop. Check the GitHub Copilot sign-in and network path. No streamed text appears Check the session enables streaming and the handler listens for parent assistant.message_delta events. Restricted data reaches the handler Stop. Check the exact tool name and parsed requestId in onPreToolUse, then rerun the denial test. Collector is unreachable Check Docker Compose health and the OTLP HTTP endpoint http://localhost:4318. Jaeger shows no trace Check the Collector exports to Jaeger, select the configured service name, and widen the time range. Output appears twice Check whether both message deltas and the final assistant message are printed as primary output.

Point learners to lab/README.md. They add the same controls to the starter project one layer at a time and run the focused checks at each checkpoint.

Tool and denial Do the test results show the handler did not run? Failure hooks Is unknown data reported without invention or broad retry? Tests Are assertions stable without matching model prose? Traces Can the learner connect terminal output to one Jaeger trace?

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Implement and review one Bookmark API slice: POST /api/bookmarks. The accepted GitHub issue limits what you change, and the Session M5-02 specification standards apply. You finish with test results and a handoff another engineer can use.

The capstone stays small on purpose. Authentication, persistent storage, deployment, and every other bookmark endpoint are out of scope. Use synthetic data and the existing dependencies.

docs.title: Learning outcomes
docs.text:
• Keep scope decisions in the accepted GitHub issue.
  • Check a prepared specification for testable behavior and named non-goals.
  • Turn the accepted specification into one implementation-ready issue.
  • Check the Bookmark creation slice with executable tests.
  • Record a review decision, deferred scope, and the next action.

docs.title: Materials
docs.text: Resource Location Trainer guide trainer-content/README.md Slides slides.md Lab lab/README.md Starter files lab/starter/ Reference solution lab/solution/
